ISE’s 2025 employer surveys put the average graduate salary at £33,000 (up 2%), with 140 applications per graduate vacancy; graduate vacancies fell 8% while apprentice vacancies rose 8%.

Financial and related professional services account for over 2.4 million jobs in Great Britain, two thirds of them outside London, and the UK was the world’s largest net exporter of financial services in 2024 (£92.6 billion).

The UK hires graduates through structured schemes that open almost a year ahead: an online application, tests, a video interview and an assessment day, often in person. Large employers fill a share of these places from their own summer interns first.
Applying is open to anyone, but the timetable, not the CV, is where most Europeans lose.
Graduate schemes

Applications open from July to October and close when full, in order of arrival, for jobs that start the next September. Employers received 140 applications per graduate vacancy in 2025, a record, and ISE members cut graduate hiring by 8% in a year.
This is the ranked first route because it is where the volume is: the 100 leading graduate employers still plan graduate intakes of their own,. The Big Four alone took about 5,400 in 2024.
Summer internship to return offer

A ten-to-twelve-week internship in the penultimate summer is the main door to banks, consultancies and law firms; a good intern leaves with an offer for the following year. Competition is fierce: 101 applications per internship vacancy and 123 per undergraduate placement in 2025.

A High Fliers survey for 2016 hiring reported that recruiters expected a third of that year’s graduate positions to go to graduates who had already worked for them, and 77% of employers in the 2025 ISE survey say former interns are more work-ready. Year-long placements and first-year insight weeks feed the same schemes, but they are for undergraduates; a one-year master’s student has usually missed them.
Civil Service Fast Stream and public-sector schemes

The Fast Stream is a competition, not an exam: for the 2026 intake 69,046 first-preference applications led to 703 people recommended for appointment, a 1.0% success rate against 654 vacancies. Stages run from online tests and a recorded video interview to an online assessment centre and, on most schemes, a final selection board.

Nationals of the UK, the Republic of Ireland, the Commonwealth and the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Liechtenstein and Turkey can apply if they can live and work in the UK, but some security and intelligence posts need British citizenship.
Degree and school-leaver apprenticeships

81% of ISE employers recruited apprentices in 2025, and employers hired 1.8 graduates for every apprentice, down from 2.3 a year earlier. 77% of apprenticeships went to school and college leavers and 16% to graduates, so this route is mainly for people who skip or interleave university, and apprenticeships at KPMG are not sponsored.
Smaller firms and direct applications

Start-ups, small firms and research groups often fill roles through direct approaches: not all internships and graduate roles are advertised, and many large companies do not accept speculative applications. Imperial’s careers service advises a named contact, a short personal email and a follow-up after 7 to 10 days.
Start-ups and small firms hire all year, often through networks and speculative approaches to a named person.
Experienced hire: advertised roles and lateral moves

With two to three years in a bank, lateral moves one tier at a time (boutique to middle market to bulge bracket) are the practitioner route in London, and openings come unpredictably so networking has to be continuous. This rests on one publisher’s accounts, not on counts.
Direct entry roles are advertised all year on boards such as Indeed, CV-Library, S1 Jobs and LinkedIn and often start soon after hiring.

Recruitment at the 100 leading graduate employers fell 24.5% between 2022 and 2025, and their targets for 2026 were 0.5% lower still. ISE members cut graduate hiring by 8% in a year while internship hiring rose 2%: firms kept the cheaper, earlier pipeline.
With fewer places, firms visit fewer campuses rather than widen their search.

London banks run campus events at a short list of universities (Oxford, Cambridge, LSE, Imperial, Warwick, then UCL, Durham, Bristol, Edinburgh and others). Applications open in July and close from October; a September arrival for a one-year master’s is already late.
The strongest master’s feeders are LSE, LBS, Imperial, Oxford and Cambridge; LBS’s Masters in Financial Analysis placed 92% within three months, two-thirds of them in the UK.

The Big Four take the largest graduate intakes in the country, but they shrank: about 6,500 in 2023 against 5,400 in 2024. Deloitte started 1,353 in September 2026, 44% of them outside London, so applying for Leeds, Manchester or Birmingham is a real lever.
Schemes fill in order of arrival and screen on grades (often a 2:1, and A-levels at EY) and online tests, not on the university’s name.
Consultancies open applications from October to December and hold final rounds from November to February, with case interviews.

Consumer-goods firms hire through rotational schemes open to any degree: Unilever’s Future Leaders Programme pays £35,000 and L’Oréal takes up to 40 marketing trainees a year in London. Both cap the time since graduating at about two years, and a failed P&G test means a twelve-month wait.
Industrial groups run graduate programmes with short September windows; Airbus’s UK programme does not sponsor visas.
The Civil Service Fast Stream is the main graduate route into government, with its own annual application window and assessment centre.
London is Europe’s largest tech market, but graduate hiring in UK tech fell 46% in a year. The median advertised graduate software engineer salary was £32,500, with London roles from about £40,000.

Big tech and fintech graduate programmes screen on hard skills: Revolut’s asks for at least a 2:1 in a STEM subject and working SQL, Python or R even for strategy roles. In one analysis of staff at Amazon, Apple, Google and Microsoft, Cambridge was the most common British university and the Open University, mostly part-time learners, the third.

Research roles at London’s AI labs and trading firms want a PhD or at least an MSc plus publications; IMC’s graduate machine-learning researcher needs an MSc, PhD preferred. Master’s graduates enter through data-science, analytics and applied engineering roles instead.
Quant desks recruit from mathematics and computing at Cambridge (Part III), Oxford and Imperial, and decide on coding and maths tests.

The government’s CyberFirst bursary pays students and gives summer placements leading to jobs at the NCSC, GCHQ and partner firms, but it is for British citizens only. In industry, most people start as security-operations (SOC) analysts.

Target universities matter for banks, top consultancies and Magic Circle law; most other employers screen on grades (often a 2:1) and tests, and many use contextual recruitment that credits strong results from a weaker school.
Autumn campus presentations, careers fairs and society events at target universities; employer insight days; case competitions with industry judges.

Autumn term is the peak: employers post and close most graduate vacancies then, some now advertise from July, and large schemes fill in order of arrival. Outside the peak, small employers, unfilled vacancies and direct roles are open all year.

Schemes screen on the class of the first degree, not on a master’s: the Fast Stream asks for a 2:2 or better in any subject on most schemes, and most employers screen on grades (often a 2:1). Research roles in AI are the exception and ask for an MSc or PhD.

Employers take foreign degrees as awarded: KPMG tells applicants to list overseas qualifications exactly as awarded, without UK equivalents. UK ENIC, run by Ecctis for the government, issues Statements of Comparability for those who need one, and regulated professions such as law, medicine, teaching and architecture have their own recognition bodies.

Target universities matter for banks, top consultancies and Magic Circle law; most other employers screen on grades and tests, and EY UK uses Rare’s contextual system to read applications against socio-economic background.

Apprenticeships are widespread but mostly for school leavers: 81% of ISE employers recruited apprentices in 2025, 77% of apprenticeships went to school and college leavers and 16% to graduates. There is no dual-study tradition like Germany’s.

The Fast Stream alone had 654 vacancies in the 2026 intake and 78,407 registrations. A recent ISE conference noted that the graduate downturn is concentrated in areas hit by public-sector cuts, such as education and local and central government.

Only licensed sponsors can sponsor, and large firms ration it: KPMG sponsors only London Audit, Tax, Consulting and Technology programmes and all Consulting Actuarial, and says the position may change at short notice; Airbus’s UK programme does not sponsor. See Visas for the rules.

Leave off the photo and date of birth: Prospects says you need a photo only for acting or modelling and that date of birth is irrelevant. Two pages for most graduate CVs, one page for finance and consulting, with grades shown.
Two A4 pages is the standard maximum for a graduate CV, and one page if the employer asks for it; a page and a half looks worse than one full page. Finance and consulting banks expect one page.

Many scheme forms replace the cover letter with application questions, or skip them altogether in a strength-based process; send a letter when it is asked for or when it explains a gap or a missed grade requirement.
Leave referees off the CV unless told otherwise, and ask your referees first. Offers are normally conditional on references and right-to-work checks.

You type your grades into the form and the employer checks them against transcripts or certificates later. KPMG asks for overseas qualifications as awarded and, for student-visa holders, a letter from your institution with your course completion date.
Scheme salaries are published, so the application does not ask for an expectation: the Fast Stream starts at £31,186 and Unilever’s Future Leaders Programme pays £35,000.
Employers must check the right to work before employment starts, and large firms add reference and qualification checks to the offer.

Online applications are the main channel for schemes; a referral gets the CV read but does not pass the tests. Smaller employers and research groups also take speculative approaches to a named person.

Applications are online and tests and video interviews remote, but the final stage is often in person in the UK: KPMG’s Launch Pad is a half-day at venues in London, Birmingham, Manchester, Bristol, Glasgow and Leeds. Non-UK citizens need a visa route, and employers want the right to work shown before the start.
English; extra European languages are an asset in London. The Skilled Worker visa asks for English at CEFR B2.

Most schemes run in four to six steps: an online form, online tests, a live or recorded video interview, then an assessment centre or final interview. KPMG’s graduate route has four stages: an application with a job-preview quiz, online skills and cognitive tests (the cognitive test is timed at 36 minutes), a video interview of 6 pre-recorded questions put by an AI avatar (about 40 minutes), and a half-day in-person Launch Pad.

PwC lists seven stages for most programmes: online application, numerical, verbal and logical reasoning tests, a behavioural assessment, a video interview and an assessment centre. It applies a once-a-year rule: one application per cycle, and a failed or withdrawn one means waiting for the next.

Assessment centres are essentially group interviews: an ice-breaker, a group exercise (often a business case), a group or individual presentation and an individual interview, with time to meet staff. They run from an afternoon to overnight, you are assessed throughout, including informal time, and some are held virtually.

The Civil Service Fast Stream has five stages: choose up to 4 schemes, online tests (work scenarios, a case study and a data test to finish within 5 days of activation), a timed recorded video interview, an online assessment centre (a written advice exercise, a stakeholder communication exercise and a development conversation) and, on most schemes, a final selection board.

Dress smartly even for video interviews and choose a quiet room. KPMG requires assessments to be done without outside help or AI tools and can withdraw an application or re-test you if it finds a breach.

From first test to offer, KPMG gives an offer within 2 working days of the Launch Pad, which runs on set dates from November to May. No source gives a median time for the whole process; it depends on when you apply, because schemes fill in order of arrival.
Probation has no set statutory length: Acas says it can be any length, and during it you still give the notice in your contract or the statutory minimum.

The statutory minimum notice is one week from either side once you have been employed for a month, rising for the employer to one week per year of service from two years, up to 12 weeks. A contract can set longer notice, not shorter.

Offers from large firms come quickly after the final stage and are conditional: KPMG gives an offer within 2 working days of the Launch Pad, subject to immigration status and right to work being confirmed before the start. There is no thirteenth-month salary in the UK; pay is one annual figure.

Scheme salaries are published and fixed, so there is little to negotiate: ISE’s 2025 average is £33,000 for graduates and £24,000 for apprentices, and the Fast Stream starts at £31,186. KPMG’s sponsored hires must accept their offer at least three months before joining.

Only employers with a sponsor licence can offer a Skilled Worker visa; the Home Office publishes the register of licensed sponsors. Ask early whether the employer holds a licence and whether the specific programme is covered, because large firms ration it.

KPMG sponsors only Audit, Tax and Consulting and Technology programmes based in London and all Consulting Actuarial ones; it cannot sponsor any other graduate programme and says this may change at short notice.

A Graduate visa needs no sponsor, which is why many employers hire on it first: it lasts 2 years for applications made by 31 December 2026 and 18 months after, and cannot be extended, so a sponsor must be found within that time.

Student visa holders must show the course completion date before the programme start, and a government scholarship that covered fees and living costs needs unconditional written consent to stay in or re-enter the UK.

The Civil Service Fast Stream takes nationals of the UK, Ireland, the Commonwealth and several European countries who can live and work in the UK, and some security posts need British citizenship; the CyberFirst bursary is for British citizens only. Student Circus lists employers that can sponsor international students.

Civil Service Careers (civil-service-careers.gov.uk) carries the Fast Stream and government jobs, and its nationality page sets who can apply. Large employers’ own early-careers pages (KPMG, PwC, Deloitte and others) take applications directly.

TARGETjobs lists graduate jobs and schemes, internships and placements, the UK 300 most popular employers and offers CV review and an interview coach; Prospects, run by Jisc, covers graduate jobs, work experience and employer profiles.

General boards named by university careers services include Indeed, CV-Library, S1 Jobs and LinkedIn. Student Circus, provided to Imperial students, lists verified full-time and internship jobs from employers that can sponsor international students.

Employers tour universities in the autumn and large graduate recruitment fairs run in the same term; KPMG holds its Launch Pad assessment days on seven dates in six cities, from London to Glasgow, between November and May. University careers services run the fairs and host employer talks.

Starting in the wrong window: autumn is the peak and some employers open from July, while graduate programmes usually open in August or September with deadlines as early as October; some multinationals recruit more than a year ahead. A one-year master’s student who begins looking in September is already late.
Sending the wrong CV: more than two A4 pages, a photo or a date of birth. If the employer asks for one page, send one page.
Using your single application too early: PwC lets you apply once per cycle, and a failed P&G test means a twelve-month wait, so do the practice tests first.
Using AI to answer assessments: KPMG can withdraw you, and in the 2025 ISE survey 61% of employers reported candidates using AI in interviews without disclosure.
Skipping the summer internship or placement that is the real entry route, and assuming sponsorship will be available: it covers only some programmes and can change at short notice.

Interviews, tests and the assessment centre are in English and fluent business English is assumed; a second European language is an advantage in London. No certificate is asked on the scheme form, though the Skilled Worker visa asks for CEFR B2.
Case interviews and written exercises are in English, so the evidence is the interview itself rather than a certificate.
Consumer-goods schemes assess in English through online tests, a video interview and an assessment centre.
The Fast Stream assesses a written advice exercise and a stakeholder communication exercise at its online assessment centre, all in English.
Software roles interview in English with coding and technical tests; Revolut’s programme asks for working SQL, Python or R, and no second language is asked.
Research roles are assessed on publications, coding and maths in English; the Skilled Worker visa baseline is CEFR B2, which a UK degree or an approved test proves.

Competition is at a record: employers averaged about 140 applications per graduate vacancy in 2025, up 14% on the year and more than three times the 38 of two decades earlier; retail, FMCG and tourism averaged about 290 and legal about 69.
Among 2022/23 postgraduate-taught leavers, 13% of international graduates were unemployed and seeking work against 3% of UK graduates (Jisc, 2026); graduate unemployment overall rose to 6.1%.

PolyU’s career office lists the portals students use: JobsDB, CTgoodjobs, eFinancialCareers, foundit Hong Kong, Jump, Recruit, Government Jobs, the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants and the Labour Department’s Interactive Employment Service (iES), besides JIJIS.
Civil-service joint recruitment (permanent residents)

The 2026-27 joint recruitment exercise opened on 12 September and closed on 2 October 2026, with 40 Administrative Officer, 100 Executive Officer II and 39 other posts; it is open to permanent residents, and the joint exam is on 5 December in Hong Kong or in seven cities abroad.
Work first on the post-study stay (Hong Kong-degree graduates)

A graduate of a Hong Kong degree can apply for the Immigration Arrangements for Non-local Graduates (IANG) with just the graduation letter and stay 24 months with no job offer and no quota, free to look for work or start a business; the Top Talent Pass offers the same 24 months to recent graduates of listed universities, with a quota of 10,000 a year for those with under three years of experience.
Entry-level hiring is shrinking: vacancies in the universities’ job system fell 55% in 2025, management-trainee posts fell 25%, and an HR consultant blamed a weak economy and fast AI adoption.
Graduates still mostly find work: in HKU’s 2025 survey 69.3% of graduates were employed, 27.8% in further study and 0.8% unemployed, at a median of HK$26,000 a month.

Recruitment runs through the universities: JIJIS is open only to students of the UGC-funded universities, and JPMorgan’s Hong Kong summer analyst notice was circulated by CityU’s business-school career office, among others.

HSBC filters on grades, not on a named school: a GPA of at least 3.2 of 4.0 (or 4.0 of 5.0) on an official transcript or degree certificate, with an overseas equivalent accepted. How far the university name counts beyond that was not stated on any page we read.
The Joint Recruitment Examination for the civil service is held on 5 December 2026 in Hong Kong and in Beijing, Shanghai, London, New York, Toronto, Vancouver and Sydney.
Cathay Pacific asks applicants for its next intake to join its Talent Community, with the 2026 summer internships already closed and the next intake opening later in the year.

HSBC runs Hong Kong graduate programmes across banking, markets, research and technology, starting from July; applications for the 2026 programmes closed on 31 October 2025 and those for 2027 close on 31 October 2026, though HSBC recruits on a rolling basis and may close earlier once vacancies are filled.

JPMorgan’s Hong Kong 2027 summer analyst programmes were asset and wealth management and the commercial and investment bank (deadline 31 August 2026) and corporate functions (30 September 2026); its technology, data and product programme was listed only for Singapore.
Graduate vacancies at the eight public universities’ job system fell 55% in 2025, to 30,798, and management-trainee posts fell 25%, at an average graduate pay of HK$20,961 a month.

The 2026-27 civil-service joint exercise had 179 posts: 40 Administrative Officer, 100 Executive Officer II, 10 Assistant Information Officer, 4 Assistant Trade Officer II, 14 Management Services Officer II and 11 Transport Officer II. Appointment needs Level 2 in the Chinese and English papers of the Common Recruitment Examination, its aptitude test, and the Basic Law and National Security Law test.

Tech roles for graduates sit mostly in the banks’ technology programmes and in corporate IT: HSBC’s 2026 list includes an engineering (technology) programme, and Cathay Pacific has digital and IT and engineering graduate trainee programmes. Local universities (HKU, HKUST, CUHK) are the usual source.

The finance calendar runs a year ahead: JPMorgan’s 2027 summer deadlines were 31 August and 30 September 2026 and HSBC’s is 31 October 2026, while the civil-service round ran from 12 September to 2 October 2026. Portal hiring continues through the year.

The programmes we read set a bachelor-level bar: HSBC asks for a GPA threshold and under two years of experience, and asks for no master’s. A master’s from a Hong Kong university is still the route to the 24-month post-study stay for many foreign students.

No recognition centre screens degrees for ordinary jobs: HSBC reads the GPA on the official transcript or degree certificate and accepts an overseas equivalent. The IANG visa needs only the graduation letter or certificate.

Banks fix a GPA threshold and recruit through university career offices; no page we read says how far the school name counts. Listed universities matter for the Top Talent Pass, which uses a list of 200 institutions.

University graduates reach employers through summer internships, graduate programmes and portals; apprenticeship or dual-study contracts are not a route we found in any source for university graduates.

The 2026-27 civil-service joint exercise offered 179 posts against 30,798 graduate vacancies in the universities’ job system in 2025, and is open to permanent residents only, so the public sector is a small door for a foreign graduate.

Graduates of a Hong Kong degree need no sponsor for the first 24 months (IANG); otherwise the General Employment Policy needs a Hong Kong-registered employer and a genuine full-time job at market-level pay, and the visa is tied to the employer. The rules themselves are under Visas.
None of the Hong Kong application pages we read asks for a photo. Treat it as optional, in our reading.
The banks’ programmes use an online form with CV and transcript; we found no page that sets a CV length, so treat one to two pages as our reading.
No page we read asks for a cover letter for the bank programmes; it is a matter for the individual employer, in our reading.
References are not part of the first application in the bank programmes we read; they are checked at offer stage, in our reading.
HSBC asks for a GPA shown on an official transcript or degree certificate; no page we read asks for certified or translated copies at application.

Pay is raised at offer; HKUST’s taught-postgraduate survey puts the median at HK$25,000 a month and HK$30,000 in banking and finance, and HKU’s 2025 survey at HK$26,000. No page we read asks for a salary expectation in the application.
No page we read says how routine background or reference checks are in Hong Kong hiring; for financial-services employers they are common, in our reading.
The banks take applications online on fixed calendars, but outside finance most local hiring runs through contacts, in our reading.
A degree from Hong Kong gives 24 months to look for work without a sponsor, and graduates of listed top universities may come under the Top Talent Pass.

English in international finance; Cantonese and often Mandarin for local firms and client-facing roles serving mainland clients. The civil service requires Level 2 in both the Chinese and English papers of its exam.

The banks’ route is an online application, then assessments and interviews; HSBC says it recruits on a rolling basis and may close earlier once vacancies are filled, and JPMorgan reviews on a rolling basis too, so apply well before the deadline. Neither page we read describes the assessment stages.

The civil-service route is a joint exam: Level 2 in the Chinese and English papers of the Common Recruitment Examination, its aptitude test, the Basic Law and National Security Law test, and then the Joint Recruitment Examination on 5 December 2026.
Interviews and dress follow the London pattern in international banks and are in English; no page we read states norms for assessment centres.

Under the Employment Ordinance a contract on probation can be ended with no notice in the first month; after that the notice is as agreed in the contract but not less than 7 days. Outside probation, a continuous contract with no notice clause needs not less than one month.

An end-of-year payment (the “13th month” or a bonus) is due only if it is contractual; for contracts made after 27 June 1997 an annual payment is presumed not to be gratuitous. A probation period of up to three months is excluded from the qualifying service for a pro rata payment.
New graduates averaged HK$20,961 a month in the universities’ job system in 2025, up 0.5%; median pay was HK$26,000 for HKU graduates and HK$25,000 for HKUST taught-postgraduate respondents.
Graduate programmes set pay on the bank’s own scale; negotiation is for experienced hires, in our reading.

The decisive fact for an employer is whether you need a sponsor: a graduate of a Hong Kong degree can apply for IANG on the graduation letter alone and work for 24 months with no job offer and no quota, so the employer files nothing.

Otherwise an employer files under the General Employment Policy: a Hong Kong-registered company, a genuine full-time job at market-level pay, and the graduate’s degree; the visa lasts 36 months but is tied to the employer, and a change of employer needs the Immigration Department’s written approval.

Ask early whether the employer has filed for a foreign graduate before, and never start a trial or internship on visitor status: working on a visitor visa is a criminal offence for the worker and the employer.

JIJIS for students of the UGC-funded universities; JobsDB, CTgoodjobs, eFinancialCareers, foundit Hong Kong, Jump, Recruit, Government Jobs, the HKICPA job board and the Labour Department’s iES for everyone else.

The banks’ own graduate pages: HSBC’s Hong Kong graduate and internship programmes (listed on GradConnection and university career pages) and JPMorgan’s summer analyst programme, applied for through its careers site; Cathay Pacific’s early-careers page and Talent Community.
For the civil service, the Civil Service Bureau (csb.gov.hk) and the Administrative Officer recruitment site (ao-recruitment.gov.hk).
Applying in the new year. JPMorgan’s Hong Kong 2027 summer deadlines were 31 August and 30 September 2026 and HSBC’s is 31 October 2026, with positions filling before the deadline.
Assuming the market is as it was. Graduate vacancies in the universities’ job system fell 55% in 2025, so a fallback plan outside investment banking is needed.
Working or interning on visitor status. Italian and EU citizens can visit for 90 days, but working on visitor status is an offence for both worker and employer.
Planning on the civil service as a foreigner. The 2026-27 exercise is for permanent residents, and appointment needs Level 2 in the Chinese and English papers and a Basic Law test.
Missing the 24-month cliff. The IANG and Top Talent Pass stays end at 24 months, so a regular contribution record or a sponsored employment visa has to be in place before the renewal.

International banks recruit in English: HSBC’s and JPMorgan’s Hong Kong programme notices are in English and state no Chinese requirement. Cantonese or Mandarin helps for client-facing roles with mainland clients, in our reading.
Local firms hire in Cantonese and Mandarin as well as English; no page we read states a level for business roles.
Appointment to the civil-service grades needs Level 2 in both the Use of Chinese and the Use of English papers of the Common Recruitment Examination, or an accepted equivalent.
Cathay Pacific’s early-careers page is in English with Traditional and Simplified Chinese versions and states no language requirement; HSBC’s technology programme notice is in English.

HKU’s 2025 survey of its UGC-funded bachelor’s graduates found 69.3% employed, 27.8% in further studies, 0.8% unemployed and 2.2% other, with a median monthly salary of HK$26,000 (average HK$33,338); the employment rate, counting only those employed or unemployed, was 98.9%.
For master’s students from abroad the picture is different: of 2,452 HKUST MSc and MA respondents in 2025, 65.5% had left Hong Kong or returned home.

Graduates of Hong Kong universities who apply within six months get 24 months with no job offer needed. Renewal at month 24 needs a market-rate job or an operating business.

Download and print your e-Visa before you fly. Hong Kong applies the apostille convention: Italian certificates need only an apostille, plus a sworn English translation that also carries one.
Banks ask for proof of a residential address issued in the last 3 months: a lease stamped by the Inland Revenue Department, a utility bill in your name or a university housing certificate.
At the border you get a landing slip with your limit of stay instead of a passport stamp: keep it in your passport, as banks, employers and universities ask for it.

Admitted for more than 180 days, you must register for a smart identity card (HKID) within 30 days of entering, or face a HK$5,000 fine: book online as soon as you have the e-Visa. The receipt (ROP 140) lets you work until the card is ready, after about 10 working days.
Salaries tax is territorial: you pay the lower of progressive rates up to 17% after allowances, or a flat 15% on gross income. The tax year runs from 1 April to 31 March.
Foreign employees are exempt from the Mandatory Provident Fund for their first 13 months; after that, 5% of pay from you and 5% from your employer.

Banks (HSBC, Standard Chartered, Bank of China HK, Hang Seng) want passport, e-Visa, landing slip, HKID or ROP 140, contract or enrolment letter and proof of address, plus your home tax number: for Italians, the 16-character codice fiscale. Virtual banks (ZA Bank, Mox) accept only the physical HKID.
A first application gives no right to stay or work while it is pending; a renewal filed before your visa expires lets you wait in Hong Kong on the same terms.
Leaving for good, your employer files form IR56G and holds your last pay until the tax clearance letter is issued.
Register for a Smart HKID within 30 days if you stay over 180 days; slots run out weeks ahead.
Working as a visitor, even a few hours or a trial while waiting for the e-Visa, is a crime carrying up to two years in prison.
Bought sponsors and shell companies are prosecuted; false statements carry up to 14 years.

IDA-backed multinationals employed 312,468 people in 2025, about 11% of national employment, across more than 1,800 operations; 54% of these jobs are outside Dublin.
Dublin hosts the European headquarters of US tech firms, fund administration and aircraft leasing.
English is the working language: only 2.4–2.8% of Irish job postings say English is not required.

Eurostat counts 339,530 people in work in the Cork metropolitan region in 2021: 16,660 in information and communication (second in Ireland, after Dublin) and 8,150 in finance and insurance (second in Ireland, after Dublin). The region’s GDP was €115.7 billion in 2021.

Eurostat counts 1,073,000 people in work in the Dublin metropolitan region in 2021: 97,700 in information and communication, 65% of Ireland’s 149,400 and the most of any Irish region, and 80,700 in finance and insurance, 68% of the national 118,800.

Among the 152 European metropolitan regions with 2021 figures, Dublin ranks tenth by jobs in information and communication (97,700) and fourth by jobs in finance and insurance (80,700), behind only Paris, Warsaw and Milan; London, Berlin, Frankfurt and Madrid report no figure for that year.
Dublin is 30th in the world in the Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) and 10th among Western European centres; Cork is not ranked among the ones listed.

Irish Funds says the funds and asset-management industry directly employed 19,519 people in Ireland in 2023, according to an Indecon report it commissioned, with over 37,500 jobs in total once indirect effects are counted.
The CSO counts 3,005 people employed in aircraft leasing in Ireland in 2024, at average earnings of €206,324 a year.

IDA-supported companies employed 142,501 people in the Dublin region in 2025 and 53,535 in the South-West (Cork and Kerry), 32,562 in the West, 28,125 in the Mid-West and 169,967 outside Dublin in all; information and communication accounted for 112,300 of the 312,468 jobs and business, financial and other services for 61,155.

One year after graduating, the median weekly earnings of the 2022 cohort were €650 for master’s graduates in business, administration and law and €855 for those in information and communication technologies (€570 and €770 for bachelor’s graduates); 84% of the cohort were in substantial employment and the all-graduate median was €625 a week.
Ireland’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 5.0% in September 2026, and 12.5% for 15-to-24-year-olds.
KPMG Ireland runs graduate programmes and says its new Dublin headquarters, Harcourt Square, opens in 2026.
Deloitte Ireland runs a graduate programme, its Future Leaders Academy, with intakes it says are always 50/50 by gender.
EY Ireland lists a 2026 Graduate Programme, with routes including Tax and Law and Technology.
Bank of Ireland says its 2027 Graduate Programme is closed for applications and invites candidates to register interest in the 2028 programme.

Apple’s job-creation page shows Cork as the base of its Irish facility, which it says builds iMac for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and of a team giving telephone support to customers across Europe.

Ireland hires graduates mostly through structured programmes at the Big Four, banks and the multinationals based in Dublin, and through work placements built into Irish degrees. Unlike the UK, most Irish employers have no fixed deadline and take applications for most of the year.
The professional-services firms are the exception: Deloitte’s 2027 audit programme closes at 17:00 on 21 October 2026, and its page says you can apply to only one graduate programme.
Graduate programmes
The Big Four, Bank of Ireland, AIB and Citi run graduate intakes in Dublin, with online tests and assessment days.

Gradireland’s survey of graduate employers found 46% use a telephone interview, 42% online ability or technical tests, 39% online psychometric tests and 37% video interviews; 54% look for a 2:1 or better.

KPMG Ireland offers a Chartered Accountant (ACA) route and a STEM and non-ACA route, Deloitte’s Future Leaders Academy takes any discipline with a 2.1, and EY takes any degree and discipline with a 2:1.
Work placements
Many Irish degrees include a paid placement of several months, which employers use as a trial before the graduate offer.
PwC Ireland’s summer internship applications open on 2 December 2026 and close on 29 January 2027, and State Street runs a 12-month in-person internship in Dublin.
Direct applications and referrals at multinationals
Google, Meta, Microsoft, Apple, Pfizer and the payment firms hire graduates in Dublin, often in multilingual operations and sales roles that welcome other European languages.
Experienced hires apply through the same online portals and recruiters; a Critical Skills permit lets a non-EU hire with an offer of at least €40,904 start without a labour-market test.
Careers fairs and campus events

The Gradireland Graduate Careers Fair took place on 6 October 2026 at the RDS in Dublin with over 80 employers; first-term fairs and presentations still happen, but are now used mainly to engage finalists, not to set closing dates.
University fairs follow: the Trinity engineering fair and UCC Recruitment Festival on 8 October, ATU Galway on 20 October, and the University of Limerick spring fair in late January and February.
Public service and apprenticeships

publicjobs.ie is the public service recruitment site, with job search, alerts and guidance on applications, tests and interviews; its page lists a news item on graduate opportunities in the civil service.

Apprenticeships now reach professional work: 87 programmes in 17 sectors, 30,536 apprentices and 10,191 companies by mid-2026, including a two-year accounting technician and a three-year insurance practitioner route that ends in a BA (Hons).
Just over 80% of the class of 2024 were in work nine months after graduating; in the 2026 employer survey, 66% planned to hire graduates as planned and a further 24% were hiring more cautiously.
Dublin depends on a few multinationals, so a round of tech lay-offs hits graduate hiring quickly.

The old model of campaigns with deadlines before Christmas is no longer the reality: gradireland says the majority of companies in Ireland do not have a specific deadline, and EY says that unless a closing date is stated, applications close once the roles are filled.
The vacancy rate is low at 1.3% in the last quarter of 2025 (2.5% in professional, scientific and technical activities), so competition for graduate places is stiff.
Employers say they look for core competencies and employability skills (65%) and a 2:1 or better (54%); the Big Four pages read name no target universities and accept any discipline.
Careers services across 26 universities, technological universities and institutes belong to AHECS, which works with gradireland and runs the Early Careers Employers Survey.
A foreign qualification gets a non-binding comparability statement from NARIC Ireland (QQI); formal recognition decisions are made by institutions, professional bodies and employers.

Gradireland Graduate Careers Fair, RDS Dublin, 6 October 2026, 11:00 to 17:00, open to students and graduates, with over 80 employers and talks on CVs, interviews and working in Ireland as an international student.

Trinity College Dublin Engineering and Environment Fair and UCC Recruitment Festival on 8 October; ATU Galway Careers Fair on 20 October; University of Limerick spring fair on 27 and 28 January and 10 and 11 February.
Firm deadlines: Deloitte’s 2027 Future Leaders Academy closes on 21 October 2026, and PwC’s summer internship opens on 2 December 2026 and closes on 29 January 2027.

Dublin’s funds industry hires graduates into fund accounting, administration and depositary roles: State Street, the largest fund administrator in Ireland, runs a 12-month in-person internship, and administrators backed a new master’s in investment fund administration with two Irish universities.
Bank of Ireland says its 2027 Graduate Programme is closed and invites registration of interest in the 2028 programme.
The Big Four and Accenture are named the top employers for Irish graduates; PwC Ireland’s annual drive has been reported at about 250 to 280 graduates, most into training contracts in Dublin.
KPMG Ireland’s ACA route runs the Chartered Accountant qualification alongside client work; EY applications go through an online form, an online assessment and two interviews.

Consulting graduates come through the Big Four and Accenture programmes: KPMG Ireland hires into Consulting and Deal Advisory teams, and Deloitte’s Future Leaders Academy welcomes commerce, science and engineering backgrounds.
The public service recruits through publicjobs.ie, which lists civil-service graduate opportunities, state boards and Garda trainees; the page does not state nationality or right-to-work conditions.

Graduate software roles come from multinationals and their Irish sites, such as Mastercard’s launch programme in Dublin and Stryker’s R&D graduate programme in Cork; employers keep hiring full-stack, mobile and embedded engineers, with Python, JavaScript and C/C++ most in demand.
Information and communication had a vacancy rate of 1.6% in the last quarter of 2025, and a software development apprenticeship of two years at NFQ level 6 exists alongside the degree route.
Data and AI teams at Google, Meta, Microsoft and the payment firms in Dublin hire mainly experienced staff; graduates enter through analyst and operations roles first.

Gradireland says the majority of companies in Ireland have no specific deadline and accept applications for most or all of the year; the professional-services firms are the exception, with fixed closing dates such as Deloitte’s 21 October 2026.
The routes read ask for a bachelor’s degree with a 2.1 or 2:1 in any discipline (Deloitte, EY) and name no master’s requirement; a master’s matters for fund administration and some technical roles.

NARIC Ireland, hosted by QQI, gives free non-binding comparability statements for foreign qualifications, covering over 1,800 qualifications from 170 countries; recognition for a regulated profession is decided by the professional body.
The selection criteria employers report are competencies (65%) and a 2:1 or better (54%), and the Big Four pages accept any discipline without naming schools.
Paid placements are built into many Irish degrees, and apprenticeships have grown to 87 programmes with 30,536 apprentices, including degree-level routes in insurance.
The public service recruits through publicjobs.ie and runs civil-service graduate and ICT apprenticeship routes, but the large graduate intakes read are in the Big Four, banks and multinationals.

A Critical Skills Employment Permit needs an offer of at least €40,904 (€36,848 for a degree under 12 months old) for two years, no labour-market test, and an employer with at least 50% EEA staff; Deloitte’s programme asks for the legal right to work in Ireland. See Visas for the rules.
Irish CVs follow British practice: no photo, two pages.
Careers-service guidance says including a photograph is not the convention in Ireland.
An Irish CV is two A4 pages with a personal profile, in reverse chronological order; leave off date of birth, PPS number, marital status and nationality.
Gradireland says a cover letter is needed when a role asks for a traditional CV, but most graduate employers now use online application forms.
Named referees are common in Ireland and the UK, provided they have agreed to be listed; otherwise a line saying references are available on request is used.
The application routes read (KPMG, Deloitte, EY) ask for an online form and CV; none asks for transcripts or certified copies at the first stage.
The online applications read do not ask for a salary expectation; pay is discussed at the offer stage. Critical Skills thresholds count basic salary and qualifying health insurance but not bonuses.
No page read describes routine background or reference checks; right-to-work is checked, since Deloitte requires the legal right to work in the Republic of Ireland.
Online applications to graduate programmes are the main channel.
Gradireland’s survey found the first screening is usually a telephone interview (46%) or online tests (42% ability, 39% psychometric), not a personal introduction.
EU citizens can apply from anywhere; non-EU graduates of Irish universities can stay one or two years to work.
Stamp 1G gives non-EEA graduates of Irish awards 12 months at Level 8 or 24 months at Level 9 and above, with full-time work for any employer.
English; other European languages are in demand in multinationals’ operations.
Only 2.4 to 2.8% of Irish job postings say English is not required.

Typical graduate selection: an online application, then online tests or a telephone interview, then interviews. EY runs an online form and CV, an online assessment (scenario ranking, sliders and written answers), an interview with a team and a final strengths-based interview with leadership, in person or on MS Teams.

Gradireland’s employer survey: 46% use a telephone interview, 42% online ability or technical tests, 39% online psychometric tests and 37% video interviews. EY’s case-study interview for Financial Services Consulting lasts 90 minutes and the competency interview 45 minutes.
Interviews are in English. The pages read give no typical time from application to offer, nor assessment-centre norms beyond the stages above.

Since 16 December 2022 a probation period is generally limited to six months, extendable to a maximum of 12 months only in exceptional cases in the employee’s interest; it must be stated in the written terms of employment.
After 13 weeks’ service statutory notice from the employer starts at one week and rises to eight weeks after 15 years, and the employee owes one week unless the contract says more.
The ACA route at KPMG Ireland combines the Chartered Accountant qualification with client work; the pages read do not state salaries, bonuses or how long you have to accept an offer.

The Critical Skills Employment Permit needs a job offer of at least two years paying €40,904 a year (€36,848 if the degree is under 12 months old) or more than €68,911 in any eligible occupation; the employer must apply at least 12 weeks before the start, pay a €1,000 fee (90% refunded if refused) and have at least 50% EEA employees.

Graduates of Irish awards who hold Stamp 2 can work full time for any employer on Stamp 1G for 12 months (Level 8) or 24 months (Level 9 and above), so an employer need not sponsor you at first; Deloitte still asks for the legal right to work in Ireland.
Ask early: a Critical Skills application must reach the Department at least 12 weeks before the start date, so an employer needs notice well before the offer is signed.
Graduate content: gradireland (graduate jobs, programmes, internships, employer A-Z, events, CV and interview guides); employers’ own pages (KPMG, Deloitte, EY, PwC, Bank of Ireland).
University careers services: 26 institutions in AHECS, which lists fairs such as UCC Recruitment Festival, the Trinity engineering fair and the University of Limerick autumn and spring fairs.

Waiting for a UK-style December deadline: most firms take applications all year, but Deloitte closed on 21 October 2026 and EY closes once its roles are filled.
Applying to many programmes at one firm: Deloitte lets you apply to only one graduate programme, and EY lets you name two preferences.
Copying a generic CV template: gradireland warns against it, and the CV should be two pages without photo, date of birth or PPS number.
Ignoring the degree grade: 54% of graduate employers look for a 2:1 or better, and Deloitte and EY both set a 2.1 or 2:1 as the minimum.
Not mentioning Stamp 1G: after an Irish degree it allows 12 or 24 months of work for any employer, so a non-EU graduate does not need a sponsor at the start.
The fund administrators and banks hiring in Dublin work in English; multilingual operations roles at multinationals add German, Dutch, French or Swedish.
The Big Four graduate pages read (KPMG, Deloitte, EY) state no language requirement beyond English, which is the language of the application and interviews; no certificate is asked.

Only 2.4 to 2.8% of Irish job postings say English is not required, so English is the working language; recruiters report the most requested second languages in sales and support roles are German, Dutch, Swedish and French.
Technology employers in Dublin and Cork work in English; the technical stack (Python, JavaScript, C/C++) is what is tested, not a language certificate.

Just over 80% of the class of 2024 were in work nine months after graduating (HEA); Eurostat puts the employment rate of 20-to-34-year-olds with a tertiary degree at 91.6% in 2025 and 92.0% for those who left education within three years.
The vacancy rate stayed low at 1.3% in the last quarter of 2025 (1.2% a year earlier), against 3.9% in the Netherlands and 3.5% in Belgium.
No source read gives a return-offer or conversion rate for Irish work placements or graduate programmes, nor a time to first job for internationals.

Israeli high-tech employed about 391,000 people in 2024, about 5,000 fewer than in 2023, the first decline in at least a decade; its share of all employees has stayed at about 11.5% for several years.
About 51% of high-tech employees, some 200,000, worked in R&D roles in 2024, against 37% in 2012; headquarters roles fell from 41% to 29%.

Of the 14 representative offices of foreign banks on the Bank of Israel’s list, 10 are in Tel Aviv, among them J.P. Morgan, BNP Paribas, Julius Baer and Pictet; the others are in Herzliya and Ramat Gan.

The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Gaza, within 500 m of its border, to parts of the northern West Bank and to areas near the northern border and the Golan Heights, and against all but essential travel to most of the rest of the West Bank; it also reports Iranian strikes in the region since 8 July 2026.
The Adani–Gadot group, owner of Haifa port since 2023, calls it the second-largest port in Israel.

Startup Genome’s 2026 report says Tel Aviv holds the top spot in the Middle East and North Africa and sits in the global top five, with an ecosystem value of $250 billion; Israeli tech companies raised about $15.6 billion in 2025, alongside exits of roughly $46 billion.

The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) ranks Tel Aviv 94th of 117 financial centres (88th in the March 2026 edition), the only Israeli centre listed; in the Gulf, Dubai is 9th, Riyadh 46th and Doha 52nd, and in the region Istanbul is 89th.

The Central Bureau of Statistics’ preliminary 2023 figures give Jerusalem 1,028,366 residents, Tel Aviv-Yafo 495,230, Haifa 298,312 and Be’er Sheva 218,995; it noted in June 2024 that Jerusalem had passed one million.

In the first half of 2025 the average monthly wage in Tel Aviv was NIS 22,359, against NIS 11,415 in Jerusalem and NIS 15,098 across Israel, whose median was NIS 10,586; Jerusalem had the most employees of any large city, 287,984.
Check Point says it has more than 7,000 employees, more than 3,500 of them security experts, and gives its international corporate headquarters as 5 Shlomo Kaplan Street, Tel Aviv.

Mobileye’s careers page listed 187 open positions worldwide, 67 of them in Jerusalem, 33 in Ramat Gan, 25 in Haifa, 23 in Petah Tikva and one in Tel Aviv, against two in Munich, four in Koblenz and 12 in Shanghai.

Elbit Systems gives its headquarters as P.O.B. 539, Haifa, and says it employs over 21,000 people in dozens of countries, with revenues of $2,287.1 million in the quarter to 30 June 2026 and an order backlog of $32.0 billion.

The Technion says more than 10,200 undergraduate and about 4,400 graduate students are enrolled, that it has awarded about 92,500 bachelor’s degrees since 1924, and that many students work in industry during their studies.

Intel Israel employs about 9,300 people, around 4,000 of them at the Kiryat Gat plant, with R&D centres in Haifa and Petah Tikva, and has been cutting jobs, including at Kiryat Gat for the first time.

The Har Hotzvim Hi-Tech Park in Jerusalem says its tenants include Intel, Mobileye, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, Ophir Optronics, Elbit Systems Rokar and Alpha Tau, alongside medium-sized firms and start-ups.

Israeli employment contracts should be drafted in Hebrew, Nefesh B’Nefesh says a CV sent to an Israeli employer should usually be in Hebrew but that this matters less in hi-tech, and one of its interviews rates Hebrew 8 out of 10 in essentiality for financial jobs, while Check Point’s programme pages are in English; no source measured Hebrew levels or certificates by employer.

Israel has no national graduate season: Tel Aviv University holds a technology career fair each winter (7 January 2026) and a general job fair each spring, vacancies are posted all year (AllJobs showed 33,500 jobs), a 2019 survey of Viola Group portfolio companies put average hiring time at 6 to 8 weeks, and a foreign hire adds 60 to 90 working days for the work permit.

Unemployment was 2.8% in May 2026 according to the Central Bureau of Statistics, but university graduates’ share of job seekers rose from 14% in August 2022 to 20.5% in August 2026 according to the Employment Service, and only 88 of 5,641 tech vacancies in June 2025 were aimed at people without experience.

Israeli tech hires largely through networks formed in service and at university: in a 2019 survey of Viola Group portfolio companies 90% ran a friend-referral programme and 47% named it their most effective source, and a Salesforce Engineering profile says unit experience convinced a team to interview one candidate. Juniors face a thin market, with 88 of 5,641 tech vacancies in June 2025 aimed at people without experience; outside tech Hebrew is the working language, and a foreign graduate needs an employer ready to sponsor a B/1 work permit, so the market is built for Israeli graduates.
Referral through army, university and employee networks

In a 2019 survey by Viola Group of its portfolio companies’ HR heads, 90% of the Israeli companies ran a friend-referral recruitment programme and 47% named it their most effective source; the survey is old and covers one investor’s companies.

Globes reported in June 2025 that candidates with industry connections are favoured and often have them before landing a first job; a Salesforce Engineering profile has one engineer reaching the firm through a classmate from the degree programme.
University job fairs and student-union recruitment days

Tel Aviv University holds a technology career fair each winter for engineering and exact-sciences students and alumni (7 January 2026, dozens of technology companies, CVs handed in on the spot) and a larger general job fair each spring; the Hebrew University business school’s student union organises recruitment days where firms visit the campus.
Employers also go to students directly: IAI lists university recruitment fairs, open days, site tours, hackathons and meetups among its student activities.
Student jobs and final-year projects that turn into offers

Check Point lists a Student Program for R&D Israel and says some students move into full-time roles after graduating; IAI lets students do their final-year project inside company projects under engineers’ supervision and says it supports combining work and study.

The route is for students already enrolled in Israel: the library’s visa guide finds no stand-alone internship visa, A/2 students may not work outside the university except as teaching assistants, and an internship on a tourist or ETA-IL status is illegal work.
Direct application through employer sites and Hebrew job boards

AllJobs, which calls itself Israel’s largest job site, showed 33,500 jobs when we read it, with student-job and no-experience categories; JobMaster has categories for students, no experience, discharged soldiers, government jobs and internships. Both front pages we read are in Hebrew.

The market for juniors is thin: Globes counted 88 of 5,641 tech vacancies (1.5%) aimed at candidates without experience in June 2025, and told of a student who sent about 300 CVs in six months and received one response.
Bank training programmes and defence-industry student schemes

Nefesh B’Nefesh says the big banks (Leumi, Hapoalim, Mizrahi-Tefahot, Discount) run training programmes that are often not advertised, and advises sending a CV with a cover letter to each bank’s HR department.

IAI’s student programmes include Engineers for Industry, a funded track for women students at Ben-Gurion University, the Hebrew University, Tel Aviv University and the Technion, with placement during the degree and a job offer after graduation, and Atidim for Industry for students from development towns and lower socio-economic backgrounds, linked to the IDF academic reserve.
Employer-sponsored foreign-expert hire (B/1)

The library’s visa guide records that the employer applies and pays: a base salary of at least NIS 27,132 a month in 2026 (twice the national average), NIS 1,420 for the application, NIS 11,525 a year for the permit and 60 to 90 working days; firms certified by the Israel Innovation Authority can use a fast track of 6 to 10 working days.

Graduates of Israeli universities in STEM fields are exempt from the double-average wage threshold for up to 3 years after graduating, within 500 permits a year; a degree from Italy or elsewhere in Europe gets no such exemption.

Junior tech openings are scarce: 88 of 5,641 open tech vacancies in June 2025 were aimed at candidates without experience, and Globes reported in January 2025 that the average junior job search had risen to 11 months and that new junior openings per month had fallen from an average of 300 to a single digit.

There is no single graduate season: Tel Aviv University’s technology fair falls each winter (7 January 2026) and its general job fair each spring, while vacancies are posted all year (AllJobs showed 33,500 jobs).

Military service shapes the calendar: Wikipedia gives the minimum for men as 2 years and 8 months as of 2022, and a December 2025 plan would lift it to 36 months but was not yet law when reported; “reserved jobs” for newly discharged soldiers are time-limited and pay around the minimum wage.

Hiring takes weeks: the 2019 Viola survey put the average at 6 weeks for general and administrative roles, 7.5 for marketing and 8 for R&D, and a foreign hire adds 60 to 90 working days for the work permit (6 to 10 on the fast track).

Tel Aviv University’s Career Development Center offers one-to-one counselling, workshops, company presentations and the two fairs; Ben-Gurion University, the Hebrew University, Tel Aviv University and the Technion are the four universities IAI names for its women’s engineering programme.
The Hebrew University’s business school says many of its accounting graduates land internships with the Big Four in Israel and that it revamped the degree with the Israel Accountancy Council.
Foreign universities do not recruit here, and we found no ranking of schools by Israeli employers. This is our reading.

Tel Aviv University Technology Career Fair: 7 January 2026 at 10:00, for students and alumni of the Faculties of Engineering and Exact Sciences, dozens of technology and high-tech companies, CVs handed in on the spot; the page calls it an annual event.
Tel Aviv University general Job Fair: held each spring for students of all fields; the page gives no date or number of employers.
Hebrew University business school recruitment days, organised by the student union with visiting firms; the page gives no dates.

A Nefesh B’Nefesh interview rates Hebrew 8 out of 10 in essentiality for financial jobs, with niche players such as private banks, hedge funds, private equity and fintech not always requiring the best Hebrew; the training programmes at the big banks are often not advertised.
Bank Leumi’s careers page invites applicants who are residents of Israel and hold a recognised academic degree, in fields such as economics, business, accounting and computer science.

The Israeli affiliates of the Big Four (Deloitte’s Brightman Almagor Zohar, EY’s Kost Forer Gabbay & Kasierer, KPMG’s Somekh Chaikin, PwC’s Kesselman & Kesselman) hire CPAs and non-CPAs for tax, audit and advisory; one interviewee in the Nefesh B’Nefesh guide says a newly qualified accountant can expect NIS 7,000 to 8,000 gross a month, and another puts junior to senior auditors at NIS 6,500 to 8,500.

The same guide says Israel requires 15 exams for the CPA licence, held twice a year, and gives the mandatory internship (staj) as 6 months in one place and two years in another, so confirm with the Israel Auditors Council; Hebrew is called crucial for dealing with the tax offices.

Nefesh B’Nefesh says civil-service posts are often filled before they are announced publicly, that all communication is in Hebrew and that selection includes intelligence and psychological (psychotechnic) exams; it names the Civil Service Commission, Jobiz and GovJob as places where government jobs are posted.

Israel’s tech workforce fell to about 409,000 at the end of 2025 from about 417,000, which Ethosia called the first contraction in more than a decade; the Central Bureau of Statistics counted 401,800 salaried tech jobs in September 2025.

Check Point’s programmes page lists a Student Program for R&D Israel; Mobileye’s careers page lists posts in Jerusalem, Ramat Gan, Petah Tikva, Haifa and Tel Aviv and sends applicants to its jobs page, and states no programme for graduates.

Hatzava describes itself as a community of alumni of the IDF’s technology units that helps members with job search, career advice and relocation; the description comes from a start-up directory profile and we found no membership figure.

Check Point’s Global Associates Program is an 18-month programme for aspiring cybersecurity professionals with up to 3 rotations through sales, sales engineering, marketing, sales operations and customer success; its page does not state locations or eligibility.

There is no national graduate season: Tel Aviv University’s technology fair is in winter (7 January 2026) and its general fair in spring, and job boards post openings all year, AllJobs showing 33,500.

A Nefesh B’Nefesh banking interview says it matters less what you studied and more what job you pursued, and the student schemes read (IAI, Check Point) take students before they finish a bachelor’s; no posting read asks for a master’s. This is our reading.

Only licensed professions strictly need recognition: medicine, law, engineering and psychology need a licence from the relevant government office, and the CPA licence runs through the Israel Auditors Council. For new immigrants the Ministry of Aliyah and Integration issues an evaluation (45 working days) that Nefesh B’Nefesh says both private and public employers should accept; trade.gov advises overseas accountants who are not CPAs to have the degree evaluated.

Employers build on named universities: IAI’s women’s programme works with four (Ben-Gurion, the Hebrew University, Tel Aviv and the Technion), and the Hebrew University business school says many graduates land Big Four internships; we found no ranking of schools by employers. This is our reading.
Working during the degree is normal in tech and defence: Check Point has a student programme for R&D, and IAI places students in final-year projects and says it supports combining work with study.

State bodies and state-owned defence firms hire graduates, but the civil service works in Hebrew, fills posts through tenders and often before announcing them; we found no figure for the public sector’s share of graduate hires. The weight is our reading.

A sponsor must pay a base salary of at least NIS 27,132 a month in 2026 plus government fees, and with 88 of 5,641 tech vacancies aimed at people without experience a foreign junior competes with Israeli graduates; the only wage exemption is for STEM graduates of Israeli universities. See Visas for the rules.

The Nefesh B’Nefesh CV guide says to leave out address, marital status and children to avoid discrimination and does not mention a photo; JobMob adds that Israeli CVs usually carry a national ID number. No page read requires a photo. This is our reading.
Nefesh B’Nefesh recommends a one-page CV; Israeli CVs usually have a section on army service.

Nefesh B’Nefesh recommends a short cover letter in the body of the email, 3 to 5 sentences, and says olim who sent it in Hebrew got more follow-up calls; the large employers’ processes read (IAI) start from a CV and do not mention a letter.
No page read asks for references with the first application; IAI’s five stages go from CV to phone interview, professional interview, suitability tests and contract. This is our reading.

For a foreign hire the work-permit file needs the degree with a Hague Apostille and a notarised translation, plus a police certificate issued within 90 days with a double Apostille; an Israeli employer asking for copies at offer stage is our reading.

Nefesh B’Nefesh advises not raising salary in a first interview and, if asked, saying you want your market value; JobMob says salaries are rarely published up front and employers may ask what you want to earn. We found no page on whether application forms ask.

IAI’s jobs page links a personal questionnaire for security suitability, one for spouses of staff in classified positions and a form listing foreign contacts; for a work permit the library’s guide requires a police certificate. We found no page on routine reference checks at private employers.

Referrals dominate tech hiring: 90% of the Viola portfolio companies surveyed in 2019 ran a friend-referral programme, 47% called it their best source, and army service creates wide contact networks, says JobMob.

A hire from abroad needs the employer to file a B/1 permit first, taking 60 to 90 working days (6 to 10 on the fast track), and entry to work on a visit status is illegal; Rivermate says the authorities prefer the company where the person will physically work to be the sponsor.

Hebrew is the working language for most employers: Israeli employment contracts should be in Hebrew, Nefesh B’Nefesh says a Hebrew CV is the general rule and critical in some fields but less important in hi-tech, and IAI’s hiring pages are in Hebrew; Check Point’s programme pages are in English.

IAI lists five stages: choosing a post and submitting a CV on its site, a phone interview, a professional interview with the hiring manager, suitability tests that vary by post, and contract signing; the security questionnaire is a separate form.

In Viola Group’s 2019 survey, 55% of portfolio companies used a four-step process (a preliminary interview, a second interview with more senior people, an HR interview and a test), 25% used five to eight steps and 5% used no more than two; Check Point candidates report take-home assignments, but those accounts are self-reported and we did not open them.

Nefesh B’Nefesh advises arriving 10 minutes early, dressing business casual and sending a thank-you email, and warns that interviewers may be late, take calls or ask personal questions; Israeli law bars rejecting candidates for marital status or army profile. JobMob (2015) adds that some interviews take place in cafes. We found no source on assessment-centre norms.

Rivermate (28 July 2026): contracts should be drafted in Hebrew; probation typically runs three to six months, probation staff keep all statutory rights, and a formal hearing is still required before ending employment.

Statutory notice for monthly-paid staff is 1 day per month in the first 6 months, 6 days plus 2.5 days for each month after the sixth, and 1 month after a year; severance after a full year is one month’s salary per year of service, often held in the severance component of the mandatory pension. The pre-dismissal hearing was created by court rulings, not legislation.

Rivermate gives the legal minimum wage as NIS 6,443.85 a month from April 2026, an employer pension contribution of 6.5% and an employee one of 6.0%, an employer severance set-aside of 8.33%, and total employer cost of 20.8% to 24.33% of salary. We did not establish whether graduates negotiate or how long employers give to decide.

The employer applies for and pays the B/1 permit: base salary of at least NIS 27,132 a month in 2026, NIS 1,420 for the application and NIS 11,525 a year for the permit, with 60 to 90 working days for a general expert and 6 to 10 on the Hi-Tech fast track for firms certified by the Israel Innovation Authority, whose spouses also get an open work permit. Rivermate adds that the authorities prefer the company where the employee works to be the sponsor.

Graduates of Israeli universities in STEM fields can be hired by certified tech firms without the double-average wage, for up to 3 years after graduating and within 500 permits a year; a graduate of an Italian or other European university does not qualify and must be paid the standard threshold.

With 88 of 5,641 tech vacancies aimed at people without experience, a foreign junior competes with Israeli graduates, so sponsorship is realistic mainly for specialists. Ask in the first interview whether the firm has sponsored foreign staff before and which entity would be the sponsor. This is our reading.

Job boards: AllJobs (Israel’s largest by its own description, 33,500 jobs, student and no-experience categories) and JobMaster (categories for students, no experience, discharged soldiers, government jobs and internships); both front pages we read are in Hebrew. Public-sector jobs are posted on the Civil Service Commission site, Jobiz and GovJob, according to Nefesh B’Nefesh.

Employer pages: IAI’s jobs and students pages (jobs.iai.co.il, in Hebrew), Check Point’s programmes page and Mobileye’s careers page, which sends applicants to its jobs listing; we could not open Rafael’s careers page.

Fairs and communities: Tel Aviv University’s Career Development Center and its winter and spring fairs, the Hebrew University business school’s recruitment days, and Hatzava, a community of alumni of the IDF’s technology units.

Planning to work or intern on a tourist, ETA-IL or student status: the library’s visa guide records arrest by the immigration authority’s enforcement unit and expulsion with a re-entry ban of 5 to 10 years, and A/2 students may not work except as university teaching assistants.
Counting on a junior tech job: only 88 of 5,641 vacancies in June 2025 were aimed at people without experience, and an average junior search had reached 11 months by January 2025.

Sending only an English CV and cover letter: Nefesh B’Nefesh says the general rule is a Hebrew CV, critical in some fields, and that a Hebrew cover letter drew more follow-up calls; tech is the exception.

Putting address, marital status, children or a senior-sounding past job title on the CV: the guide says the first invites discrimination and the second implies high salary and managerial expectations.
Raising salary in the first interview: Nefesh B’Nefesh advises waiting and, if asked, answering that you want your market value.

A Nefesh B’Nefesh interview rates Hebrew 8 out of 10 in essentiality for financial jobs and calls English a plus for certain projects; niche players such as private banks, hedge funds and fintech do not always need the best Hebrew.

The Nefesh B’Nefesh accounting guide quotes interviewees calling financial Hebrew the most important skill, crucial for dealing with the tax offices, and essential at a high level; no certificate is named.
Nefesh B’Nefesh says Hebrew fluency is essential for government work because all communication is in Hebrew.
Rivermate says Israeli employment contracts should be drafted in Hebrew, and Nefesh B’Nefesh says a CV sent to an Israeli employer should usually be in Hebrew; no level or certificate is named.

Nefesh B’Nefesh says a Hebrew CV is less important in hi-tech, and Check Point’s programme pages are in English; IAI’s hiring pages are in Hebrew. No source tested English or Hebrew levels for graduates.

Check Point’s cybersecurity programmes are posted in English, while defence-sector hiring such as IAI’s runs in Hebrew with a security-suitability questionnaire; we found no stated language level for cybersecurity graduates.

The Central Bureau of Statistics put unemployment at 2.8% in May 2026 (126,500 of 4,469,000 in the labour force), with the Jerusalem district highest at 4.1% and Tel Aviv and the centre lowest at 2.4%.

University graduates’ share of Israel’s job seekers rose from 14% in August 2022 to 20.5% in August 2026 (16.7% in 2023, 19% in 2024, 19.6% in 2025), per the Employment Service via Calcalist, with software and application-analysis job seekers up 6.4% between June and August 2026; this is a share of job seekers, not a graduate unemployment rate.

In June 2025 Globes counted 88 tech vacancies (1.5%) aimed at candidates without experience and about 500 for candidates with one to three years of experience, against about 1,400 job seekers at that level; we found no return-offer rate or time to first job for graduates.

For a programme at an institution accredited by the Council for Higher Education, applied for at a consulate before travelling, also for an exchange semester. Valid a year at a time, renewed in Israel.

There is no internship visa, and an internship on an ETA-IL is illegal work. Students enrolled in Israel may do a required placement; otherwise a company must hire you on a B/1, or you join an accredited Masa Israel programme (ages 18 to 35) on an A/2.
Hi-tech route for Israeli STEM graduates

There is no post-study visa. The one exception: companies certified by the Innovation Authority can hire graduates of Israeli universities in tech fields without the double-average-wage rule, for three years after graduating, within 500 permits a year. A European degree does not qualify.
B/1 foreign expert

The employer must pay a base salary of at least twice the national average, with no bonuses or allowances counted; one year at a time, up to 63 months. Ordinary jobs below that level are closed to foreigners.
Tech companies certified by the Innovation Authority get a decision in 6 to 10 working days, and the spouse gets an open work permit.
For tasks of up to 90 days a year, the STEP route skips the salary rule for visa-exempt nationals.

Visiting researchers, post-docs and PhD students on a fellowship hold an A/2, and fellowships from recognised institutions are free of income tax. Researchers on an employment contract hold a B/1.
Weizmann, Technion, Tel Aviv and Hebrew University offer international PhD students full packages with a stipend and no tuition.
Working holiday

Only for Germans, Austrians and Czechs among EU citizens (plus Australians, New Zealanders and South Koreans): aged 18 to 30, up to 12 months, at most three months per employer. Italy and other EU countries have no agreement.
Israel has no working-holiday agreement with the UK.
Since 1 January 2025 visa-exempt visitors need an ETA-IL before boarding: valid two years, up to 90 days a visit, with no work, internship or formal study.

Visitors need the electronic travel authorisation ETA-IL before flying. At Ben Gurion, security officers may ask to see your phone, chats and social media, and past travel to Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq or Yemen triggers long extra checks.

Israel does not stamp passports: at the border you get a light-blue slip (Form 294) with your visa category, the only proof that your stay is legal. Keep it in your passport until you leave and photograph it straight away.

Israeli banks (Hapoalim, Leumi, Discount) are built around the 9-digit citizen ID number, which B/1 and A/2 visa holders do not have: there is no online onboarding, so go to a branch with an international desk.

Work (B/1) and student (A/2) visas are single-entry: before any trip abroad, apply through the MyVisit app 21 to 30 days ahead for a re-entry visa (inter-visa, 205 NIS), or the visa lapses as you leave. Emergency extensions in wartime do not count as one.
B/1 and A/2 visas are single-entry: leave without a re-entry permit, requested 21 to 30 days ahead, and the visa is cancelled at the border. Automatic wartime extensions do not count as one.
Passports are not stamped: the blue entry slip is your only proof of legal stay. Keep it until you leave.
Security staff at Ben Gurion may ask to see phones and social media; past travel to Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Yemen or the West Bank means long questioning.
Without an Israeli ID number you cannot open a bank account online: it takes a branch with an international desk.

Whether the 500 permits for Israeli STEM graduates run out during the year.
Consular appointments in Rome for B/1 and A/2 visas take 2 to 8 weeks.
