The Kuwait Investment Authority’s Fresh Graduate Training Program, eleven months long with a ten-week international assignment and more than 600 alumni since 1995, is "designed for high-performing nationals"; applicants must be no older than 26 and hold a bachelor’s awarded within three years.

Kuwait Petroleum Corporation hires fresh graduates in non-engineering and non-science majors only through announced recruitment campaigns, which it says are "restricted to nationals"; engineering and science graduates apply through Kuwait Oil Company or Kuwait National Petroleum Company.
The 2021 census counted 4,385,717 people in Kuwait, 574,839 of them in the Capital governorate, which includes Kuwait City; Farwaniya (1,110,560) and Hawalli (926,170) were larger.

Employment contracts in Kuwait must be in Arabic, with a translation allowed, and the Kuwait Investment Authority asks its Kuwaiti applicants for proficiency in Arabic and English in reading, writing and conversation; no source read measured the language of work for foreign graduates.

Kuwait has no national graduate season: Kuwait Petroleum Corporation opens fresh-graduate campaigns only when it announces them, Zain’s 2026 graduate posting closed on 28 February 2026, the Australian University’s career fair was held on 16–17 October 2022 and on 24 October 2024, Kuwait University held its fair in July 2022, and a Career Fair at the Kuwait International Fair was listed for 9 September 2026; a foreign hire waits about 4 to 8 weeks for the work visa after a formal offer.

On 30 June 2026 unemployment among Kuwaiti citizens was 6.45% (31,794 people, up from 6.2% at the end of 2025) against 0.18% for expatriates; 80.1% of employed Kuwaitis worked in the public sector and non-Kuwaitis were 96.4% of the private-sector workforce; no graduate-specific figure was found.

Kuwait’s private sector runs almost entirely on foreign staff, 96.4% of its workforce in mid-2026, while 80.1% of employed Kuwaitis work for the government. Every graduate programme we could read (KIA, KPC, NBK Academy, the central bank’s programme, Zain) is for Kuwaitis only, so foreign graduates are hired by private firms mostly through recruiters and contacts, and the state is raising the cost of hiring expatriates for roles Kuwaitis could fill.
Direct application or recruiter for a sponsored private-sector job

No survey ranks the routes in Kuwait. Non-Kuwaitis are 96.4% of the private-sector workforce and 80.1% of employed Kuwaitis work for the government, so the private sector is where a foreign graduate is hired; Rivermate says a formal employment offer is needed to start the work visa, which usually takes about 4 to 8 weeks.
Roles Rivermate lists as in demand include software engineers, project managers, marketing specialists and digital marketing experts.
Personal introductions (wasta) and networking

An independent guide to working in Kuwait calls networking essential and says referrals and reputation, “often referred to in the region as wasta”, open doors that a CV cannot; it is one author’s account and its “85% of offers” claim is unsourced, so we do not use it.
University fairs

The Australian University (AU) in Kuwait held its career fair on 16–17 October 2022 with 60 companies, among them NBK, Kuwait Finance House, Gulf Bank, Boubyan, Kuwait Airways and Schlumberger as sponsors, and again on 24 October 2024 with over 60 organisations (the page gives no year; its files point to 2024), where students and graduates could hand in CVs and take part in on-the-spot interviews. Kuwait University ran a Human Capital Investment Exhibition and Career Fair for students and fresh graduates of all colleges in July 2022, with Zain as main sponsor; a Career Fair at the Kuwait International Fair on 9 September 2026 listed universities, oil, banks, insurance, telecom and government employers.
Graduate programmes for Kuwaitis

The Kuwait Investment Authority’s Fresh Graduate Training Program needs Kuwaiti nationality, an age of 26 or less, a bachelor’s from a recognised Kuwaiti institution within three years and a GMAT score; KPC’s fresh-graduate campaigns are restricted to Kuwaiti nationals; NBK Academy and the central bank’s Kuwait Graduate Development Program are built for Kuwaiti graduates; Zain Kuwait’s graduate posting required a copy of Kuwaiti nationality.
A foreign graduate cannot use any of them.
Government posts (for Kuwaitis)

Of 495,697 employed Kuwaitis on 30 June 2026, 397,165 (80.1%) worked in the public sector; the library’s visa guide says the state sector is almost entirely reserved for Kuwaiti citizens, with exceptions for specialist doctors, university teachers and top technical advisers.
Internships

The library’s visa guide finds no internship visa: an internship, even unpaid, on a tourist, business or visit visa counts as illegal work, with arrest and expulsion; the only exception is an unpaid curricular placement for students already resident in Kuwait. Zain’s 2026 summer programme took 30 interns for five weeks and was aimed at young Kuwaitis.

Kuwait has no national graduate season. KPC says applications open only when it announces a campaign in newspapers, on its website and on social media; the KIA page gives no application window; Zain’s graduate posting closed on 28 February 2026.

Fairs fall in autumn, at the start of the academic year, and in summer: the Australian University (AU) in Kuwait on 16–17 October 2022 and 24 October 2024, Kuwait University’s fair in July 2022 and the Kuwait International Fair’s Career Fair on 9 September 2026.

For a foreign hire the timetable is the visa: Rivermate puts the work visa at about 4 to 8 weeks after a formal offer, and the library counts 3 to 5 weeks for the Public Authority for Manpower and Interior Ministry steps before travel.

The Australian University (AU) in Kuwait, whose fairs drew 60 companies in October 2022 and over 60 organisations in October 2024, and Kuwait University, whose fair is run by its admissions deanship for students and fresh graduates of all colleges, are the two Kuwaiti universities whose employer fairs we could read; GUST and AUM are other accredited universities the library names.

Foreign universities do not recruit here, and we found no ranking of schools by Kuwaiti employers. Law 78 of 2019 punishes use of foreign degrees not recognised by the Ministry of Higher Education with up to five years in prison, so accreditation matters more than brand.

Career Fair at the Kuwait International Fair, Mishref: 9 September 2026, with universities, banks, oil, insurance, telecom, airline and government participants; the listing does not name the organiser or the entry terms.

Australian University (AU) Career Fair: 24 October 2024, over 60 organisations (platinum sponsors included Kuwait Petroleum Corporation, Kuwait Finance House and Gulf Bank); the earlier fair was 16–17 October 2022 with 60 companies. We found no announcement of the next date, so check the university.
Zain Summer Program, 7th edition: five weeks, 30 interns in 22 branches, closing ceremony reported on 12 August 2026, aimed at young Kuwaitis.
Banks are among the private employers most pressed to hire Kuwaitis; foreign graduates are hired mainly into specialist and experienced roles.

The bank-linked graduate programmes read are for Kuwaitis: NBK Academy (seven months, January to August 2023, for Kuwaiti fresh graduates) and the central bank’s one-year Kuwait Graduate Development Program run through the Institute of Banking Studies. A 2026 guide says banks must keep at least 70% Kuwaiti staff but gives no date and warns the rules change.

KPC hires fresh graduates in non-engineering and non-science majors through announced campaigns restricted to Kuwaiti nationals, with a two-year onboarding programme; engineering and science graduates apply through Kuwait Oil Company or Kuwait National Petroleum Company.

Of the 495,697 Kuwaitis employed on 30 June 2026, 80.1% worked for the government; the private sector is 96.4% non-Kuwaiti, and unemployment among Kuwaiti citizens was 6.45% against 0.18% for expatriates.
IT roles open to foreigners are advertised mostly for experienced staff, with visa sponsorship; there is no graduate pipeline for non-nationals.

Zain Kuwait’s “Technical Opportunities for Recent Graduates” posting (closing date 28 February 2026) asked for a bachelor’s in MIS, engineering, telecom engineering or computer science, some internship exposure and a copy of Kuwaiti nationality from Sahel.
There is no national season for foreign hires: employers recruit when a post opens, KPC opens campaigns only when it announces them, and the visa takes about 4 to 8 weeks after an offer.
The programmes read ask for a bachelor’s (KIA: awarded within three years, GPA of 3.00 and a GMAT score); none requires a master’s. This is our reading.

Kuwait is not party to the Hague Apostille Convention: a foreign degree needs the traditional consular legalisation chain, and the Ministry of Higher Education issues the equivalence certificate (Moadala); Law 78 of 2019 punishes use of unrecognised foreign degrees with up to five years in prison. Engineers are verified through the ministry and the Public Authority for Manpower.
The programmes read set a GPA of 3.00 or higher (KIA) and accredited institutions (Ministry of Higher Education); we found no ranking of schools by employers. This is our reading.
We found no apprenticeship or dual-study route into graduate jobs; the library finds no internship visa for foreigners. This is our reading.
80.1% of employed Kuwaitis (397,165 of 495,697) worked in the public sector on 30 June 2026, but it is almost entirely closed to foreigners.

Foreign staff are 96.4% of the private-sector workforce, so private employers do sponsor, but entry-level expatriate hiring is the first target of the localisation policy and each work permit needs a Public Authority for Manpower approval and a 150 KWD recruitment fee. See Visas for the rules.
Zain Kuwait’s graduate application asks for a CV, a passport-size photograph, the highest qualification and a copy of the Civil ID or passport; this is one employer’s form.
No page we read states a CV length for Kuwait; we assume the regional default of up to two pages. This is our reading.
The Zain, KIA and KPC application flows read run on an online portal with tests and a form, with no cover letter mentioned. This is our reading.
None of the application pages read asks for references up front; KPC makes its offer conditional on pre-employment requirements under Kuwaiti labour law. This is our reading.

The library’s guide asks for the degree and a police-clearance certificate (issued within three months) translated into Arabic and legalised through the consular chain, with the Foreign Ministry stamp in Kuwait; the work contract must be in Arabic, with a translation allowed.
None of the application pages read asks for a salary expectation; the contract states salary in KWD, allowances and notice terms. We did not establish how often recruiters ask. This is our reading.

The state does the checking for a foreign hire: a legalised police-clearance certificate, a medical screening at the Ministry of Health and fingerprints at the Interior Ministry before residence is issued; KPC adds pre-employment requirements for nationals.
Personal recommendation (wasta) and recruiters carry most hiring.

A foreign hire can be recruited from abroad: the employer files the Public Authority for Manpower approval and the Interior Ministry entry visa (3 to 5 weeks), then the medical, fingerprints and Civil ID follow in Kuwait within 60 days of entry; no work or internship can start on a visit visa.

The contract language is Arabic by law, with a translation allowed; KIA asks for proficiency in Arabic and English. For foreign staff in banks and multinationals English is the working language, but no source measured it. This is our reading.

KPC’s fresh-graduate process has five stages: an announced campaign, a preliminary review, assessment tests, a personal interview and a conditional offer after pre-employment checks; the page gives no timing, test format or language. KIA applicants who meet the requirements take an assessment test on finance, accounting and economics.

Zain Kuwait’s graduate application starts with account registration and uploads of a CV, photograph, qualification and ID copies. These are the nationals’ flows; we found no page describing interviews, assessment centres or dress norms for foreign graduates.

Rivermate (6 August 2026): probation is at most 100 working days and cannot be repeated for the same role, and either party can end the contract in it without notice; notice is generally three months for monthly-paid staff; end-of-service pay starts after one year at 15 days’ salary per year for the first five years, then one month per year.

A written contract is mandatory and its official language is Arabic, with a translation allowed; it states duties, workplace, salary in KWD, allowances, hours, leave and notice. The guide gives a 48-hour week, 36 in Ramadan, and 30 paid days of annual leave after six months, but is inconsistent on hours, so verify. The employer pays the recruitment fee, visa, residence and medical costs. We did not establish whether graduates negotiate or how long employers give to decide.

The employer needs an active file with the Public Authority for Manpower, a Kuwaitisation quota in good standing and prior approval to recruit from abroad; the recruitment fee is 150 KWD per new permit and the library counts about 305 KWD of first-year government costs, all on the employer. Fines for missing Kuwaitisation targets were reported in 2024 as set to rise from 100 to 300 KWD, with proposed rates of 50% in oil and about 30% in other sectors.

Because the private sector is 96.4% non-Kuwaiti, employers do hire foreigners, but the state is pressing them to replace expatriates where Kuwaitis could do the job, and a 2026 legal guide says banks must keep at least 70% Kuwaiti staff and other sectors between 1% and 30%, without dating it. Ask early who sponsors, which entity employs you and whether the post is inside a quota. This is our reading for the last point.

Employer portals: KPC’s recruitment portal (recruitment.kpc.com.kw), the Kuwait Investment Authority’s portal (portal.kia.gov.kw) and Zain Kuwait’s careers site (careers.zain.com); all three are for Kuwaiti graduates. We could not open the pages of the Big Four, KOC or the other banks.

Fairs and universities: the Australian University (AU) in Kuwait’s fair, Kuwait University’s fair and the Career Fair at the Kuwait International Fair; the Public Authority for Manpower, which was a silver sponsor at the 2022 AU fair, supervises work permits and quotas.
Applying to the national programmes (KIA, KPC campaigns, NBK Academy, the central bank’s programme, Zain’s graduate posting) as a foreign graduate: they require Kuwaiti nationality.
Starting an internship or trial work on a visit or tourist visa: the library says it is illegal work, with arrest, detention and expulsion with a ban across the Gulf states.
Relying on an Apostille: Kuwait is not party to the Hague Convention, so a degree or police certificate with only an Apostille is rejected and needs the consular chain.
Handing over your passport to the employer: the library notes the law bans employers from keeping it without written consent, yet many ask; do not give it up without a formal receipt.
Missing the 60-day deadline after entry to finish residence: the library cites daily fines of 2 KWD in the first month and 4 KWD after, up to 1,200 KWD.
The Kuwait Investment Authority asks its Kuwaiti applicants for proficiency in Arabic and English in reading, writing and conversation; we found no bank page stating a level for foreign graduates.

Employment contracts must be in Arabic by law, with a translation allowed, and Rivermate notes that local graduates are often fluent in both Arabic and English. For foreign staff in multinationals English is the working language, but no source measured it. This is our reading.
Government posts are almost entirely reserved for Kuwaiti citizens, so Arabic is the working language there; no page gave a level. This is our reading.
Zain Kuwait’s graduate posting asks for strong communication skills and does not state a language level; IT roles for foreigners are mostly for experienced staff. This is our reading.

On 30 June 2026 unemployment among Kuwaiti citizens was 6.45% (31,794 people, up from 6.2% at the end of 2025) against 0.18% for expatriates. We found no graduate-specific figure, return-offer rate or time to first job for Kuwait.

Kuwaiti workers in the private sector were about 72,800 at the end of June 2024 against about 404,900 in government; by June 2026 the Kuwait Times figures imply about 98,500 in the private sector, a rise driven by the localisation policy. This second step is our reading.

Student residence (Article 23)

A university accredited by the higher-education ministry, such as Kuwait University, GUST or AUK, sponsors the visa. Kuwait is not in the Apostille Convention: diplomas and records need full consular legalisation, with wet-ink signatures.
Paid work off campus is forbidden.

visa 10 KWD; residence 20 KWD a year; health insurance 100 KWD a year

Kuwait has no visa for interns. An internship on a tourist, business or visit visa, even unpaid, is illegal work leading to detention and expulsion; only students already resident may do unpaid curricular placements.
After graduating
There is no grace period. A graduate with a formal offer before the student residence is cancelled can move straight to a private-sector work residence; otherwise you must leave.
Private-sector work residence (Article 18)
The employer obtains the work permit and entry visa; within 60 days of arrival come the medical, fingerprints, residence and Civil ID. The employer pays all first-year fees by law.
Engineers need degree equivalency from the higher-education ministry, doctors the Kuwait licensing exam; enter with a downgraded job title and it cannot be corrected later.
Employer, first year
You cannot move to a new employer in the first three years without the current sponsor’s written consent.
Research visits and contracts

Unpaid archive work, interviews or seminars up to 90 days can be done on a tourist eVisa; structured research at KISR or Kuwait University needs a visit visa from the host, and paid research beyond 90 days a government contract. PhD students are students; KFAS or KISR funding makes them employees.
Working holiday
Kuwait has no working-holiday agreements; working, even remotely for foreign clients, on a tourist visa leads to arrest and expulsion.
Tourist eVisa
EU and UK citizens get an eVisa or visa on arrival for up to 90 days, with no work. A visit visa can become residence only exceptionally, with a 150 KWD surcharge.

Kuwait is not in the apostille convention: have your criminal record (under 3 months old) translated into Arabic and fully legalised at the Kuwaiti consulate in Milan or embassy in Rome (€25 a stamp), then countersigned by the Foreign Ministry in Kuwait (5 KWD a document).
Since an inactive lung scar counts as unfit, a high-resolution chest X-ray at home before you resign or pay for the move is a prudent check.
Entering on the work entry visa starts a 60-day deadline to complete residence. You may not start work, even informally, before the Civil ID or its digital version is issued.
A positive or doubtful result in the medical screening, including healed tuberculosis scars, means deportation and a lifetime ban from all Gulf states.
Register with the civil information authority (PACI) for the Civil ID: the digital ID appears at once in the Hawiti app, and the chip card costs 5.250 KWD.

After arriving, have the compulsory medical screening at the Ministry of Health centres in Shuwaikh or Sabhan, and pay the state health insurance (100 KWD a year, or 130 KWD through Dhaman); for workers the employer pays.
The Central Bank has frozen the cards and accounts of anyone who did not complete the biometric registration with the Interior Ministry; salaries are paid through the Wages Protection System.
Any old scar or calcification on the chest X-ray is treated as TB: medically unfit, deportation and a lifelong Gulf ban, with no appeal. Get a chest X-ray at home first.
An employer can file an “absence” report: the Civil ID is revoked, accounts frozen and a travel ban imposed.

At the end of 2025, 248 fintech companies operated in Lithuania with about 7,800 employees; 231 of them were in Vilnius, and Lithuania ranks first in the EU by fintech licences issued.

Lithuania’s business-service centres employ more than 27,000 people in 100 companies, 37% of them for US-headquartered organisations and 36% in tech roles; brands include Danske Bank, Nasdaq, Western Union, SEB and Moody’s.

Eurostat counts 278,880 people in work in the Kaunas metropolitan region in 2021: 9,890 in information and communication (second in Lithuania, after Vilnius) and 2,560 in finance and insurance. The region’s GDP was €11.7 billion in 2021.

Hubs added on 3 October 2026 are rated only from Eurostat’s 2021–22 metropolitan employment counts: strong means second or third in the country for jobs in finance and insurance, or in information and communication, with at least 5,000 such jobs.

A small market centred on Vilnius, which has about two-thirds of the country’s ICT jobs and nearly three-quarters of its finance jobs: fintech, where Lithuania issues more licences than any other EU country, and business-service centres for Nordic banks and US firms. Non-EU graduates can stay 12 months to look for work, but rules for students were tightened in May 2026.
Tax, recruiting calendars, graduate programmes and language requirements were not researched; pay is Statistics Lithuania’s averages by sector and place, not entry pay.

Country brief: hubs, employers, pay and standing
Eurostat counts 33,980 people employed in information and communication in the Vilnius metropolitan region in 2021, 67% of Lithuania’s 50,860, and 22,380 in finance and insurance, 73% of 30,530.
In 2025 ICT specialists were 5.7% of employment in Lithuania (83,100 people), against 5.0% in the EU.

In 2025 the average gross monthly wage in Lithuania was €2,411, €4,168 in information and communication and €3,848 in finance and insurance; in Vilnius County the three figures were €2,656, €4,359 and €3,997, and in Kaunas County €2,416, €3,715 and €3,362.
Swedbank AB gives its address as Konstitucijos pr. 20A, Vilnius.
Vinted says more than 2,000 people work from its headquarters in Lithuania and offices across Europe; its careers page lists roles in Vilnius and other Lithuanian locations.
Nord Security’s careers page speaks of its Vilnius headquarters and lists offices in Vilnius, Kaunas and Madrid.
Startup Genome’s 2026 report puts the Vilnius ecosystem’s value at $8 billion, against a European average of $14.3 billion.
The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) lists Vilnius (34 assessments) and Kaunas (15) only as associate centres, too few assessments for a rank.
Vilnius University ranks 465th in the QS World University Rankings 2027, the highest of any Lithuanian university.

Invest Lithuania describes Kaunas University of Technology as the largest provider of qualified engineers in the country and Kaunas’ free economic zone as a hub of logistics and advanced manufacturing; 36% of Kaunas’ 50,000 students study engineering, manufacturing and construction.

In 2025, 92.7% of Lithuanian tertiary graduates aged 20–34 who finished within the last three years were in work (EU 85.3%), unemployment among 15-to-24-year-olds was 14.1% (EU 15.2%), and 60.8% of 25-to-34-year-olds had a tertiary degree (EU 44.8%).
Invest Lithuania reports that 58% of Lithuanian fintechs employ international staff in their Lithuanian offices, so fintech and service-centre work is possible in English.

The bank and Big Four postings read for Vilnius ask for Lithuanian as well as English: a Luminor graduate programme (fluent English and Lithuanian), an EY audit internship (English and Lithuanian) and a KPMG Baltics internship (fluent Lithuanian and effective English).
Swedbank’s Kick Start traineeships in the Baltic countries are open all year, and the bank is actively hiring trainees and junior specialists from February to May.
Vilnius University’s student-run VU Career Days ran from 23 to 27 March 2026, with the career fair and quick job interviews on 24 and 25 March and more than 70 companies.
The Vilnius Tech Career Day, now in its 23rd year, promotes registration for the 2027 edition; its page gives no date.

Vilnius hires graduates mainly into its fintech firms and global service centres: 248 fintech companies employed about 7,800 people at the end of 2025 (231 of them in Vilnius), and the business-service centres employ more than 27,000, many in jobs that are advertised in English. Banks and the Big Four also recruit, but their postings usually ask for Lithuanian as well.
Fintech firms and service centres

Fintechs are the growth door: 77% of them plan to expand their teams in 2026, 58% already employ international staff in their Lithuanian offices, and the sector counts about 14,000 compliance and risk specialists. The business-service centres employ more than 27,000, 36% of them in tech roles.

Revolut, Shift4 (its largest European tech centre is in Vilnius) and Western Union, SEB and Nasdaq are among the names Invest Lithuania lists; SEB’s Vilnius centre said in 2016 that it recruits social-science graduates and students every year.
Bank trainee and graduate programmes

Swedbank’s Kick Start takes around 200 trainees a year across the Baltic countries, hires most actively from February to May, and offers a fixed-term contract at €1,200–1,800 gross a month in Lithuania. A Luminor 12-month graduate programme in corporate banking in Vilnius (a 2023 posting) paid €1,900 gross and asked for fluent English and Lithuanian.
Paid internships at the Big Four and tech teams

Internship adverts show the going rate and the language: an EY audit internship in Vilnius paid €1,100 gross a month and listed English and Lithuanian (the advert expired in December 2024), and a KPMG Baltics ERP internship paid €1,153 gross a month and asked for fluent Lithuanian and effective English.
The KTU WANTed platform lists internships by faculty with a paid or unpaid flag and the number of places, which makes it a good place to see how many are unpaid.
University career days and fairs

Vilnius University’s student-run VU Career Days ran from 23 to 27 March 2026 with more than 70 companies, a career fair and quick job interviews on 24 and 25 March; the Vilnius Tech Career Day is in its 23rd year with 100 participating organisations and more than 10,000 visitors, and registration for the 2027 edition is open.
State-funded internships for international students (2024 round)

The UPinLT programme paid international students and recent graduates €650 a month for additional internships at Lithuanian organisations; the Vilnius University round ran from 1 February to 31 August 2024. A later Vilnius University scholarship of €650 a month for a two-month internship in 2026, for final-year master’s students, had closed its applications by October 2026.
Working while you study

Under the 22 May 2026 amendments as the library’s visa guide reads them, non-EU students with a study permit work without a separate work permit: first- and second-year bachelor’s students are capped at 20 hours a week, while master’s and PhD students can work 40.
Speculative applications and contacts

The University of Magdeburg’s guide for interns says to use your network first and calls a speculative application to the local office you want to join fairly successful; with personal contacts the formal cover letter may be replaced by a phone call or an email, although online applications are becoming more common.
Open ads and job portals (the experienced hire)

CVbankas listed 8,828 offers on 8 October 2026 (with pay ranges shown, a working-time filter for internships and popular searches for “no experience”, “internship” and “for students”); CV-Online listed 1,803 job ads, 958 of them in Vilnius and 14 internships; CV.lt shows the newest ads with no student section.

Lithuania is a small market that follows the financial and tech cycle: in 2025, 92.7% of recent graduates were in work (EU 85.3%) while youth unemployment was 14.1%, so the door is open for graduates but narrow for school-leavers.

Banks’ operations centres (SEB, Swedbank, Luminor) and the fintechs licensed in Vilnius, Revolut among them, hire graduates into compliance, risk and operations; the sector counts about 14,000 compliance and risk specialists. The bank programmes we read asked for Lithuanian as well as English.
Audit and accounting interns at EY and KPMG are advertised at about €1,100 to €1,150 gross a month, with Lithuanian and English both listed.
The country counts around 78,000 ICT specialists, and nine dedicated fintech study pathways run across universities and colleges; Shift4’s Vilnius office is its largest European tech centre.
Nord Security, founded in Vilnius, became Lithuania’s second unicorn in April 2022; we found no graduate-programme page for it.

Vilnius University and Vilnius Tech run the two large career events in the capital, and the Kaunas University of Technology runs the WANTed internship platform; employers recruit from all three through fairs and faculty postings.

VU Career Days (Vilnius University, 23 to 27 March 2026: fair, quick interviews, a LinkedIn workshop in English and a hackathon) and the Vilnius Tech Career Day (23rd edition, registration for 2027 open).

No national season; the peaks follow the student year: Swedbank hires trainees most actively from February to May, VU Career Days are in March, and the Luminor programme we read closed its applications on 30 May.
The programmes we read take a bachelor’s or a master’s (Luminor asked for a BSc or MSc with 0 to 3 years of experience) and Swedbank states no degree level; none asks for a master’s.

Only regulated professions need recognition: the competent authority decides within three months of receiving all documents and can require an adaptation period of up to three years or an aptitude test; documents are translated into Lithuanian with a certified translation. Where Lithuania does not regulate the profession, you apply directly to the employer. SKVC is the ENIC/NARIC centre for academic recognition.
Vilnius University, Vilnius Tech and the Kaunas University of Technology are the schools whose career events and platforms employers use; no programme we read names a target school.

There is no apprenticeship track for graduates; the equivalent is the curricular internship under a three-party agreement between student, university and company, and an extracurricular volunteer internship for under-29s is capped at two consecutive months and unpaid.

We could not open the Civil Service or Employment Service pages, so we have no figure for the public sector’s share of graduate hires; the fintech and service-centre numbers (7,800 and 27,000) show where most graduate hiring we could count happens.

The 2026 quota for non-EU workers (24,706) was used up on 7 September 2026, after which a permit needs a salary of at least €2,893.68 gross a month (€2,411.40 for shortage occupations); 58% of fintechs already employ international staff. The rules are on the Visas page.
The guides we read disagree on photos and none is official; leave it out unless the advert asks for one.

The University of Magdeburg’s guide calls the CV a marketing tool for getting an interview: list only relevant education, mention your English and other languages, use a clear layout with brief entries. We found no page that states a page limit; one to two pages is the usual advice.
The same guide says the cover letter should be short (maximum one page) and typed, and should say why you want this particular position.
The guide does not put references in the CV; it advises bringing copies of references and diplomas to the interview.
Bring copies of diplomas and references to the interview; certified translations are needed for degree recognition in a regulated profession, not for ordinary applications.

Since 27 July 2019 every job advert must state the base salary, as an amount or a range, whether it is gross or net, and the highest pay for the position; breaches can be fined €80 to €880. We found no page on whether application forms ask for your expectation.
We found no page on background checks in Lithuanian graduate hiring; banks and the public sector can be expected to check more.

Both work: the Magdeburg guide calls a speculative application to the local office fairly successful and says online applications are becoming more common; the portals and company career pages carry the advertised roles.
The portals and Swedbank’s steps are online and the fintechs recruit internationally; a non-EU hire from abroad needs a permit first, and the quota is already used up for 2026.

Many roles in Vilnius do not require Lithuanian, especially at multinationals, and the fintechs and service centres work in English; the bank programmes and Big Four internships we read listed Lithuanian as well, and local firms and the public sector require it.

Swedbank’s steps are an application on its recruitment portal, calls with a recruiter or interviews with a manager or mentors (possibly with job-related tests or tasks), and then a fixed-term contract; some roles ask for answers in video format.

The Magdeburg guide says the interview is the most important part of the application in Lithuania: look interested, ask questions, back up achievements with examples, wait to be invited to sit and never criticise former employers.
We found no page on assessment-centre norms, online tests at the banks and the Big Four, or the time from application to offer.

Probation is optional and generally cannot exceed three months; one guide allows up to six months for senior management and staff who handle financial or commercial secrets. Either side may end it with three working days’ written notice if the results are unsatisfactory, and a fixed-term contract under six months gets a proportionally shorter probation.
First contracts for trainees are fixed-term (Swedbank’s Kick Start at €1,200–1,800 gross a month); the advert must state gross or net pay, so check which one the quoted figure is.
We did not find a page on negotiating, a thirteenth month, notice after probation or the time employers give you to decide, so treat these as unknown rather than as customs.

Luxembourg-domiciled UCITS funds held €6.69 trillion of net assets in June 2026, €9.07 trillion including alternative funds, up about 20% in twelve months.
Expats rank Luxembourg 4th in the 2026 Working Abroad Index and 1st for job security.

In 2022 employees under 30 in Luxembourg firms with 10 or more staff (public administration excluded) earned a mean of €48,369 gross a year, and those under 30 working as professionals €60,726, against €74,542 for all ages.

In 2025 the employment rate of Luxembourg residents aged 20 to 34 with a tertiary degree was 90.5% (88.2% for those who finished within the last five years); unemployment was 6.5% overall, 21.6% for the 15-to-24s in 2024, and GDP was €89.5 billion.

The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) ranks Luxembourg 17th in the world (down 1 place) and fourth in Western Europe after London, Zurich and Geneva; in the investment-management sector table it is second in the world, behind Hong Kong, and it is 12th for banking.

Luxembourg has 510,990 jobs (2023): 115,420 of them in public administration, defence, education and health, 90,490 in professional, scientific, technical and administrative services, 54,220 in finance and insurance and 22,730 in information and communication.

Of the 152 metropolitan regions for which Eurostat publishes jobs by sector (latest year, 2021 or 2022; German, British and Swiss regions are not in the table), Luxembourg has the 11th-most jobs in finance and insurance (53,040, just behind Brussels with 63,000) and the 45th-most in information and communication (21,830).
The European Investment Bank says it has more than 4,000 employees in Luxembourg and in offices around the world.
The CSSF, Luxembourg’s financial-sector supervisor, says it has over 950 employees working in many specialised departments.

Startup Genome’s 2026 report puts the value of Luxembourg’s start-up ecosystem at $4 billion (Europe’s average $14.3 billion), with $271 million of seed and Series A funding in H2 2023–2025 and $1 billion of exits in 2021–2025.

Luxembourg recruits from abroad by necessity: about 47% of employees commute from France, Belgium and Germany. Graduate hiring is dominated by the Big Four and the fund industry, which take large intakes every year, mostly from internships and graduate applications.
There is no national season, but the large firms hire in waves: the Big Four peak in September and January, and the European Investment Bank takes trainees in two intakes a year.
Big Four graduate intakes
The four firms employ about 9,100 people in Luxembourg; in 2022 their recruitment targets ran from about 500 to 910 each.

Hiring peaks in September and January and targets graduates as well as experienced people; Deloitte and KPMG use online assessments of analytical skills followed by several interviews. English and French are described as essential.
Internship under an agreement

A practical internship needs an agreement and is open to enrolled students and to people who finished secondary school or a first higher-education cycle (Bachelor, BTS); in the last two cases the whole internship must fall within 12 months after the last enrolment. It cannot exceed 6 months in 24 with the same host.

Pay is set by law: from 4 weeks, at least 40% of the unskilled minimum social wage for 4 to 12 weeks and 75% for over 12 to 26 weeks; for holders of a Bachelor or BTS the reference is the skilled minimum wage.
Direct application and job fairs

Applications go through employer portals and boards such as jobs.lu, which lists a "Graduate" and an "Internship" category and shows the vacancies in English, French and German. In 2025 the national employment agency ADEM passed more than 123,000 candidate profiles to employers and organised 106 job fairs.
Moovijob Day, held on 20 March 2026 at Luxexpo The Box, had more than 150 companies confirmed and is open to anyone, including students, for jobs and internships.
EU institutions and the civil service

The European Investment Bank takes trainees in two intakes a year, March-April and September-October, announced about 4 months ahead; they must be in their final year or have less than 1 year of work experience, be EU or candidate-country nationals and be proficient in English and/or French.

The state recruits civil servants by competitive exam: candidates must be nationals of an EU state and show sufficient Luxembourgish, French and German; in general administration the general aptitude test stays valid for 5 years, and posts are listed on GovJobs.lu.

The job market has softened since the post-pandemic peak: ADEM reports unemployment of 6.2% at the end of 2025 and 6.3% at the end of March 2026, and vacancies well below their earlier highs, although employment passed 530,000 in March 2026 and about 143,000 new contracts were signed in 2025.
Fund administration, depositary, compliance and risk work hire juniors in large numbers and train them; English is the main working language in the financial sector.
The Big Four are among the country’s largest employers, about 9,100 people, and take hundreds of graduates a year into audit and advisory, many of them from France, Belgium and Germany.

The European Investment Bank (more than 4,000 staff in Luxembourg and worldwide) and the financial supervisor CSSF (over 950 staff, recruiting from entry level to senior) are the main public-interest employers for finance graduates.
IT roles sit mostly in banks, fund administrators and the Big Four, which need people who understand both regulation and systems; English is enough in most of them.
No single school is the gate: employers draw on graduates from France, Belgium, Germany and well beyond, so the degree and the language mix count more than a school ranking.

Moovijob Day (20 March 2026, Luxexpo The Box, more than 150 companies) is the largest job fair; the Big Four and the EIB announce their own intakes and events on their careers pages, and ADEM organised 106 job fairs in 2025.
The Big Four’s hiring peaks in September and January, and the EIB takes trainees in March-April and September-October, with intakes announced about 4 months ahead.

The pages read name no degree level for entry roles: the EIB takes final-year students and graduates with less than 1 year of work experience, and the Big Four take graduates into audit and advisory. A master’s is common but not the stated condition.

Recognition matters for regulated professions; for other jobs employers read the degree, and foreign documents may need a certified translation. Expatica names the Ministry of Education, Children and Youth for academic qualifications and the Department for the Recognition of Diplomas for professional ones.
Employers recruit across the border and abroad, so the CV and the language mix count rather than a short list of schools.
The graduate route runs through internships and graduate intakes, not dual study; the pages read describe no dual-degree programme for graduates.

Of 510,990 jobs in 2023, 115,420 were in public administration, defence, education and health (Eurostat). The state recruits by competitive exam in the three administrative languages, and the EIB and the CSSF recruit separately.

Employers are used to hiring non-residents, but a non-EU graduate needs a permit. The EU Blue Card asks for a gross salary of at least €65,652 a year (for applications from 3 March 2026), a contract of at least 6 months and the qualifications the job needs. See Visas for the rules.
A photo is not required; it is acceptable in some sectors and many international companies expect none. Expatica still advises a passport-sized photo, top right.

One A4 page, or one to two pages; entry-level candidates can stay on one, and a second page is for highly qualified or experienced people. Write it in the language of the job posting and list language levels on the CEFR scale.
A concise cover letter explaining your motivation and what you would bring to the role is recommended, submitted with the CV through the online portal or by email.
Some companies ask for references from previous employers early; others ask for additional documents such as diplomas or references later. Keep reference letters ready in English and/or French.
Include a copy of your diploma if you studied in Luxembourg; list each degree with institution, country and year, and expect foreign documents to need a certified translation in some cases.
Salary is usually discussed in the first or second interview stage, often with the interviewer asking about your expectations; research typical pay first.
Employers can ask for diplomas and references at a later stage, and a language level may be tested in the interview; the pages read describe no routine background screening.
Applications to the large firms work through their portals and events; the EIB considers only applications for advertised positions. Networking also helps with smaller employers.
Employers are used to hiring people from abroad and from across the border: about 47% of employees are cross-border commuters and another 26% are foreign residents.

English and French for the Big Four; French, German or Luxembourgish for about half of all postings in one recruiter’s estimate (English named by the other half), and all three administrative languages for the civil service.

Expect four or five rounds of phone, online and in-person interviews of about 30 to 60 minutes each; confirm the interview language in advance and use formal address ("vous") in French. Deloitte and KPMG start with an online assessment of analytical skills and then hold several interviews.
The EIB process is screening, interview and additional tests for shortlisted candidates, then an offer; only applications for advertised positions are considered.

Civil service posts need a competitive exam: in general administration the general aptitude test (EAG) stays valid for 5 years, followed by a ministry-specific test for each post; language tests in Luxembourgish, French and German come first.

Probation is 2 weeks at least and at most 6 months for graduates (3 months for those without a CATP/DAP-level qualification, 12 months from a high gross monthly salary, €4,938.75 in the source read); it must be in the contract, and during the first 2 weeks neither side can end it without agreement.

After probation, an employer’s notice is 2 months under 5 years of service, 4 months from 5 to under 10 years and 6 months from 10 years; an employee’s notice when resigning is 1, 2 or 3 months for the same bands. Severance applies from 5 years of service.
Salary is discussed in the first or second interview, usually when the interviewer asks your expectations; check the contract for any thirteenth month, since the pages read do not state one.
Employers hire widely from abroad: about 47% of employees commute across the border and another 26% are foreign residents, so recruiters are used to cross-border and relocation questions.

For non-EU graduates the highly qualified route is the EU Blue Card: a gross salary of at least €65,652 a year for applications from 3 March 2026, a contract of at least 6 months and the qualifications the job needs. A job below that pay level needs a different permit.
What an employer wants to hear is that your right to work is settled or how it will be: say it in the first message, with the contract length and pay the Blue Card needs.

Employers to look up: the Big Four’s Luxembourg offices, the European Investment Bank (job portal erecruitment.eib.org, traineeships and GRAD programmes) and the CSSF careers site.
Applying in the wrong language: write the CV and letter in the language of the job posting, and do not overstate your language level, which may be tested in the interview.
Missing the internship window: a practical internship after a Bachelor or BTS must fall wholly within 12 months after the last enrolment, so waiting a year loses the route.
Assuming the civil service is open in English: candidates must show sufficient Luxembourgish, French and German, and some posts need Luxembourg nationality.
The Big Four describe fluency in English and French as essential, and German or Luxembourgish as improving prospects.

English is the main working language in the financial sector; the national picture is mixed, with French, German or Luxembourgish named in about half of all postings in one recruiter’s April 2026 estimate and English in the other half.
IT roles sit in banks, fund administrators and the Big Four, where English is enough in most.
The civil service requires sufficient knowledge of Luxembourgish, French and German, at a level that depends on the pay group; the EIB asks for English and/or French.

The hub is the island’s built-up core around Valletta’s two harbours: employer addresses run from Valletta and Sliema to Birkirkara and Santa Venera, and statistics are for the island of Malta or the country, since none is published for the harbour towns alone.

The gaming regulator and Eurostat count jobs, not role families: finance is rated from the sector’s share of jobs and output and from named bank headquarters, information technology from Eurostat’s share of jobs in information and communication; gaming itself is not a role family and the report does not say how many gaming jobs are technical or commercial.

Pay is Eurostat’s 2022 survey for the whole country (older than 2023, no split for graduates or by region); there is no rent, because no citable rent source (the Housing Authority’s rent tools included) was available, and no official one-bedroom rent was found.

Graduate programmes were read for Deloitte and KPMG only, without intake sizes or dates; no page was read for the banks, PwC, EY or the gaming operators, and the National Statistics Office figures were not available to cite.
Startup Genome has no Malta ecosystem page and no start-up ranking of Malta was read; no university ranking was read.
All Maltese immigration, visa, residence permit and salary rules are consolidated from primary sources in visas_immigration/malta/malta_visas_immigration_guide.md.

At the end of June 2025, 304 companies held 312 gaming licences from the Malta Gaming Authority and employed 14,797 full-time equivalents working in Malta.

At the end of 2025, 302 companies held 311 gaming licences from the Malta Gaming Authority and employed 15,039 full-time equivalents working in Malta (14,357 a year earlier); the authority estimates 19,150 jobs directly or indirectly tied to gaming, about 6.5% of the national workforce, and the sector’s gross value added at €1,422 million, about 6.3% of Malta’s output.
Eurostat counts 532,997 residents on 1 January 2025 in the island of Malta (NUTS 3 region MT001, 93% of the country’s 574,250) and a GDP of €22.1 billion in 2024 (96% of Malta’s €23.1 billion).
In 2025 Malta had 338,190 people in employment: 16,250 in information and communication (4.8%, against 3.5% in the EU) and 17,100 in finance and insurance (5.1%, against 2.3% in the EU).
Malta’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 3.4% in August 2026, and 9.7% for under-25s, against 6.1% and 15.4% in the EU.
In 2025, 92.8% of Maltese tertiary graduates aged 20 to 34 who left education up to three years earlier were in work, against 85.3% in the EU.

In the 2022 structure of earnings survey, mean monthly gross earnings of Maltese employees in firms with ten or more staff were €2,080; €1,832 for those under 30, €2,749 in information and communication and €2,781 in finance and insurance, against annual mean earnings of €30,960 for all sectors and €39,711 and €39,899 in those two sectors.

In the Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) Malta ranks 63rd in the world, down five places, is profiled among the “international specialists” and is outside the Western European top 15; for fintech it is 89th, up 12 places.

In 2025 financial and insurance activities generated about €1.3 billion of gross value added, 7.3% of Malta’s total (about 4% in the euro area), and employed about 6.2% of the national workforce at pay about 36% above the national average; the MFSA supervised 2,413 authorised entities with 575 staff, 45 of them students in its Pre-Graduate Programme, and partnered with the University of Malta on a postgraduate programme in financial regulation and compliance.

For 2026 a single resident pays no tax on the first €12,000 of taxable income, 15% from €12,001 to €16,000, 25% from €16,001 to €60,000 and 35% above that; employee and employer each pay social security of 10% of salary, at a fixed €55.93 a week for annual salaries above €29,084.

Deloitte Malta’s International Graduate Programme is for people who have recently graduated or are about to graduate in accounting, with work in its Audit & Assurance business in Malta, a salary package, a relocation allowance and a permanent contract; the page gives no pay figure or dates.
KPMG in Malta says it houses over 600 professionals in its offices in Pietà, including students enrolled in its Graduate Recruitment Programme.

FDJ UNITED says its sites in London (Kindred London Limited), Stockholm (Kindred People AB) and Malta (Kindred Group) support the group’s online betting and gaming operations and have ISO 14001 environmental certification.
Malta’s official EU languages are Maltese and English.
Bank of Valletta has its headquarters at Cannon Road, Zone 4, Central Business District, Santa Venera.
HSBC Bank Malta has its headquarters at 116 Archbishop Street, Valletta.
APS Bank has its headquarters at APS Centre, Tower Street, Birkirkara.
Lombard Bank Malta has its headquarters at 67 Republic Street, Valletta.
The Central Bank of Malta has its headquarters at Castille Place, Valletta.
The Malta Stock Exchange has its headquarters at the Garrison Chapel, Castille Place, Valletta.
Kindred Group plc has its headquarters at The Centre, Tigné Point, Sliema.

Malta is small and runs on reputation and word of mouth: recommendations in expat groups, coworking spaces and meet-ups often weigh more than job ads. Its iGaming, financial-services and tech firms need more people than the island supplies, so they hire foreigners in English.
Referrals and networks

Two Malta recruitment guides describe a market where recommendations and reputation carry real weight, and advise going to industry events, expat communities and LinkedIn. No survey puts a share on it, so the rank rests on practitioners’ accounts.
Agencies and job portals

Recruiters such as GRS Recruitment and Konnekt place people in iGaming, IT and financial services, and Jobsplus runs the national job portal, which feeds EURES. Many small and mid-sized employers screen CVs by hand, while some recruitment platforms parse them first.
iGaming and tech

Operators and suppliers recruit continuously, including for juniors in customer, compliance and marketing roles; industry events in Malta are frequent and are where many first contacts are made. Betsson’s Malta vacancy list shows customer roles that ask for German, Danish, Nordic or Lithuanian beside English.
Big Four and bank graduate programmes

Deloitte, PwC and KPMG run student and graduate programmes in Malta, and bet365 runs an 18-month Graduate Trainee scheme; Bank of Valletta invites students on a degree at MQF level 6 or above to its Graduates’ Programme. These are the structured entry points read, but none of the pages gives an intake size.
Internship to offer

The Malta Gaming Authority takes students from banking, business, technology, law and other fields for summer or longer placements, and Betsson offers a paid one-year infosec internship through MCAST. HSBC Malta’s summer interns come from the University of Malta, MCAST and JA Malta; no page read gives how many are hired.
Hired from abroad (experienced)

For a non-EU hire the employer advertises on Jobsplus and EURES first, for three weeks in the two months before applying (two weeks for the Key Employee Initiative, Specialist Employee Initiative, EU Blue Card and Skilled Occupation List). A Key Employee Initiative application is processed in 5 working days once all documents are uploaded.

There is no single graduate season. Deloitte Malta’s Graduate Programme takes people who finished their studies within the last year or finish within 12 months; its team was at the students’ union Freshers’ Week stand on 5–7 October 2026. A bet365 trainee listing ran only from 4 to 19 November 2025.
Internships follow the academic year: Betsson’s MCAST infosec internship is full time from July to September and part time, 10 to 20 hours a month, from October to May.

Employers name two local feeders: the University of Malta and MCAST. Deloitte’s student hub lists an Undergraduate Programme for university students and internship and apprenticeship programmes for MCAST students, and HSBC Malta’s summer interns came from the University, MCAST’s Institute of Business Management and Commerce, and JA Malta.

The students’ union (KSU) holds a Careers’ Expo on campus in spring (an exhibitor post is dated 10 March 2026); Bank of Valletta met students at a three-day Careers Expo at the University of Malta in March 2023.
iGaming industry events in Malta, such as those of SiGMA, are where many first contacts are made, and a Deloitte team member joins the KSU Freshers’ Week in early October.
The Big Four in Malta train graduates through sponsored ACCA programmes and have looked abroad, for example to Greek graduates, to fill places; the funds and gaming industries keep audit demand high.
Deloitte’s International Graduate Programme places recent accounting graduates in Audit & Assurance with a relocation allowance and a permanent contract, and you apply through its job search page.
Finance and insurance are 5.1% of Malta’s jobs, against 2.3% in the EU. Bank of Valletta runs a Graduates’ Programme, and HSBC Malta takes summer interns.

The MFSA had 575 staff in 2025, 45 of them students in its Pre-Graduate Programme, and works with the University of Malta on a postgraduate programme in financial regulation and compliance. The Malta Gaming Authority takes student interns.
More than 300 iGaming firms operate from Malta; the industry body works with MCAST and the University of Malta on a student placement scheme that feeds developers and analysts into it.
Betsson’s one-year paid infosec internship, posted by the MCAST ICT Institute, works with the Information Security Governance Team on governance, risk and compliance.
No national season: employers recruit when they have a vacancy, and Jobsplus lists them all year. Programme windows are short and set by each employer, such as bet365’s two weeks in November 2025.

The programmes read ask for a first degree: Bank of Valletta takes MQF level 6 or above and bet365 a 2:1 gained within three years. A postgraduate course matters for regulation and compliance, where the MFSA partners with the University of Malta. Recent graduates with a first degree already find work: 92.8% of those aged 20 to 34 were in work in 2025.

EU degrees go in as plain copies of certificates. For some work-permit routes (Specialist Employee Initiative, EU Blue Card) Malta’s qualifications recognition centre, MQRIC, validates a tertiary degree of at least three years; regulated professions need their own recognition.
Employers name the University of Malta and MCAST and nothing more, and no page read ranks schools. In a market this size the reputation that counts is the candidate’s own.
Deloitte offers an MCAST apprenticeship for students who must complete one as part of an advanced diploma or degree, and Betsson runs its infosec internship through MCAST.
Public administration, defence, education, health and social work employed 70,440 people in 2025, 20.8% of Malta’s 338,190 jobs, against 24.4% in the EU.

Employers hire from abroad: Deloitte runs an international programme with a relocation allowance, and Malta’s labour migration policy sets a workforce growth limit by company size. Rivermate notes that visa quotas and local rules can limit sponsorship. Rules are on the Visas page.
A photo is optional: Konnekt calls it unexpected and advises against it, and leaves out the date of birth.
EURES Malta says the CV is usually no longer than two pages; Konnekt advises one page for graduates and two for experienced candidates, as a PDF with a clear file name.
EURES asks for a brief covering letter of a few paragraphs, and the Malta Gaming Authority asks for a CV and covering letter for internships.
EURES lists references among the application documents, while Konnekt says to write that they are available on request and give contact details only when asked.
EURES says to send copies of certificates with the application, and typed documents; some employers use their own application form with open questions.
The Malta Gaming Authority says its offer is meant to meet the salary expectations candidates state at the start of the process, so be ready to name a figure early.
A law-firm guide says staff whose work relates directly to the gaming system must be vetted as fit and proper persons, and EURES says some jobs need a medical certificate before you start.
Word of mouth and recommendations carry real weight; in a small market a firm’s and a candidate’s reputation travel fast.

Employers do hire people still abroad: the policy has a “still abroad” application route, and Deloitte’s International Graduate Programme is built for it. A non-EU applicant should expect the employer’s advert and the labour market test before any permit.
English is an official language (with Maltese) and enough for most private-sector roles; Maltese matters in the public sector.

The Malta Gaming Authority describes five stages: a first interview, a task showing what the job involves, a second interview where you present the task, a behavioural profiling test, then the offer. Deloitte’s international programme starts with a first conversation arranged by a team member after you apply online.
No page read gives a time from application to offer. For a non-EU hire add the employer’s three-week advert on Jobsplus and EURES and the permit processing before a start date.
The CV is in English, and some jobs require a medical examination before employment.

Either a contract or a written statement of core conditions is required, covering the job, pay, hours, leave, probation and notice. Probation is six months as standard, up to a year for managerial or technical roles paid at least double the minimum wage.
In probation either side can end the job without a reason, with a week’s notice once you have worked more than a month; after that notice rises from one week to twelve weeks at ten years’ service.

Deloitte’s international programme offers a permanent job, a salary package and a relocation allowance; the Malta Gaming Authority aims the offer at the salary you named at the start. No page read says whether extra statutory months of pay apply or how long you have to decide.

For new non-EU hires the employer must advertise on Jobsplus and EURES for at least three weeks in the two months before applying; the period is two weeks for the Key Employee Initiative, Specialist Employee Initiative, EU Blue Card and Skilled Occupation List. Health, care, regulator-endorsed cases, sportspersons and change of employer are exempt.

The monthly labour market test looks back 12 months at the employer’s recruitment and redundancy record and the 2% disability quota, and caps growth through non-EU hires by size: up to 200% for firms of 1–9 staff, 100% for 10–49, 50% for 50–249 and 25% for 250 or more.

In practice this favours established employers with headcount to spare, such as the Big Four and gaming operators; raise your status at the first conversation, since the advert comes before the application.

Jobsplus, the national employment agency, runs the “Find a Job” portal, a traineeship scheme and the Youth Guarantee; vacancies posted there pass to EURES. Employer pages worth knowing: Deloitte’s “Join Deloitte” search, PwC’s student page, the Malta Gaming Authority’s Talexio portal and Betsson’s careers list.

Bank of Valletta takes enquiries for its Graduates’ Programme by email at resourcing-graduates@bov.com. Recruiters GRS Recruitment and Konnekt publish Malta job-search guides, and the KSU Careers’ Expo and Freshers’ Week are the campus events.
Sending a Europass CV to private employers: Konnekt says recruiters find it forgettable and keeps it for public-sector roles and EU bodies.
Assuming a non-EU offer is enough: the employer has to advertise the job on Jobsplus and EURES and pass the labour market test before a permit can be requested.
Waiting for a graduate season: programme windows are short, as with bet365’s two weeks in November 2025, so follow each employer’s page.
Leaving out your languages: Betsson’s Malta list asks for German, Danish, Nordic or Lithuanian beside English in customer roles, and EURES lists language proficiency as a CV section.
English is the working language of the programmes read: EURES asks for a CV written in English, and the Deloitte and Malta Gaming Authority pages are in English with no other language required.
The Deloitte International Graduate Programme page states no language requirement and is written in English.
Maltese and English are the official languages, and Maltese matters in the public sector; the Malta Gaming Authority’s careers page is in English.

In iGaming operations a second market language is the entry ticket: bet365 asks for fluency in one or more supported languages including English, and Betsson’s customer roles name German, Danish, Nordic or Lithuanian. Evidence is an interview and the language on the CV.
English is the working language in Malta’s tech and iGaming firms; Betsson’s infosec and AI internships in Malta are posted in English.

No return-offer or conversion rate was found for any programme above: HSBC Malta, Deloitte and the Malta Gaming Authority give no hiring share for their interns. Treat the national figure as the guide: 92.8% of tertiary graduates aged 20 to 34 who left education up to three years earlier were in work in 2025.

For graduates of the last two years or students abroad, with a training agreement, a tutor and the host’s written commitment to cover your living costs; up to six months, 12 at most, not convertible to work on the spot.
Permit to look for work or start a business after graduating

After a bachelor’s, master’s or PhD in Malta, apply before your student permit expires: nine months, not renewable. It does not itself allow work; a job offer converts it to a single permit without leaving Malta.
Key and specialist employee schemes, EU Blue Card

The Key Employee Initiative gives a decision in five working days for senior or highly specialised roles; the Specialist Employee Initiative in 15. Both need a degree or three years of relevant experience.
The Blue Card needs a contract of at least six months and a three-year degree; family joins at once with the right to work.

Senior roles in finance, gaming and aviation earning at least €65,000 can pay a flat 15% on employment income.

Rent only a flat whose lease is registered with the Housing Authority (rentregistration.mt): since 1 September 2024 a bedroom may hold at most 2 people, and permit applications need the authority’s approval letter and an attestation form signed by a notary or lawyer in Malta.

Since 1 August 2025 you cannot enter as a visitor and apply for a work permit in Malta: your employer files the single permit (€600) while you are abroad, and you then get the D visa (€100). Since 1 March 2026 workers must also pass a 20-hour online pre-departure course (€250).
Students on courses over 90 days, UK and US citizens included, need the study D visa (€100) before travelling.
Your address is the registered lease: the Housing Authority approval is what Identità checks for any residence document.

You may work from day one. Within 90 days, apply online to Identità with form A (employment), your contract, the Jobsplus engagement form and registered lease; after biometrics in Msida you get a free eResidence card valid 5 years.

Workers book biometrics at Valley Road, Msida, bring their €100,000 health policy, and get an interim permit; the plastic card takes 4 to 8 weeks. Students apply online within 30 days of arriving (form N.01): €50 plus €27.50 for the card.
Your employer’s Jobsplus engagement form, filed by your first day, generates your social security number, and the tax office assigns your tax identification number.
Your European Health Insurance Card covers you until you work; employees are covered by public health care through their Class 1 contributions.
Every non-EU permit needs health insurance of at least €100,000 for hospital and medical care in Malta: travel policies of €30,000 are refused.
If your job ends, a new employer has only 30 days to file a complete change of employer (€600); do not start the new job before it is approved.

The interim receipt and the employer’s “still working” letter let you keep working while a renewal is processed, but are valid only in Malta: leaving, even for a Schengen stopover, can mean refused boarding and losing the application.
Students may not work at all in their first 90 days; from day 91, up to 20 hours a week with a Jobsplus licence the employer requests.
The interim receipt and “still working” letter are valid only in Malta: leaving while a renewal is pending can strand you abroad.
Leases must be registered with the Housing Authority, with at most two people per bedroom; Identità refuses applications without the approval letter.
Ordinary €30,000 travel insurance is refused: cover must reach €100,000.
The Skills Pass may be extended beyond hospitality.
EU citizens working in hospitality will need the Skills Pass from 1 January 2027, unless postponed again.
Visa appointments at VFS centres in India and elsewhere take 6 to 16 weeks, with slots resold illegally.
A reform of the non-domiciled tax regime is announced for 2027.

Entry for EU passports, graduate pay, tax and language expectations were not researched.

Kuala Lumpur’s economy grew 5.2% in 2025 to RM265.1 billion; as the capital it remained the second-largest contributor to Malaysia’s economy after Selangor, and services made up more than 90% of it, with finance, insurance, real estate and business services growing 5.3%.
Deutsche Bank (Malaysia) Berhad is a licensed commercial bank with its office on Jalan Sultan Ismail, Kuala Lumpur.
Bank of America Malaysia Berhad is a licensed commercial bank and principal dealer with its office in Menara Merdeka 118, Kuala Lumpur.

The UK Foreign Office advises against all but essential travel to the islands and dive sites off eastern Sabah, from Sandakan to Tawau, because of the threat of kidnapping; this does not apply to mainland Sabah.

Pulau Pinang’s economy grew 7.3% in 2025 to RM130.3 billion, led by electrical, electronic and optical products, up 12.7%; the statistics office calls it Malaysia’s leading electrical and electronics hub.
Johor grew fastest of all states in 2025, by 8.0% to RM171 billion, nearly 10% of Malaysia’s economy, driven by data centres; the statistics office calls it the nation’s digital economy hub.

Penang’s IT rating rests on one employer’s design and shared-services functions: the statistics office describes its electronics manufacturing, not graduate hiring by role. Johor’s IT rating rests on data-centre growth, which creates more construction and operations jobs than graduate IT roles.
The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) ranks Kuala Lumpur 39th in the world, up three places, and Labuan 44th.

CIMB says it has grown from its headquarters in Kuala Lumpur to around 33,000 employees serving over 30 million customers across ASEAN and beyond.
In December 2025 the median monthly wage of formal-sector employees was RM3,167 across Malaysia: RM4,391 in Kuala Lumpur, RM3,500 in Pulau Pinang and RM2,982 in Johor.

Intel Malaysia was established in Penang in 1972 and, in the investment agency’s words, is Intel’s largest and most diverse site outside the United States, covering manufacturing, product design and development and global shared services.
Infineon says its Penang team is in the Phase 2 Bayan Lepas Free Industrial Zone and invites applications to its jobs there.
Micron lists Penang and Muar in Malaysia among its manufacturing locations.

Malaysia recorded RM385.7 billion of data-centre investment from 2021 to the first half of 2026; the investment authority names AWS, Microsoft, Google, Bridge Data Centres, DayOne, AirTrunk and Vantage Data Centres as operators present, particularly in Greater Kuala Lumpur and Johor.
