English is the default language of private-sector and multinational recruiting in Malaysia, while Bahasa Malaysia is sometimes required for government, government-linked and some local or front-line roles.

Graduate windows are mixed rather than one national season: CIMB’s Complete Banker has intakes in April and October, its Protégé takes applications all year round, and the 2026 fairs ran on 25 and 26 July (myStarjob, Johor Bahru) and 1 August (TalentBank, Penang); industrial training placements usually last 3 to 6 months.

In 2024 graduate unemployment was 3.2% (165,900 people), down from 3.4%, with 5.14 million graduates in the labour force; about 67.8% of employed graduates were in skilled occupations, skill-related underemployment was 32.2%, and the median monthly salary was RM4,521.

Malaysian students usually do an industrial training placement before graduating, typically 3 to 6 months, and graduate hiring runs through structured programmes at banks, government-linked groups and the Big Four, many of them limited to Malaysian citizens. Graduate unemployment was 3.2% in 2024, but the entry market is crowded and about a third of graduates work below their skill level.
Industrial training placement

Industrial training puts students in a company, agency or other organisation for supervised work before they receive a certificate, diploma or bachelor’s degree; it usually lasts 3 to 6 months depending on the institution and programme.

The national Structured Internship Programme (MySIP) of TalentCorp sets a minimum allowance of RM600 a month for bachelor’s-level placements and RM500 for diploma-level ones; government agencies pay RM5 an hour for up to 90 working days.
No conversion rate from placement to job offer was found in the pages read, so this ranking rests on the structure of degrees, not on a survey.
Graduate and trainee programmes

Banks and government-linked investors run the visible schemes: CIMB’s Complete Banker is a 24-month regional programme with intakes in April and October and a minimum CGPA of 3.25, its Protégé programme is 8 months of on-the-job training taking applications all year round, and Khazanah’s Graduate Trainee Programme lasts 12 months with a minimum CGPA of 3.0.
Many are for citizens only: Khazanah’s programme is open to Malaysian citizens, and Maybank’s graduate and trainee schemes are restricted to Malaysian citizens.
Big Four and professional-services intake
The Big Four are a main door for accounting and business graduates, usually asking for a CGPA of about 3.0; KPMG says it takes about 400 graduates a year.
FDM Group Malaysia lists graduate programmes in data engineering, software engineering, business analysis and project management, and technical engineering on SEEK Grad.
Public service posts
The Public Service Commission (SPA) takes applications online through its SPA9 system, requires Malaysian citizenship and sets a probation period of 1 to 3 years for appointments.
Career fairs and job portals

Commercial fairs run through the year: the TalentBank Career Fair was on 1 August 2026 in Penang for graduates and experienced professionals, and the myStarjob Fair on 25 and 26 July 2026 in Johor Bahru offered on-the-spot interviews.
Mass hiring happens in manufacturing: about 1,000 people queued for up to 500 vacancies at an Infineon open interview in Melaka, with RM3,500 starting pay for production operators and technicians.
Graduate unemployment was 3.2% in 2024, but about 36% of tertiary-educated workers were in jobs below their skills.

Programme windows are mixed rather than a single national season: CIMB’s Complete Banker has two intakes a year (April and October) and its Protégé takes applications all year round, while Khazanah’s assessments run in stages after applications close.
Maybank’s graduate and trainee schemes are restricted to Malaysian citizens.

CIMB’s Protégé is open to fresh graduates from all disciplines with at least a diploma and is a contract post; its Complete Banker needs a minimum CGPA of 3.25 and runs five stages from an online application to a final interview with the Group Chief People Officer.

Khazanah, the sovereign investor, runs a 12-month Graduate Trainee Programme with an Investments track and a Khazanah track covering strategy, governance, sustainability, legal and research, for citizens who are fresh graduates or in their final year, or who have up to two years of work experience.

Grab opened its seventh R&D centre in Kuala Lumpur and aimed to bring on 100 tech staff in its first year, including software engineers, data scientists and data analysts; the electronics and semiconductor plants of Penang hire engineers, and Intel in Penang employs about 9,000 Malaysians.

The pages read set academic bars by grade, not school: CIMB’s Complete Banker asks for a CGPA of at least 3.25 (second class upper or a WAM of 75), Khazanah for 3.0 (second class upper or a WAM of 70%), and the Big Four typically about 3.0.

The TalentBank Career Fair was held on 1 August 2026 in Penang (internships, graduate programmes and full-time roles in business, accounting, engineering, IT and semiconductors), and the myStarjob Fair on 25 and 26 July 2026 in Johor Bahru; TalentCorp’s Minggu MyBakat is a talent-development week for students and fresh graduates.

Windows differ by employer and are often open for long periods: CIMB’s Protégé takes applications all year round, its Complete Banker has intakes in April and October, and Khazanah moves candidates through online assessment, video, phone and final interviews as applications arrive.

The programme pages read ask for a degree and a grade, not a master’s: Khazanah takes fresh graduates or final-year students of undergraduate or postgraduate study with a CGPA of at least 3.0, and CIMB’s Protégé asks for at least a diploma. Degree holders had a median monthly salary of RM5,724 against RM3,390 for diploma holders in 2024.
The Malaysian Qualifications Register lists accredited programmes of local and foreign providers, and any interested party can use it to check the status of a qualification.
The programme pages read name no target schools: CIMB, Khazanah and the Big Four set a minimum CGPA (3.25, 3.0 and about 3.0) and CIMB’s Complete Banker accepts all fields of study.

The route into work is a short industrial training placement of usually 3 to 6 months, with allowances set by the organisation or under MySIP and the HRD Corp Industrial Training Scheme (up to RM500 a month); the pages read show no dual-study degree.

The public service recruits through SPA with citizenship required, and government-linked groups such as Khazanah run their own graduate programmes; no headcount of graduate hires in the public sector was found in the pages read.

Citizens-only schemes (Maybank, Khazanah, the public service) shut out foreigners, and the lowest Employment Pass category needs a basic salary of at least RM5,000 a month from 1 June 2026, above the RM4,521 median monthly salary of all graduates in 2024. See Visas for the rules.

A photo is optional, but many local employers still expect a recent headshot on a plain background in business attire; multinationals can omit it. Leave off your full IC (MyKad) number, religion, race and exact date of birth.
One to two pages; fresh graduates and people with under about 5 years of experience should aim for one page, and longer documents are discouraged outside academia and senior roles.

The government guide on industrial training tells students to prepare an updated resume and a specific application letter; the programme pages read (CIMB, Khazanah) describe an online application with a CV and assessments.
The pages read ask for a CV and assessments first; none of the programme stages read (Khazanah: CV, online assessment, video interview, phone interview, final interview) asks for referees up front.
Applications ask for a CV and a result measure (CGPA, class or WAM) rather than certified copies; the public service sets qualification levels in its application requirements.

Include your expected monthly salary in ringgit if the advert asks for it; if it does not, it can be left out and discussed at interview. The Malaysian Employers Federation warned in 2023 that graduate pay demands that are too high may not be affordable, putting honours-degree starting pay at about RM2,700 a month.
No source read describes background checks for graduate programmes, so how routine they are is not established; qualification status can be checked in the Malaysian Qualifications Register.

Formal schemes and public portals sit beside walk-in channels: SPA takes applications online, Khazanah runs a staged online process, and fairs such as myStarjob offer on-the-spot interviews and face-to-face networking.

A foreign graduate faces citizens-only schemes and an Employment Pass whose lowest category needs RM5,000 a month from 1 June 2026, a pay level that entry roles rarely reach (the median graduate salary was RM4,521 in 2024).
English is the default for private-sector and multinational roles; Bahasa Malaysia is sometimes required for government, government-linked and some local or front-line roles.

Khazanah’s selection has five stages: application with CV, an online assessment, a recorded video interview, a phone interview and a final interview, and it may take a few months after applications close.

CIMB’s Complete Banker also has five stages: online application, aptitude test, case study and group assessment, an interview with the Regional Head of Talent Acquisition and a final interview with the Group Chief People Officer.

If the contract names no notice period, the Employment Act sets 4 weeks for under 2 years of service, 6 weeks for 2 years up to 5, and 8 weeks for 5 years or more; either party can end the contract by paying wages in lieu of notice.
Public service appointments carry a probation period of 1 to 3 years; CIMB’s Protégé is a contract post of 8 months of on-the-job training after one week of classroom training.

Pay expectations are modest: the median monthly salary of all graduates was RM4,521 in 2024 (RM5,724 for degree holders), while the Malaysian Employers Federation put honours-degree starting pay at about RM2,700 in 2023.
Most graduate schemes read exclude foreigners: Maybank’s schemes are restricted to citizens, Khazanah is open to Malaysian citizens and the public service requires citizenship.

Where an employer does sponsor, the Employment Pass has three categories from 1 June 2026: RM20,000 and above for up to 10 years, RM10,000 to 19,999 for up to 10 years with a succession plan, and RM5,000 to 9,999 for up to 5 years with a succession plan.

No source read lists which employers sponsor graduates. Multinationals with large Malaysian sites, such as Intel in Penang (its largest site outside the United States, with about 9,000 Malaysians), are the places to ask; ask early and expect the question of pay level.

Portals and boards: the SPA9 system for public service posts, SEEK Grad Malaysia (GradConnection), which showed 24 graduate and internship programmes the day it was read, and the career pages of CIMB, Khazanah and Maybank.
Fairs: the TalentBank Career Fair (1 August 2026, Penang) and myStarjob (25 and 26 July 2026, Johor Bahru); university career offices and TalentCorp’s MySIP place students in industrial training.
Skipping industrial training: it is the standard exposure to work before the degree, usually 3 to 6 months, and the national scheme sets a minimum allowance of RM600 a month.
Applying to citizens-only schemes as a foreigner: Maybank’s schemes, Khazanah’s programme and public service posts require Malaysian citizenship.
Putting your full IC (MyKad) number, religion or date of birth on the CV: the guide says never include the full IC number, because of identity-fraud risk.
Expecting a high start: the median salary of all graduates was RM4,521 in 2024 and about 36% of tertiary-educated workers were in jobs below their skills.
CIMB’s regional Complete Banker and the Protégé listing are in English; the pages read name no language test.
The Big Four recruit in English; Bahasa Malaysia is not a stated requirement on the guides read.
Bahasa Malaysia is sometimes required for government and government-linked roles, and the SPA pages and its application requirements are in Malay.
Grab’s Kuala Lumpur R&D centre and the multinational plants in Penang work in English; the sources read name no language test.

In 2024 Malaysia had 5.98 million graduates, 5.14 million of them in the labour force; graduate unemployment was 3.2% (165,900 people), about 67.8% of employed graduates were in skilled occupations, and skill-related underemployment of graduates was 32.2%.

Early job absorption is weaker for graduates in education, services, agriculture, social sciences, journalism, information, and arts and humanities, while engineering, software and advanced manufacturing face talent shortages.
No return-offer rate from industrial training to a graduate post was found in the pages read.

Students of Malaysian universities intern on their Student Pass. Students of foreign universities need a Professional Visit Pass requested by the host company: typically 3 to 6 months, 12 at most, with an allowance but no salary. An internship as a tourist is illegal, even unpaid.

A 12-month pass to look for work after a degree from a Malaysian university, open only to citizens of 32 listed countries, among them Germany, France, the Netherlands and the Nordic countries. Italy is not on the list.
British graduates of Malaysian universities can get a 12-month pass to travel, work part time and look for a job.

The employer first gets labour-department approval, then applies; since 1 June 2026 all three categories may bring family. Foreign-owned sponsors need RM 500,000 of paid-up capital.

Up to 90 days with no work; fill in the free Malaysia Digital Arrival Card within three days before arriving. Repeated border runs to reset the 90 days lead to refusal and a blacklist.
Fill in the Malaysia Digital Arrival Card before you travel. Students apply through Education Malaysia Global Services (EMGS); workers through their employer and the Expatriate Services Division.
Expect to pay 2 months’ damage deposit, 1 month in advance and half a month’s utility deposit when you rent.
Have the lease stamped with stamp duty on e-Duti Setem (MyTax) within 30 days of signing: an unstamped lease is not valid proof of residence for a bank account or utilities.

On arrival you get a temporary special pass, usually 30 days. Your employer or university then hands your passport to immigration for the visa sticker and the i-Kad card, which takes 2 to 6 weeks; meanwhile you cannot leave the country or fly to Sabah or Sarawak.

Register your tax identification number online on MyTax. Until you have spent 182 days in Malaysia, your employer withholds a flat 30%; for arrivals in the second half of the year, more than 14 days abroad on holiday can break the count.
Since 1 October 2025 employees on an Employment Pass pay 2% into the EPF pension fund, matched by 2% from the employer, refundable when you leave for good.
Your employer must cover you under the SOCSO employment injury and invalidity schemes; expatriates are excluded from the unemployment insurance scheme.

Banks (Maybank, CIMB, Public Bank, RHB) refuse accounts on a tourist visa or approval letter: bring your passport with the visa sticker, the i-Kad, a letter from your employer or university addressed to the branch, and the stamped lease.
When you leave for good, the visa cancellation (check-out memo) and tax clearance are needed to withdraw your EPF savings.
Until you have spent 182 days in Malaysia in the year, employers withhold a flat 30% tax.
Malaysia does not accept apostilles: documents need consular legalisation at the Malaysian embassy.
A positive urine test is a crime even if the drug was taken legally abroad; CBD products are banned.
Same-sex relations are criminalised, with prison sentences of up to 20 years.
While your passport is with immigration for the pass sticker, 2 to 6 weeks, you cannot travel abroad or to Sabah and Sarawak.
Employers renewing category II and III passes must file a local succession plan from 1 January 2027; the criteria are not out.

De Nationale Carrièrebeurs ran on 24 and 25 April 2026 at RAI Amsterdam with 250 employers, and Career Expo Eindhoven on 3 and 4 March 2026 at TU/e.

The Dutch job vacancy rate was 3.9% in the last quarter of 2025, down from 4.1% a year earlier: 5.0% in professional, scientific and technical activities, 4.8% in information and communication and 3.4% in finance and insurance.

RSM reports that 95.8% of its master’s graduates were employed within six months of graduating (512 responses from 2,055 graduates who finished between 1 September 2024 and 31 August 2025; school-reported, surveyed in April 2026).

The most English-friendly large job market on the continent. Amsterdam takes about 40% of the international graduates who stay and work, with trading firms, fintech and European headquarters; Rotterdam is Europe’s logistics gateway; Eindhoven is built around ASML’s chip machines. Only a quarter of international graduates are still in the country five years on.

Graduate labour market
7.8% of Dutch job postings say Dutch is not required — the highest share of the large European markets — and about 5% are written in English.
25% of international graduates still live in the Netherlands five years after graduating; EEA graduates stay at about half the non-EEA rate (20.3% against 38.5%).

The 30% facility can exempt part of a recruit’s pay from tax if they lived more than 150 km from the Dutch border for 16 of the last 24 months; under 30 with a master’s it needs €36,497 a year (2026).
Greater Amsterdam hosts about 40% of the international graduates who are working in the Netherlands five years after graduating.
The proprietary trading and market-making firms Optiver, IMC and Flow Traders have their headquarters in Amsterdam.
The Port of Rotterdam handled 428.4 million tonnes and 14.2 million TEU of containers in 2025 and describes itself as Europe’s logistics hub.
ASML, headquartered in Veldhoven, plans a campus at Brainport Industries Campus for 20,000 more employees.

Eurostat counts 850,000 people in work in the Utrecht metropolitan region in 2021: 55,000 in information and communication (second in the Netherlands, after Amsterdam) and 34,000 in finance and insurance (second in the Netherlands, after Amsterdam). The region’s GDP was €83.3 billion in 2021.

Eurostat counts 645,000 people in work in the The Hague metropolitan region in 2021: 27,000 in information and communication and 14,000 in finance and insurance. The region’s GDP was €56.0 billion in 2021.

The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) ranks Amsterdam 26th in the world (down 6 places) and eighth among Western European centres, behind London, Zurich, Geneva, Luxembourg, Lugano, Paris and Copenhagen.

Of the 152 metropolitan regions for which Eurostat publishes jobs by sector (latest year, 2021 or 2022; German, British and Swiss regions are not in the table), Amsterdam has the seventh-most jobs in information and communication (114,000) and in finance and insurance (67,000), and Utrecht the 19th (55,000) and 18th (34,000).

Greater Amsterdam (Groot-Amsterdam) has 1,144,700 jobs (2023): 91,300 in information and communication, 60,100 in finance and insurance and 297,600 in professional, scientific, technical and administrative services.

Startup Genome’s 2026 report ranks Amsterdam-Delta joint 23rd in the world with Stockholm, with an ecosystem value of $83 billion, $2.5 billion of seed and Series A funding in H2 2023–2025 and $21 billion of exits in 2021–2025.
Adyen says it was founded in 2006 in Amsterdam and has 4,000+ employees of 115+ nationalities in 28 offices (page undated; its processed-volume figure is for 2023).
The University of Amsterdam has over 44,000 students, 6,200 employees, 3,000 PhD researchers and an annual budget of €850 million.
In 2024 Rotterdam handled 397.3 million tonnes of goods, the most of any port in the EU, followed by Antwerp-Bruges (244.2 million) and Hamburg (97.0 million).

The Port of Rotterdam Authority puts the port’s employment at about 182,000 jobs, directly and indirectly, in the Rotterdam-Rijnmond area and its added value at €23.3 billion, 2.2% of Dutch GDP; the Authority itself has about 1,440 employees.

Groot-Rijnmond (the Rotterdam region) has 831,500 jobs (2023): 46,200 in manufacturing, 249,000 in trade, transport, hospitality and information and communication, and 204,600 in finance, real estate and professional and business services.

ASML’s 2025 annual report counts more than 44,000 total employees (FTEs) of 143 nationalities; its global headquarters is ASML Veldhoven, De Run 6501, and it operates in more than 60 locations worldwide.

The Eindhoven region (Zuidoost-Noord-Brabant) has 502,100 jobs (2023), 80,400 of them (16%) in manufacturing, 16,300 in information and communication and 106,400 in professional, scientific, technical and administrative services.
The Utrecht region has 891,800 jobs (2023): 60,800 in information and communication, 37,000 in finance and insurance and 177,800 in professional, scientific, technical and administrative services.
NS, the Dutch railway company, gives its head-office address as Laan van Puntenburg 100, Utrecht.
Utrecht University reports over 38,000 students, over 8,800 staff members, over 650 professors and an income of about €1.3 billion.

The Hague agglomeration has 514,200 jobs (2023): 191,400 of them (37%) in public administration, defence, education and health, 20,000 in information and communication and 12,300 in finance and insurance.
The Hague is home to some 200 international organisations, including the International Court of Justice in the Peace Palace, Europol and the International Criminal Court.
The International Criminal Court’s permanent premises are at Oude Waalsdorperweg 10 in The Hague.

In 2022 employees under 30 in Dutch firms with 10 or more staff (public administration excluded) earned a mean of €34,109 gross a year, and those under 30 working as professionals €45,349, against €50,942 for all ages.

In 2025 the employment rate of Dutch people aged 20 to 34 with a tertiary degree was 92.7% (91.8% for those who finished within the last five years); unemployment was 3.9% overall and 8.8% for the 15-to-24s, and GDP was €1,170.6 billion.

Eurostat counts 998,000 people in work in the Rotterdam metropolitan region in 2021: 72,000 in manufacturing, 29,000 in information and communication and 19,000 in finance and insurance, third in the Netherlands for both of the last two.

Brainport Eindhoven describes itself as a high-tech region with Eindhoven at its centre, where companies, knowledge institutes and governments develop technology together; it lists Eindhoven University of Technology, Fontys, Avans and Tilburg University as its universities.

Dutch graduates usually move into work through a graduation internship (afstudeerstage) or a company traineeship, and half of Rotterdam School of Management’s master’s graduates had a job before they graduated. The largest employers of business graduates are the Big Four and the banks.
English opens more doors than anywhere else on the continent, but the first year is still hard for internationals.
The big programmes run to short fixed windows and ask for existing work rights: Heineken’s 2026 window ran from 31 August to 20 September, and Unilever fills on a first-come, first-served basis.
Graduation internship and thesis in a firm
Many master’s theses are written inside a company over several months; it is the usual way a firm tries out a graduate before offering a contract.
Of the 381 RSM master’s graduates who gave timing, 197 (52%) had a job before they graduated, and 95.8% of respondents were employed within six months of graduating.
Traineeships

Large firms run multi-year traineeships with rotations: FrieslandCampina’s lasts two years with two one-year assignments, starting in March and September; Heineken’s three-year programme starts with two six-month rotations in the Netherlands.

ING runs two-year traineeships in Amsterdam in retail banking, wholesale banking, tech and HR, ABN AMRO’s last 18 months to two years, and Unilever’s Future Leaders Programme has three rotations and a permanent contract.
Direct entry and open applications
A motivation letter carries real weight, and open applications to a named person are normal.
Recruitment agencies are a channel too and may ask for an assessment; for experienced hires the usual path is a posted vacancy, with salary discussed only in the second or third round.
Career fairs and in-house days

De Nationale Carrièrebeurs at RAI Amsterdam (24 and 25 April 2026) had 250 employers; Career Expo Eindhoven ran on 3 and 4 March 2026 at TU/e, and ABN AMRO and Heineken hold in-house days for graduates.
Central government and public bodies

Werken voor Nederland, the central government’s job portal, filters vacancies by field and education level and promotes traineeships, internships and starter positions; there is no national civil-service exam.
Referrals and open networking

Dutch directness extends to networking: say plainly what you want and why. Magnet.me lists employer events for early-career candidates, such as McKinsey’s Future Talent Program, aimed at people with up to one or two years of experience.

A year after graduating, 41.8% of international graduates who stayed had a paid job, against 64.9% of Dutch graduates; the gap narrows to 79.6% against 89.6% by year five. Dutch-language requirements are one likely reason.

Programme windows are short. Heineken’s Netherlands tracks took applications from 31 August to 20 September 2026, with an online assessment on 21 to 27 September and calls from 28 September; ING’s October 2026 class held interviews in May and June 2026.
Fairs fall in spring: Career Expo Eindhoven in early March and De Nationale Carrièrebeurs in late April; Delft’s orientation days ran from 16 to 18 February 2026.

The banks hire through traineeships of 18 months to two years: ABN AMRO holds in-house days for graduates with at most two years of experience, and ING’s two-year traineeships in Amsterdam take a CV, motivational questions and grade lists in English.
Amsterdam’s trading firms (Optiver, IMC, Flow Traders) hire graduate traders and engineers from mathematics, physics, econometrics and computer science, and decide on tests.
The vacancy rate in finance and insurance was 3.4% in the last quarter of 2025, against 3.9% for the whole economy.
The Big Four are the largest employers of Rotterdam School of Management graduates and take trainees through graduation internships and traineeships.
Unilever’s Dutch Future Leaders Programme fills first come, first served and ends with an in-person day in Rotterdam where the offer is decided; it requires the right to work in the Netherlands.

Heineken’s Global Graduate Program (commerce and finance tracks) took graduates from January 2026 to March 2027 who speak Dutch and English and already hold work rights, and FrieslandCampina’s corporate traineeship starts in March and September.
Central government recruits through Werken voor Nederland, with traineeships that rotate across several state organisations; The Hague is the seat of government, so most of the work is there.

Booking.com’s graduate software and data programmes in Amsterdam are open only to graduates of Dutch universities, which makes a Dutch degree a direct key. ASML in Veldhoven is a major employer of Eindhoven University of Technology graduates.
Information and communication had a vacancy rate of 4.8% in the last quarter of 2025, higher than finance (3.4%) and the whole economy (3.9%).

Data and AI roles cluster in Amsterdam (Booking.com, Adyen, ING, the trading firms) and around ASML and Philips in Eindhoven; the University of Amsterdam, TU Delft and Eindhoven are the usual sources, often through a thesis in the company.

Employers lean on the universities near them: Erasmus/RSM for Rotterdam, the University of Amsterdam and VU for Amsterdam, TU Delft and Eindhoven for engineering. Master’s graduates who also did their bachelor’s in the Netherlands stay more often.
RSM’s top five employers are Deloitte, PwC, EY, KPMG and Rabobank, a local list of Dutch Big Four offices and a cooperative bank.
A foreign diploma is checked by Nuffic or SBB through the IDW portal, but the evaluation is advisory and Dutch employers decide who they hire.
De Nationale Carrièrebeurs, RAI Amsterdam, 24 and 25 April 2026, with 250 employers and a free ticket; the Match&Meet tool shows beforehand which companies fit you.

Career Expo Eindhoven at TU/e on 3 and 4 March 2026, and Delft Career Days’ orientation days on 16 to 18 February 2026, described by CERN as the largest technical career fair in the Benelux with over 150 companies.
Company in-house days: ABN AMRO’s In-house Day for traineeships, and Heineken’s Global Graduate Program in-house days, one of them on 20 August 2026.

Programmes open once a year for a few weeks and fill early (Heineken 31 August to 20 September 2026, Unilever first come, first served, ING interviews in May and June), while ordinary vacancies are posted all year.

ING asks for grade lists of both the bachelor’s and the master’s, Heineken takes graduates within a year of their degree, and RSM’s employer list is made of master’s graduates; none of the pages read says a master’s is compulsory.

Only regulated professions need recognition: teaching through DUO, healthcare through the BIG register. For other jobs, Nuffic and SBB offer a credential evaluation through IDW (at least 10 working weeks), which is advisory and which the employer decides whether to ask for.
The employers recruiting most visibly are tied to nearby universities (RSM and the Big Four, TU/e and ASML), but Heineken, ING and Unilever select on tests and interviews, not on a school list.
For university graduates the Dutch counterpart of dual study is the graduation internship and the thesis written inside a firm; formal dual degrees were not researched here.
Central government hires through Werken voor Nederland, with traineeships across state organisations and a starters section, but the largest graduate programmes read are in banks and industry.

A highly skilled migrant permit needs an employer recognised by the IND, which appears in a public register; Heineken’s Netherlands programme postings ask for existing work rights. See Visas for the rules.
A photo is not required, and employers may not select on age or origin; most Dutch CVs fit on one page.
Expatica says photos are not usually expected and should be included only when the employer asks.
Expatica puts the CV at one A4 page for entry-level roles and no more than two for senior ones; Inburgering.org says one or two pages is usually enough and to follow the vacancy’s instructions.
The motivation letter should be no longer than one A4 page and explain your motivation; Heineken’s programme asks for a CV and a cover letter, and ING for motivational questions.
References are given when asked or noted as available on request; ask the person’s permission first, and expect employers to call them.
ING asks for grade lists with the application; for interviews bring copies of your CV, certificates and references.
Do not raise salary in the first interview: it usually comes up in the second or third round, and pay scales set by collective agreements cannot be negotiated.

Employers may search for you online only with a strong job-related reason and must tell you beforehand; a medical exam is allowed only for special medical requirements, after selection, and some employers ask to see the original ID.
Applications work, and Dutch directness extends to them: say plainly what you want and why.
Open applications to a named person are normal, and employer events on Magnet.me and at fairs are a second door.
International employers recruit from abroad in English; for most others, a Dutch degree and a local network come first.

Some programmes close the door to those without existing work rights or a Dutch degree: Heineken’s asks for work rights and Booking.com’s graduate programmes are open only to graduates of Dutch universities.
7.8% of ads say Dutch is not needed, the highest share Indeed found, but graduate roles in client-facing work still ask for Dutch.
ING asks for the application in English and fluent English, while Heineken’s programme asks for both Dutch and English.

Programmes run in steps: ING takes a CV, motivational questions and grade lists, then HR interviews and business panels at its Amsterdam headquarters (18 to 22 May and 1 to 5 June 2026 for the October class), with a second round only if places remain; a failed assessment or interview cannot be retried.

Heineken asks for a CV and cover letter, then an online assessment of situational scenarios and a cognitive test, then an introductory call; Unilever runs an online application, a digital assessment of motivation, personality and cognitive ability, a digital interview, and an in-person Discovery Centre in Rotterdam where you learn the outcome the same day.

Ordinary interviews are conversational, last 30 to 90 minutes, and second and even third rounds are common; you may get a job-related test or tasks. Dress smartly, arrive early, expect direct questions and value modesty over bragging.
Interviews are normally in English for international employers and in Dutch for Dutch-speaking ones; no source read gives a typical time from application to offer outside the programme calendars.

A probation period must be agreed in writing and be equal for both sides: none in a contract of six months or less, at most one month in a contract of more than six months and under two years, and at most two months otherwise.

Holiday allowance is at least 8% of gross annual salary, normally paid in May or June; the default notice period for the employee is one month. Pay scales set by collective agreements cannot be negotiated.

Successive fixed-term contracts become permanent after three contracts or 36 months, whichever comes first, and a gap of more than six months breaks the chain; a law adopted in July 2026 extends that gap to three years from 1 January 2028.

After you accept an offer there is a short conversation about employment terms; before accepting, check the contract for trial period, hours, salary, holiday pay and the collective agreement. The pages read do not say how long you have to decide.

The employer must be a sponsor recognised by the IND, listed in a public register updated once a month, and the IND must decide within 90 days; the employer applies and pays the €423 fee. Ask early whether a prospective employer is on the register.

For 2026 the gross monthly salary floors are €4,357 for under-30s, €5,942 for 30 and over and €3,122 for those within three years of graduating or on the orientation-year permit; fixed allowances count, holiday allowance does not.

Some graduate programmes ask for existing work rights and offer no visa support: Heineken’s Netherlands programme asks for Dutch, English and the right to work, and Booking.com’s graduate programmes are for Dutch-university graduates.
Central government: Werken voor Nederland, filterable by field and education level, with traineeships, internships and starter positions.

Graduate programmes and events: employers’ own pages (ING, ABN AMRO, Heineken, Unilever, FrieslandCampina) and Magnet.me, which lists employer events such as McKinsey’s Future Talent Program and Strategy&’s Own Your Impact.

Fairs: De Nationale Carrièrebeurs (RAI Amsterdam), Career Expo Eindhoven at TU/e and Delft Career Days; Career Compass Netherlands, on 28 May 2026 at Eindhoven, was aimed at international students and graduates.
Permits: the IND’s register of recognised sponsors shows which employers can hire from abroad; the UWV (via werk.nl) supports jobseekers on benefit.
Missing the window: Heineken’s Netherlands tracks were open for about three weeks, and Unilever fills first come, first served and requires you to finish the digital interview before the period ends.
Assuming English is enough: the 7.8% of ads that say Dutch is not needed is the highest in Europe, but still means about nine in ten want Dutch in some measure.
Raising salary in the first interview, bragging, or taking direct questions personally: Dutch interviewers value honesty and modesty.
Putting a photo, date of birth or marital status on the CV out of habit, or sending a letter longer than one page.
Applying twice to ING after failing its assessment or interview: the posting says you cannot apply again.
ING asks for its application in English and fluent English; no Dutch requirement is named for the traineeships read, and no certificate: the motivational questions and interviews are the evidence.
Heineken’s Netherlands Global Graduate Program asks for Dutch and English; no certificate is named, and the level is judged in the interviews.
Only 7.8% of Dutch ads say Dutch is not needed, so English-only technology roles are the exception outside the large employers; Booking.com’s programmes require a Dutch-university degree.

RSM reports that 95.8% of its master’s graduates were employed within six months (512 responses from 2,055 graduates, surveyed in April 2026), and of the 381 who gave timing, 52% had a job before they graduated; this is a school-reported figure with a 25% response rate.
For internationals the picture is slower: 25% are still in the Netherlands five years after graduating, and of those who stay, 80% are employed at year five.
The vacancy rate fell from 4.1% in the last quarter of 2024 to 3.9% in the last quarter of 2025, with 5.0% in professional, scientific and technical activities.
No source read gives a return-offer rate for Dutch graduation internships or a time to first job for internationals.

EU, EEA and Swiss citizens need no visa, work permit or residence document; the immigration service (IND) can confirm your right of residence for €85 if you want proof.

Staying more than four months, register with the municipality within five days of arriving and you get your citizen service number (BSN) on the spot; for shorter stays there is the non-resident register (RNI).
A student who works, even one hour a week, must take out Dutch basic health insurance within four months; one who does not work stays on the European Health Insurance Card.
Residence permit for study
You cannot apply yourself: your university, a recognised sponsor, applies to the IND. US, UK and some other nationals need no entry visa (MVV).
Earn at least half of each year’s credits, or the university must report you and the permit is withdrawn.
Employed work: 16 hours a week in term, or full time in June, July and August, never both, and only once the employer has a work permit (TWV). Freelance work needs no TWV.
A non-EU student with a student permit from another EU country can study here up to 360 days without a Dutch permit, after the university notifies the IND.

Recruits from abroad receive 30% of their salary tax-free in 2026, falling to 27% from 2027. You must have lived more than 150 km from the Dutch border for 16 of the previous 24 months, and the employer must apply within four months of your start date to cover you from day one.

With the housing shortage, check that the lease allows registration at the town hall (“inschrijving mogelijk”) and get the landlord’s signed consent with a copy of their ID: a room without it means a fine of up to €325 and 52% tax withheld from your pay.

Bring your birth certificate: EU citizens can use the multilingual EU extract, which needs no translation; others need an apostille or legalisation, and a sworn translation unless it is in Dutch, English, French or German.

Your sponsor (employer or university) files the combined application with the IND. Unless your nationality is exempt (UK, US and a few others are), you then collect the MVV entry visa at the consulate, with biometrics. You cannot switch from a tourist stay in the Netherlands.
Staying more than 4 months, register in the personal records database (BRP) at your town hall within 5 working days of arriving, with passport, lease and landlord’s consent, and birth certificate.
Staying under 4 months, register as a non-resident (RNI) instead; since 2026 non-EU citizens can only do so at the Breda or Venlo desks.
No IND document is required; you may ask for an optional statement that you live here lawfully (€85).
When the IND writes that your residence document is ready, book an appointment at an IND desk to collect it; if you gave no fingerprints abroad, book a biometrics appointment first.
Your citizen service number (BSN) is given at the end of the BRP appointment: it is the key to your work contract, tax and health insurance.

Anyone who works, even a student working one hour a week or a paid intern, must take out basic health insurance (basisverzekering) within 4 months of starting, backdated to the first day: about €145 to €165 a month in 2026, with a €385 yearly excess. Missing it costs a €529.74 fine.
On a modest income you can claim up to €129 a month of health-care allowance (zorgtoeslag). Register with a GP near home; if all refuse, your insurer must find one within 10 working days.

Activate DigiD, the state digital ID for the tax office, MijnOverheid, health insurance and the IND, online at digid.nl with your BSN and postcode; the code comes by post within 3 working days, or at once with an NFC check of your passport.
Never pay a deposit into an anonymous fintech account before viewing the flat and checking the owner in the land registry (Kadaster).
Do not leave the Netherlands with only an IND receipt or a residence sticker: get a return visa first (€197), or you can be stopped at the border or refused boarding.

Nationals who must take it have the tuberculosis screening at the municipal health service (GGD) within 3 months of arriving. Students who earn under 50% of their credits in a year can lose the permit.
Refuse a room where you cannot register at the municipality: without registration your employer withholds 52% of your salary and your bank account can be blocked.
The IND waiting sticker or receipt is valid only inside the Netherlands: to travel before the card arrives you need a return visa (€197).
A partner can join only if both of you are at least 21 on the day you apply.
Since 1 January 2026 non-EU citizens can register as non-residents (to get a BSN for a stay under four months) only in Breda or Venlo.
Never pay a deposit to an anonymous account before seeing the flat and checking the owner in the land registry (Kadaster).
For a foreign university near the top-200 line, which year’s ranking the IND uses for the orientation year can be unclear; check with the IND before applying.
In Amsterdam, Utrecht, Rotterdam, Delft and Eindhoven many rooms are offered without the right to register.
Bills before parliament would raise naturalisation from five to ten years of residence and the civic integration level from A2 to B1.

91.8% of recent tertiary graduates in Norway were in work in 2025, and unemployment among graduates was 3.4%, the lowest in the comparison.
NHH’s 2024 master’s class reported a median gross salary of NOK 580,000 six months after graduating, for those working in Norway (52% responded).
62% of students from outside the EU and EEA who completed a Norwegian degree were still resident the year after, and 86% of those still in Norway were employed.
About half of Norway’s gross product in financial services was generated in Oslo, and finance, real estate, ICT and technical services made up 38% of Oslo’s output (2015 data).
DNB, Norway’s largest bank, runs a trainee programme in Oslo that recruits in the autumn.
Nordea’s 1.5-year Graduate Programme starts in September in Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden; the 2026 applications ran from 9 to 28 February.
Equinor has its head office at Forus in Stavanger, where about 4,500 people work; Bergen has about 3,000 and Oslo about 1,600.

Eurostat counts 334,000 people in work in the Bergen metropolitan region in 2021: 8,000 in information and communication (joint second in Norway, after Oslo) and 6,000 in finance and insurance (second in Norway, after Oslo). The region’s GDP was €36.5 billion in 2021.

Eurostat counts 245,000 people in work in the Trondheim metropolitan region in 2021: 7,000 in information and communication and 4,000 in finance and insurance. The region’s GDP was €26.1 billion in 2021.

Eurostat counts 496,000 people in work in the Oslo metropolitan region in 2021, 47,000 of them in information and communication (45% of Norway’s 105,000) and 22,000 in finance and insurance (46% of 48,000).

Eurostat counts 265,000 people in work in the Stavanger metropolitan region in 2021, 8,000 of them in information and communication (8% of Norway’s 105,000) and 2,000 in finance and insurance (4% of 48,000).

Norges Bank Investment Management, which runs the government pension fund, has its head office at Bankplassen 2 in Oslo and says it has 676 people from 37 countries, with investment offices in London, New York and Singapore.

The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) ranks Oslo 48th of 117 centres, up 16 places and sixteenth among European centres, and 33rd for fintech; Bergen, Stavanger and Trondheim are not ranked.

Startup Genome’s Oslo ecosystem page shows an ecosystem value of $12 billion against a regional average of $14.3 billion, $418 million of seed and Series A funding in 2023–2025 and $2 billion of exits in 2021–2025.
In 2025 ICT specialists were 5.9% of employment in Norway, against 5.0% in the EU, ninth highest of the 33 European countries Eurostat lists; Sweden led with 8.9%.
In 2025 unemployment among Norwegians aged 15 to 24 was 14.0% (EU 15.2%), up from 11.0% in 2023.
In 2025 average monthly earnings of all employees, by place of work, were NOK 62,070 in Norway, NOK 70,690 in Oslo, NOK 69,670 in Stavanger, NOK 64,170 in Bergen and NOK 62,760 in Trondheim.

NHH Norwegian School of Economics in Bergen has about 3,700 students and around 470 employees, holds the Triple Crown of accreditations (AACSB, EQUIS, AMBA) and has been in the Financial Times rankings since 2005.
NTNU, with its headquarters in Trondheim, has 43,500 students (9% international) and 8,560 employees.

In Norway the usual door for business and engineering students is a summer internship of six to eight weeks between the two years of the master’s, at a bank, consultancy or energy group, which leads to an offer for after graduation. Firms visit NHH, BI and NTNU each autumn to fill them.
Summer internship (sommerinternship)

Selective and short: DNB’s runs from mid-June to mid-August and drew close to 500 applications for a handful of places; Equinor’s lasts seven weeks; BCG’s six-week internship can lead to a full-time role.
The Big Four make offers to NHH students a year before they finish, after a summer internship.
Graduate and trainee programmes

DNB and other large employers recruit trainees in the autumn for the following year. NBIM’s 12-month graduate programme (the 2027 cohort) took applications from 1 to 15 August 2026, and Equinor’s two-year programme, with rotations, had closed for 2027 when read.
Aker BP’s graduate programme offers permanent positions with structured training, and offers relocation help to graduates of universities outside Norway.
Campus career fairs

BI’s Karrieredagene, run by student volunteers each autumn on the Oslo campus, brings about 100 companies; NHH’s career fair in Bergen had close to 100 companies on its main company day in 2023 and included recruitment panels and company courses (EY, Accenture, Pareto Securities).
Networks and referrals
Expat.com says many jobs in Norway are filled through referrals and personal connections rather than public ads; it recommends professional events, conferences, job fairs and industry associations.
Posted vacancies

Nav’s Arbeidsplassen is the public job service and links to EURES; FINN.no and Jobbnorge are the other big boards, and Aker BP accepts applications only for advertised positions, with a CV and a cover letter.
Recruitment agencies
Expat.com names Manpower, Experis and Adecco as agencies focused on tech, engineering and finance; it presents them as an extra channel, not the main route.
Recent-graduate employment is among Europe’s strongest at 91.8%; oil prices move hiring in Stavanger and the energy supply chain more than elsewhere.
The autumn is the recruiting season: firms visit campuses and run career days in September, the DNB cybersecurity programme closed on 1 October, and NBIM and Equinor ran their 2027 rounds in August.

NHH in Bergen is the main business feeder: the median gross salary of its master’s class in the 2025 survey was NOK 600,000 for those working in Norway, and 193 of 660 graduates answered. Most NHH graduates working in Norway are in Oslo and Bergen.

BI in Oslo runs one of the largest student-run career fairs, and NTNU in Trondheim is the main source of tech graduates; NTNU’s career service offers online courses on CVs, job applications and interviews.
HK-dir, Norway’s ENIC-NARIC centre, handles recognition of foreign education; not all professions in Norway require recognition of a foreign qualification.
Company presentations on campus in the autumn, with in-person case interviews in Bergen and Trondheim.
The NHH career fair of 4 to 7 September 2023 held its main company day on 7 September with close to 100 companies, and marked 25 years as a link between business and students.
BI’s Karrieredagene takes place every autumn at the Oslo campus, with lectures, courses from BI Career Service, internship presentations and a closing banquet.
DNB recruits its trainees in the autumn; NHH is the main feeder, and its 2025 master’s class had a median gross salary of NOK 600,000 for those working in Norway.

NBIM’s 12-month graduate programme starts with nine months on the AI team and three in a business area, and asks for a completed bachelor’s, master’s, MBA or PhD and up to two years of work experience.
Auditing and consulting have long been the largest destinations of NHH graduates, and the Big Four make offers to students a year before they finish, after a summer internship.
BCG takes visiting associates for a six-week internship that can lead to a full-time role; EY and Accenture ran company courses at the NHH career fair.

Equinor’s graduate programme lasts two years with rotations and gives full Equinor employment with the benefits of the country of work; Aker BP’s offers permanent positions and relocation help to graduates from outside Norway.
NBIM’s 2027 graduate programme is built around its AI team and asks for enthusiasm for AI and a sincere interest in finance; selection includes an AI case-study exercise.

Recent tech graduates report a harder market as consultancies hire fewer juniors, but DNB still runs a graduate programme for developers, IT architects and cybersecurity, and Equinor recruits IT and cybernetics graduates; NTNU in Trondheim is the main source.
DNB’s graduate programme includes a cybersecurity track, with applications closing on 1 October.
Public employers advertise through Jobbnorge, a board run by Grade Jobbnorge AS that also sells recruitment tools to employers; Nav’s Arbeidsplassen lists public and private posts.

The programmes recruit once a year in the autumn or late summer: NBIM took applications from 1 to 15 August 2026, DNB’s IT and cybersecurity programme closed on 1 October, and campus career days fall in September.
NBIM accepts a bachelor’s, master’s, MBA or PhD, completed before the start, and the business-school pipeline is a master’s (NHH’s class is surveyed six months after the master’s).

HK-dir, the Norwegian ENIC-NARIC centre, handles foreign-education recognition; not all professions require recognition, but regulated professions need authorisation or recognition of the professional qualifications.
Firms visit NHH, BI and NTNU, and NHH’s fair has close to 100 companies, but the programmes read name no list of schools and NBIM takes a bachelor’s to a PhD.
The entry for business and engineering students is the summer internship and the programme after the master’s; the sources read show no apprenticeship or dual-study route for graduates.
Public employers advertise on Jobbnorge and Nav’s Arbeidsplassen; the large graduate programmes read are at a sovereign-wealth manager, a bank and energy groups.

Aker BP offers graduates from universities outside Norway relocation help, immigration and work-permit support and language training; NBIM works in English and does not require Norwegian. See Visas for the rules.
A photo is optional on a Norwegian CV; the guide read advises one A4 page, two at most.

Aim for one A4 page, two at most, with a clear layout since paper CVs may be scanned; write in Norwegian for Norwegian postings and in English for English ones, and technology, oil and gas may prefer English.
Most employers expect a cover letter tailored to the company and its industry; if you are not fluent in Norwegian, state your willingness to learn it.
Expat.com lists references among the items on the CV and calls them highly important in spontaneous applications; other guides differ on whether to list them or wait until asked.
A spontaneous application should include a complete CV and your diplomas; the online programme applications read ask for a CV and academic records rather than certified copies.
Norway has no national minimum wage and many industries set minimum pay through collective agreements; the application pages read ask for a CV and letter, not a salary figure.
Expat.com calls references highly important and Equinor’s selection includes an online assessment and video interview; no source read describes background or criminal-record checks for graduates.
Applications through structured programmes and advertised posts work; elsewhere, many jobs are filled through referrals, and contacts made during the internship decide.

Equinor’s selection runs through an online application, online assessment, video interview and a virtual recruitment day; NBIM’s adds online assessments and an AI case study, with online or in-person interviews, and takes documents in English or Norwegian.

Norwegian for most roles outside global energy, tech and consulting teams; many Norwegians speak English, but Norwegian is often required for permanent roles and career advancement, while NBIM’s working language is English.

Equinor’s graduate selection has five steps: online application, online assessment, video interview, virtual recruitment day, then the offer. NBIM’s has five too: CV screening, online assessments (personality profile and psychometric tests), an AI case study, interviews online or in person, then the offer.
Ordinary interviews are straightforward and professional, with questions on experience, technical skills, teamwork, motivation and long-term commitment; punctuality is important.
Dress is professional but modest: creative and tech sectors are more casual, while finance and law expect business attire.
The first step can be very selective: DNB’s summer internship drew close to 500 applications for ten places.

A written contract is mandatory: for employment over one month it must be ready no later than seven days after the start, and a contract cannot set a shorter notice period than the Working Environment Act requires.

A trial period normally lasts up to six months; during it either side gives 14 days’ notice unless otherwise agreed in writing, and afterwards the statutory notice is one month under five years of service, two months over five and three to six months over ten.
Holiday is at least 25 working days a year (Saturdays count, so four weeks and one day); some collective agreements add a fifth week, and the holiday pay rate then rises from 10.2% to 12%.

There is no national minimum wage; collective agreements set minimum pay in many industries. NHH’s 2025 master’s class had a median gross salary of NOK 600,000 for those working in Norway; Equinor’s graduates are full employees with the benefits of the country of work.

Aker BP says graduates from universities outside Norway get relocation help, covering travel costs, housing search, a first-year housing allowance, immigration and work-permit support and language training.
NBIM says English is the working language across the organisation and Norwegian is not required, and application documents can be in English or Norwegian; its page does not mention permits.

Work-visa processing can take several weeks, so ask the employer about permits at the offer stage; the pay floors for a skilled-worker permit are in Visas. No source read describes a labour-market test or a quota.
Posted vacancies: Nav’s Arbeidsplassen (a service from Nav that also links to EURES), FINN.no and Jobbnorge for public employers; Nav’s board can be filtered for English by searching “English”.
Graduate programmes: NBIM, Equinor and Aker BP post theirs on their own career pages, DNB on jobb.dnb.no; Work in Norway offers an employer database and practical information.
University fairs: BI’s Karrieredagene in Oslo every autumn (about 100 companies), NHH’s career fair in Bergen in September, and NTNU’s career service and career days in Trondheim.
Agencies: Manpower, Experis and Adecco focus on tech, engineering and finance.
Missing the late-summer and autumn windows: NBIM’s 2027 round ran from 1 to 15 August 2026, and DNB’s IT and cybersecurity programme closed on 1 October.
Skipping the summer internship: Big Four offers to NHH students come a year before they finish, after a summer internship.
Sending a long CV or leaving out references: aim for one A4 page, two at most, and expect to be asked for references.
Sending a Norwegian CV for an English-language posting, or the reverse: write in the language of the ad, and say you are willing to learn Norwegian if you are not fluent.
Applying to Aker BP without an advertised position: it accepts applications only for advertised positions.

NBIM’s working language is English across the organisation, Norwegian is not required and documents can be in English or Norwegian; no certificate is named, the online assessments and interviews are the evidence.
Aker BP’s graduate page is in English and offers language training to graduates from outside Norway; Expat.com says Norwegian is often required for permanent roles and career advancement.
Technology, oil and gas may prefer an English CV because English is the main working language there; Nav’s board has English-language postings.
NBIM’s AI-team graduate programme works in English and asks for no Norwegian.
Public employers advertise on Jobbnorge in Norwegian; the sources read name no English route, so expect to need Norwegian.
NHH’s survey is answered by 193 of 660 master’s graduates (36%), so its NOK 600,000 median is a self-selected figure for those working in Norway; the 2024 median was NOK 580,000.

91.8% of recent tertiary graduates were in work in 2025, among Europe’s strongest rates, while youth unemployment (15 to 24) was 14.0% and rising from 11.0% in 2023; no source read gives a return-offer rate for Norwegian summer internships.

New Zealand employers fill graduate roles largely from people who have already worked for them: 77% of employers in the graduate employers’ survey filled some or all of their graduate roles with candidates who had done work experience with them.
Word of mouth is one of the channels graduates name as most common and effective, and friends and family influence the job decisions of over two thirds of graduates.
Summer internship to graduate role

In the 2025 surveys, 63% of graduates had worked for their current employer before starting their graduate role, 86% gained industry-relevant work experience during their studies, and 83% of interns want a permanent role with their internship employer.

Deloitte’s summer internship is for students in their penultimate year and ran from 16 November 2026 to 12 February 2027; its graduate roles start on 22 February 2027. Tahatū, the government careers site, advises starting to look for an internship 6 to 9 months ahead.
Competition is also at intern level: 30% of interns submitted eight or more internship applications.
Graduate programme
92% of employers in the 2025 survey have a formal graduate development programme, and 46% spend more than NZ$30,000 on graduate training and development.

The Big Four and mid-tier firms recruit for a February start: Deloitte takes people finishing their studies or within the previous 24 months, from all majors, and Baker Tilly Staples Rodway advertised 20 to 25 places at NZ$50,000 to 60,000 with February or July starts.

Employers do not all open at once: the NZ Government Procurement programme took applications from 17 July to 17 August 2026 for a February 2027 start, and Suncorp New Zealand closed most streams on 31 August for a January start.
Word of mouth and networks

Word of mouth ranks with employer websites, careers expos and LinkedIn as the most common and effective channels for graduates, and for interns word of mouth comes first; friends and family influence over two thirds of graduates and 65% of interns.
Tahatū says many jobs are not advertised, so contacting employers directly is worthwhile, and it names networking as one of the best ways to get a job.
Careers expos and campus events

Careers expos are among the channels graduates and interns use most. The University of Auckland ran a Business and Law expo on 12 March 2026 and an Internship and Graduate expo for all faculties on 29 July 2026.

Firms also come to campuses: the University of Waikato hosted a networking event with PwC, KPMG, Deloitte and EY on 13 March 2024, and Summer of Tech links tech employers with students and graduates through about 100 events a year.
Public Service graduate programmes and internships

NZ Government Jobs lists Public Service vacancies with “Graduate” and “Internship” categories; Tahatū says the government runs internships in the public service, some for students or recent graduates, and points to the Public Service Commission page on graduate programmes.
The NZ Government Procurement Graduate Programme took 10 graduates for two years, with four six-month placements across agencies in Auckland and Wellington.
Direct application and job boards

Employer websites head the channels graduates name, and experienced hires apply the same way or through boards and recruiters: Trade Me Jobs showed 8,880 jobs nationwide on the day it was read, and Tahatū lists recruitment agencies and job boards as sources of vacancies.

Applications for the main graduate cohort cluster in the year before a February start: Deloitte’s graduate roles start on 22 February 2027 and it also lets students finishing mid-year join that national cohort; NZ Government Procurement applied from 17 July to 17 August 2026 for February 2027.
Summer internships fill the Southern Hemisphere break: Deloitte’s ran from 16 November 2026 to 12 February 2027, and Summer of Tech opens candidate registration for its 2027 programme in January.
The market is crowded: 60% of employers saw more graduate applications in 2025, 13% of them by more than 50%, and 41% of graduates received two or more offers.

The Big Four recruit through campus events at the universities, and mid-tier firms run graduate programmes too: Baker Tilly Staples Rodway advertised 20 to 25 places at NZ$50,000 to 60,000, with February or July starts.
Deloitte takes all majors, but Audit, Assurance and Reporting Advisory need prerequisite papers, or bridging papers completed before starting CPA or Chartered Accountants ANZ studies.

Public Service graduate and internship roles are posted on NZ Government Jobs, and some programmes rotate graduates across agencies: the NZ Government Procurement programme placed 10 graduates in four six-month placements.
Summer of Tech helps New Zealand employers hire junior tech talent, with about 100 events a year for students and graduates; registration for its 2027 programme opens in January.
Tech graduates follow the national pattern of hiring people who have already worked for the employer: 63% of graduates had worked for their current employer before their graduate role.

The pages read set eligibility by study status, not school: Deloitte takes people finishing their studies or within 24 months of finishing, from all majors and degrees. Universities still host the expos and employer events through which firms meet students.

The University of Auckland’s 2026 expos were Business and Law on 12 March, Engineering and Technology on 21 and 22 April and Internship and Graduate on 29 July; no 2027 dates were listed. Summer of Tech opens its 2027 registration in January.

Graduate rounds cluster in the year before a February start, with different windows by employer: NZ Government Procurement 17 July to 17 August 2026, Suncorp New Zealand closing most streams on 31 August, Deloitte open by October for a 22 February 2027 start.

The programme pages read ask for a finished degree in any major, not a master’s: Deloitte takes people finishing their studies or within the previous 24 months. A level 8 or 9 qualification matters mostly for the post-study work visa, which now needs level 7 or higher.

NZQA evaluates overseas tertiary and vocational qualifications through an International Qualifications Assessment, and says to check with the organisation you apply to whether you need one; it advises applying only when you hold every required document.
The programme pages read name no target schools: Deloitte welcomes all university majors and degrees, so fit, results and work experience count more than the university name.

The graduate pages read show no dual-study route. Apprenticeship-type pathways exist beside them: Employment NZ lists Māori and Pasifika Trades Training and Skills for Industry pre-trades training as pathways to apprenticeships, but these lead to trades, not graduate roles.

Central government employed about 417,700 people, including education and health; the Public Service is a smaller part, with 42.6% of its workforce in the Wellington region. One graduate programme read there is the 10-graduate Procurement programme.

Some firms take international graduates who already hold work rights: Deloitte accepts a post-study work visa valid for three years. Formal channels carry the programmes (employer websites, expos, LinkedIn) but word of mouth ranks beside them, and friends and family influence over two thirds of graduates.

A New Zealand degree is the clearest route: the post-study work visa is for up to 3 years, and from 16 November 2026 it extends to holders of a bachelor’s degree completed in New Zealand or overseas, plus level 7 graduate diplomas studied in New Zealand.

Deloitte’s graduate selection has four steps: an application with cover letter, CV and academic transcript; a one-way video interview on HireVue; a face-to-face interview; then an offer by phone followed by a contract by email.
Poor communication is the number one reason interns withdraw from a process, and 41% of graduates received two or more offers, so speed and contact between steps matter.
Some employers run rotations rather than one role: the Procurement programme is four six-month placements over two years.
Every employee must have a written employment agreement, and employers should be open to negotiating terms if you ask; terms not written in do not remove the minimum rights set in law.

A trial period can last up to 90 calendar days for someone who has not worked for the employer before, but it must be agreed in the signed agreement before work starts and is not allowed for migrants on an accredited employer work visa. Graduate adverts state a pay band, for example NZ$50,000 to 60,000 at Baker Tilly Staples Rodway, so there is little to negotiate beyond where in the band you start.

Check the work-rights line of each advert first: Deloitte accepts international students who hold a post-study work visa valid for three years and who show evidence of the right to work for the length of the role.

An employer that sponsors an accredited employer work visa must be accredited and hold a job check for the job; the job must be full-time at 30 hours a week or more, and you need 2 years of relevant experience or a qualification at level 4 or higher, where a bachelor’s degree in any field counts.
A level 7 or higher degree studied in New Zealand lets you work for any employer for up to 3 years on the post-study visa, which removes the sponsorship question for a first job.

Portals and boards: NZ Government Jobs for the Public Service, SEEK Grad (GradConnection NZ), which listed 122 graduate and internship programmes the day it was read, Trade Me Jobs, LinkedIn, and Tahatū for advice and tools.

University career services run expos, such as the University of Auckland’s Business and Law, Engineering and Technology, and Internship and Graduate expos, and the New Zealand Association of Graduate Employers publishes the surveys cited here.
Starting the internship search late: Tahatū advises starting 6 to 9 months ahead because some programmes only accept applications at certain times of the year.
Skipping the internship: 77% of employers filled some or all of their graduate roles with people who had worked for them before, and 63% of graduates had worked for their current employer first.
Applying when the round has closed: NZ Government Procurement closed on 17 August 2026 for a February 2027 start, and Suncorp New Zealand closed most streams on 31 August.
Sending a CV with a photo or running past about 2 pages: Tahatū says not to use images and to keep to 2 pages if you can.

Counting on a trial period or visa sponsor: a 90-day trial is not allowed for migrants on an accredited employer work visa, and Deloitte asks international students for a post-study visa valid for three years.
