Oman's job-seeker rate was 3.1% in 2025 and 2.4% in June 2026 (13.2% for ages 15 to 24); among bachelor's holders it was 12.4% for women and 1.3% for men, and 0.5% for master's and doctoral holders; at the end of June 2026 Omanis held 441,737 private-sector and 392,962 government jobs, and in the Employer Survey 2025 47% of private employers had hired graduates with no work experience; no figure for expatriate graduates was found.

Oman reserves a growing list of professions for Omanis, and junior white-collar roles are among the first: marketing specialists, sales representatives and quality-control officers are already closed to new expatriate hires, systems analysts were added from 2025 and programmers and computer engineers from 2026.

Omanis were 21.8% of workers in private and family-run businesses in 2025, so the private market is large for foreigners, but the graduate programmes we could read (PDO, OQ, Oman Airports) are for Omanis, and a foreign graduate is mostly hired as an experienced specialist whose employer proves its Omanisation compliance.
Direct application or recruiter, with the employer obtaining the Labour Clearance

Expatriates were 67.1% of Oman’s 2.7 million workers in 2025 and the private sector held 68.4% of jobs, so most foreign hires come through private employers; the employer applies for the Ministry of Labour clearance, proving Omanisation compliance, and then the visa, which the library puts at 2 to 4 working weeks in practice.

Expatriates in regulated professions (engineering, logistics, accounting) must have their qualifications assessed and approved by accredited sectoral skills units before arrival, and entry permits follow the work practice licence (Gulf News, December 2025).
Graduate programmes of employers (for Omanis)

PDO’s Graduate Development Programme is for Omani staff who join with a bachelor’s degree or above and runs 2.5 to 5 years; OQ onboarded 130 graduates into its 2026 programme under an agreement with the Ministry of Labour for 600 opportunities; Oman Airports’ graduate programme (20 places, deadline 12 October 2025) was for Omani nationals only, with a GPA of at least 3.5, age 28 or under, and registration as a job seeker with the Ministry of Labour.

KPMG Middle East’s two-year graduate development programmes (Advisory, Audit, Tax) are advertised on its Oman page without a stated nationality rule; its selection runs online application, a talent-team meeting, online assessments, an assessment centre and an offer.
Campus recruiting and internship fairs

Sultan Qaboos University’s Career Fair ran on 13–15 April 2026 with Oman Arab Bank among the exhibitors and a Ministry of Labour under-secretary at the opening; Sohar University’s Career Training Fair ran on 2–4 February 2026; the Oman Internship Fair on 26 January 2026 brought more than 65 companies together for students and fresh graduates from four partner universities, including the German University of Technology in Oman.
SQU’s Centre for Career Guidance runs the fair and CV and interview support and gives employers lists of SQU graduates.
Internships through a university or training institution

The library finds no stand-alone internship status: an unpaid or privately agreed placement at a company counts as unauthorised work; a foreign trainee needs a Student Training Visa (OMR 20) requested by an authorised university or training institution, it gives only an allowance, and it cannot be converted to an employment visa inside the country.

There is no national season: fairs fall between January and April (Oman Internship Fair on 26 January 2026, Sohar University on 2–4 February, SQU on 13–15 April), while programme postings come in autumn (the Oman Airports graduate programme was posted on 1 October 2025 with a deadline of 12 October 2025) and intakes start early in the year (OQ’s 130 graduates were onboarded by 4 February 2026).

New expatriate hiring is closed by date, not by season: marketing specialists, sales representatives and quality-control officers from 2 September 2024, systems analysts from 1 January 2025, computer programmers and computer engineers from 1 January 2026, and web designers and operations analysts from 1 January 2027.

For an expatriate the library finds no job-seeker visa and about 30 days of grace after studies end, and the employer’s clearance and visa take 2 to 4 working weeks in practice (7 to 10 working days officially).

Sultan Qaboos University’s Centre for Career Guidance links the university with employers, runs the Career & Training Fair and supplies employers with lists of SQU graduates; Sohar University and the four partner universities of the Oman Internship Fair (Arab Open University, the German University of Technology in Oman, Majan University College and the National University of Science and Technology) give their students the same kind of access.

In the Ministry of Higher Education’s Employer Survey 2025, employers favoured graduates in management, commerce, engineering and information technology, especially bachelor’s holders. We found no page where Omani employers rank foreign universities; a foreign degree needs Ministry of Higher Education equivalency.
Sultan Qaboos University Career Fair: 13–15 April 2026, with Oman Arab Bank among the exhibitors and the Ministry of Labour’s under-secretary at the opening.
Oman Internship Fair 2026: 26 January 2026, 9:00 to 14:00 at The Diplomatic Club in Muscat, more than 65 companies, for students and fresh graduates.
Sohar University Career Training Fair: 2–4 February 2026, an exhibition with public and private bodies and workshops on labour-market skills.

The central bank’s 2013 circular tells banks to strive for Omanisation above 90% overall, with 100% for clerical staff and senior-management targets of 75% and 90%; foreign banks may exempt their CEO or country manager and a single-branch foreign bank may have three non-Omani staff.

Accounting is one of the regulated professions for which expatriates must have their qualifications assessed and approved by accredited sectoral skills units before arrival; KPMG Middle East’s two-year Audit track assesses English, logical and numerical reasoning and accounting online.
PDO’s Graduate Development Programme is for Omani graduates, and OQ’s programme took 130 graduates in 2026; Oman Airports’ graduate programme asked for Omani nationality.

Omanis made up 90.2% of government employment in 2025 and 47.1% of new government recruits held a bachelor’s degree or equivalent; the public sector is a graduate employer for Omanis, not for foreigners.
Marketing specialists and sales representatives are already among the professions closed to new expatriate hires.
IT is being localised step by step: systems analysts from 2025, programmers and computer engineers from 2026, web designers and operations analysts from 2027.
University fairs cluster between January and April and programme postings come in autumn (Oman Airports on 1 October 2025); the pages read show no single national season.

Employers surveyed in 2025 favoured bachelor’s holders, and the Oman Airports programme accepted a bachelor’s or a master’s; we found no posting that treats a master’s as an advantage. This is our reading.

The Ministry of Higher Education requires an equivalency certificate for qualifications issued abroad, in addition to attestation by the embassy and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Oman Observer, 2018); Oman has been party to the Apostille Convention since 30 January 2012, and the library asks for apostilled degrees with a sworn translation. Engineers, logistics and accounting professionals also need a sectoral skills-unit assessment before arrival.

Fairs are run by individual universities (SQU, Sohar University, the Internship Fair’s four partners) and the 2025 employer survey names fields, not schools; we found no ranking of schools by employers. This is our reading.

We found no apprenticeship or dual-study route into graduate jobs; the library finds no stand-alone internship status and describes only curricular internships for students enrolled at Omani universities. This is our reading.

At the end of June 2026 Omanis held 392,962 government jobs and 441,737 private-sector jobs, and they were 90.2% of government employment in 2025; the public sector is a major graduate employer for Omanis.

Every foreign hire needs the employer to obtain the Ministry of Labour clearance by showing Omanisation compliance (the library gives fees of OMR 201 to 301, doubled for non-compliant firms); more than 200 professions are closed to new expatriate visas, and the library finds that junior posts cannot be cleared for foreigners. See Visas for the rules.
A CV guide for Oman says a professional headshot is customary, especially for senior roles, but optional.
The same guide advises a concise one-to-two-page resume for private-sector roles, up to three pages for senior or academic ones, with longer CVs common in government.
The pages read (KPMG’s selection steps, OQ and Oman Airports) mention an online application and no cover letter. This is our reading.
None of the programme pages read asks for references with the application. This is our reading.
Degrees and certificates need the Ministry of Higher Education’s equivalency certificate and, per the library, a double apostille with a sworn translation into English or Arabic.

We found no page saying Omani employers ask for a salary expectation with the first application; the contract states the basic wage, bonuses and allowances. This is our reading for the application stage.

Checks run through the state for a foreign hire: equivalency of the degree, a Ministry of Health medical within 30 days of arrival (blood tests and a tuberculosis test), and, for regulated professions, a pre-arrival qualification assessment. Prosecutors reported 1,200 forgery cases between 2010 and 2016.

Applications run through portals (the Ministry of Labour’s job-seeker service, the Oman Jobs board) and employer pages; a 2016 Huddersfield thesis based on 496 questionnaires in banking, tourism and car retailing found no significant impact from wasta and nepotism on barriers to Omanisation, though it covers Omani employees, not foreign graduates.
Every job needs an employer-sponsored permit, and the employer must meet its Omanisation quota.

The employer must complete the clearance and visa before you arrive; the library says the visa-free 14-day entry cannot be converted to a work visa inside the country (ROP directive of 31 October 2023).

English is standard for multinational firms and Arabic is often required for government and local companies (CV guide); the labour contract must be written in Arabic in two copies, and KPMG’s online assessments include English.

KPMG Middle East’s graduate programmes run six steps: online application, a meeting with the talent-attraction team, online assessments (English, logical and numerical reasoning, accounting), an in-house assessment centre with interviews, a case study and a group activity, an offer, then an onboarding bootcamp.

For the Omani-only programmes the first step is registration as a job seeker with the Ministry of Labour (Oman Airports); for a foreign hire, the library gives 7 to 10 working days officially and 2 to 4 working weeks in practice for the clearance and visa, then a medical within 30 days of arrival.
We did not establish interview language, dress norms or assessment-centre practice beyond KPMG’s steps, nor the selection steps of PDO, OQ or Oman Airports.

The labour contract must be written, in Arabic, in two copies and approved by the competent authority; a fixed term cannot exceed five years, and a contract with no term, an unwritten one, or one that runs on after expiry becomes indefinite.

Probation must be in the contract and cannot exceed three months for monthly-paid workers (two months for others), only once with the same employer, with 7 days’ notice to end it. Notice for a legitimate termination is 30 days for monthly-paid workers and 15 days for others, and the worker gets up to ten paid hours a week to look for a new job.

End-of-service gratuity under the labour law in force since 31 July 2023 is not less than one basic wage per year of service; for expatriates it applies until a savings system funded at 9% of basic wage by the employer replaces it, and we did not establish whether that has started. The employer, not the worker, pays the work-permit fees.
We did not establish whether graduates negotiate, how long employers give to decide, or entry pay.

Ministerial Decree 501/2024 amends Decree 235/2022 and adds professions closed to new expatriate hires in phases (marketing specialists, sales representatives and quality-control officers from 2 September 2024; systems analysts from 2025; programmers and computer engineers from 2026; web designers and operations analysts from 2027), on top of the older list; the Ministry announced in January 2026 that more than 200 professions are covered, and existing workers may stay until their permits expire.

Banks are the clearest case: the central bank’s 2013 circular asks for Omanisation above 90% overall and 100% in clerical posts, so a foreign graduate has little room outside senior or specialist roles at foreign banks. This is our reading of the last point.

Ask early who sponsors, whether the job title is on the closed list and whether the role counts toward Omanisation; the library finds that entry-level and junior posts cannot be cleared for foreigners, and that an employer may dismiss an expatriate to replace him or her with an Omani.

Public services and boards: the Ministry of Labour (mol.gov.om) lets job seekers register, apply for private and government jobs and share their profile with employers; the Oman Jobs board (omanjobs.om) has jobseeker, employer, fresh-graduate or trainee and recruitment-consultant accounts.

Employer pages: OQ’s graduate hiring programme (oq.com/en/careers/graduate-hiring-program, for young Omanis), KPMG Oman’s graduate development programme (kpmg.com/om) and PDO’s Graduate Development Programme (for Omani staff).
University services and fairs: SQU’s Centre for Career Guidance and Career & Training Fair, Sohar University’s Career Training Fair and the Oman Internship Fair in January.

Applying under a closed title: the library says the Ministry of Labour system automatically rejects requests for marketing specialist, sales representative or HR manager roles and, from 1 January 2026, computer programmer or computer engineer.
Starting work, a trial day or an internship after a visa-free entry: the library cites a fine of OMR 1,000 to 2,000, 10 days to 1 month in prison, expulsion and a GCC blacklist.
Planning a post-study job search in the country: the library finds no job-seeker visa and about 30 days of grace, with an overstay fine of OMR 10 a day.
Arriving without the degree equivalency or, in engineering, logistics or accounting, the pre-arrival skills-unit assessment: entry permits follow the work practice licence.
Applying to the Omani-only programmes (PDO, OQ, Oman Airports) as a foreign graduate.

Omanis made up 90.2% of government employment in 2025 and a CV guide says Arabic is often required for government employers; we found no page stating an Arabic level.

Programmers and computer engineers are closed to new expatriate hires from 1 January 2026, and we found no page testing English or Arabic for graduates in software, data or cybersecurity. This is our reading.

These are Omani-population figures: we found no graduate-specific figure for expatriates, and no return-offer or time-to-first-job figure.

In 2025, 91.2% of Polish tertiary graduates aged 20–34 who finished within the last three years were in work (EU 85.3%), unemployment among 15-to-24-year-olds was 12.2% (EU 15.2%, Poland 11.4% in 2023) and 45.2% of 25-to-34-year-olds had a tertiary degree (EU 44.8%).
PKO Bank Polski opened recruitment for the second edition of its paid branch internship on 7 May 2026; the internship ran from 1 July to 30 September 2026 in branches in 20 cities.

KPMG Poland’s World of Audit held workshops on 8, 15 and 22 October and guarantees those who complete them a paid full-time audit internship starting in January; recruitment to the programme has ended for this year.
PwC Poland’s three-month All-Techclusive internship runs from early July to the end of September; recruitment for summer 2026 has closed.

The University of Warsaw’s autumn 2026 fairs are Psychological Career Days on 13 to 15 October, the Faculty of Management career day on 20 and 21 October and an IT job fair on 28 October; past years also had spring fairs in March and a public-sector day in May.

Poland’s largest door for graduates is the business-services sector: 2,081 centres run by foreign and Polish firms employed 488,700 people in early 2025, mostly in Warsaw and Kraków, and they hire juniors in volume, often for their languages. Polish banks, the Big Four and industry recruit through internships and programmes for students still at university.

Students work early and cheaply for employers: a student under 26 on a commission contract (umowa zlecenie) costs no social or health contributions, and income up to PLN 85,528 a year is free of income tax for everyone under 26.
Business-services and tech centres

Finance, risk, IT and customer operations for multinationals; a European language plus English is a paid skill, worth an allowance of about PLN 600 to 2,000 a month. Foreigners were 19.6% of the workforce, and Italians 8.3% of the foreigners.
ABSL counts foreign-owned centres at 84.3% of the employment and intelligent automation in more than 74% of centres, so the entry rung is thinner than the headcount suggests.
Paid internships at banks and the Big Four

PKO Bank Polski’s three-month paid internship for students and graduates ran from 1 July to 30 September 2026 in branches in 20 cities, and the bank says over 60% of interns continue working with it; KPMG’s World of Audit guarantees a paid full-time audit internship from January to those who complete three October workshops.

PwC runs a three-month summer programme in technology from July to September, with four recruitment stages (application, competency tests, language verification and an assessment centre); EY takes interns into audit and tax, with online tests for students and graduates before the interviews.
Working while you study

Student work is the norm and the rules favour it: a student under 26 on an umowa zlecenie pays no social or health contributions, income up to PLN 85,528 a year is exempt from income tax for under-26s, and Warsaw University of Technology says 44% of its graduates had a job before graduating. Foreign students on full-time courses can work without a permit.
University career offices and job fairs

The University of Warsaw Career Office lists faculty-level fairs: Psychological Career Days on 13 to 15 October 2026, the Faculty of Management career day on 20 and 21 October and an IT job fair at the Faculty of Mathematics, Informatics and Mechanics on 28 October; past years added a language fair and a public-sector career day in May.
Tech start-ups and scale-ups

Poland’s IT market is large but junior-thin: of about 111,000 IT postings on Just Join IT in 2025, juniors were 4.79%, while juniors apply about twice as often as experienced candidates. On 8 October 2026 the board showed 668 junior offers among 19,988.
Foreign arrivals add competition: Bending Spoons opened a Warsaw office in September 2026 and reports about 50,000 applications from Poland in the first nine months of the year.
Civil-service competitions and the public job board
The Civil Service job board listed 413 offers from 202 offices in 103 towns on 8 October 2026; you apply to the office that advertises, and a filter shows which offers are open to foreigners.
Open ads, portals and public employment services (the experienced hire)

Experienced candidates apply to open ads on the tech board Just Join IT (where mid-level and senior offers are 6,621 and 11,386 against 668 junior), on company career pages and through the public employment services, which run Zielona Linia.
Automation and a maturing sector are thinning the junior rung: process automation runs in 74.1% of centres and the junior share is falling, while the middle widens.
ABSL’s 2025 report put the centres’ headcount up 6.2% on the year, and 61 centres opened between January 2024 and March 2025, mostly in IT (42.6%) and R&D (26.2%).

Western banks’ Polish centres (Goldman Sachs and others in Warsaw, HSBC in Kraków) hire graduates into risk, finance operations and engineering, not client-facing deal roles; local banks such as PKO recruit in Polish and run branch, risk (zaRyzykuj), corporate-client and ESG internship tracks.

The Big Four take interns every year: KPMG’s World of Audit offers a paid full-time audit internship in 7 offices from January, EY hires audit and tax interns with online tests, and PwC recruits in four stages including an assessment centre. In 2010 the press counted 100 to 200 interns per firm.

Deloitte Poland lists advisory, consulting, audit, tax, legal and its Central Europe business-services centre as the areas open to students and graduates; its page promises a transparent process but gives no stages.
The service centres hire business graduates into finance operations, procurement and customer operations; the language allowance (PLN 600 to 2,000 a month) makes a second language part of the pay.

Poland’s IT market is large but junior-thin: of about 111,000 IT postings on Just Join IT in 2025, juniors were 4.79%, while juniors apply about twice as often as experienced candidates. Warsaw University of Technology says 44% of its graduates had a job before graduating.
PwC’s three-month summer programme offers nine technology paths with a mentor, and KPMG’s online tests cover numerical and verbal reasoning and English.
The state hires through the Civil Service board (413 offers on 8 October 2026), and the University of Warsaw has held a public-sector career day in May to explain internships and recruitment.

Warsaw, Kraków, Wrocław and the other university cities feed their local centres and banks through faculty career days and job fairs; the University of Warsaw’s career office lists them by faculty (management, psychology, IT, languages).
University of Warsaw, autumn 2026: Psychological Career Days 13 to 15 October, Faculty of Management career day 20 and 21 October, IT job fair 28 October.
KPMG’s World of Audit runs three workshops on 8, 15 and 22 October (the last online) before it guarantees an internship offer.

No single national season; programmes keep their own calendars. PKO recruited for its July to September internship from 7 May 2026, PwC’s summer programme runs July to September and was closed to new applicants, KPMG’s World of Audit workshops are in October for a January internship, and university fairs cluster in October and March.

The programmes we read start at the student stage: KPMG’s World of Audit takes students from their 4th year or graduates, PKO takes students and graduates, and nobody asks for a master’s. The centres hire for languages, not for degree level.

Poland’s ENIC/NARIC role is held by NAWA, which took over academic recognition on 1 February 2018 and has separate pages for professional recognition, EU/OECD/EFTA degrees and regulated professions; we could not read the rules on those pages. For a non-EU Blue Card, the degree is documented with a sworn translation.
Employers know the leading universities (Warsaw University of Technology reports 44% of graduates already employed), but no programme we read names a target school.

There is no formal dual-study culture for graduates, but working during the degree is the norm: tax and contribution rules favour students under 26, and 44% of Warsaw University of Technology graduates worked before graduating.
The public sector is small as a graduate employer next to the service centres: 413 offers from 202 offices on the Civil Service board on 8 October 2026, against 488,700 people in the centres.

The centres employ many foreigners (19.6% of staff, mostly from Ukraine, India, Belarus and Italy), but an ordinary non-EU permit needs a labour-market test by the district office and a PLN 400 employer fee; graduates of Polish full-time courses are exempt from work permits. The rules are on the Visas page.
A photo is not required, and the Zielona Linia page says an employer who demands one would not be compliant with the Labour Code, but many recruiters like one.
We found no Polish page that states a CV length; a one-to-two-page CV with the data-processing clause is the safe format.
The portals we read (KPMG, EY, PKO) ask for an online profile or form and a CV; none mentions a cover letter.
We found no page that asks for references with the application.
Employers ask for the CV and the data-processing clause; diploma copies come at the offer stage, and a sworn translation is needed for a Blue Card or recognition.

Since the Labour Code amendment of June 2025, the employer must give you the pay or range in the advert, before the interview or before the contract, and may not ask what you earned in earlier jobs. We found no page on whether forms ask for your expectation.
We found no page on background checks in Polish graduate hiring; banks and the public sector can be expected to check more.

Applications work, especially at the service centres. Add a data-processing consent clause (klauzula RODO) at the foot of the CV: many recruiters expect it, and it is needed if you want to be kept for future openings.
KPMG’s steps are all online, PKO’s interviews are online and the tech and public boards are open to anyone; a non-EU hire from abroad still needs a permit first.
English is the working language in most centres and tech firms, and KPMG tests English online (a 2010 report says the same of the Big Four); Polish is needed at local banks and firms.

KPMG’s process has four steps, all online, with an online test of numerical reasoning, verbal reasoning and English; EY’s is an online profile (about 15 minutes), a review, online tests for students and graduates, interviews in person, by phone or video with the talent team and then the team, and an offer.
PKO Bank Polski’s steps are an online form with CV, a call if you meet the requirements, an online interview that may have two stages, and an answer whatever the result.
PwC’s page lists four stages for its internships: application, competency tests, language verification and an assessment centre. We found no page on dress or on the time from application to offer.

The Labour Code allows a probation contract of up to three months: one month if a fixed-term contract shorter than six months follows, two months if it is six to twelve months, three months otherwise. Notice during probation is three working days for up to two weeks, one week above that and two weeks for three months.

After probation the notice is two weeks below six months of service, one month from six months and three months from three years. Student and intern work is often on an umowa zlecenie rather than an employment contract; PKO’s internship is on one.
The employer must state the pay or range in the advert, before the interview or before the contract; we found no page on negotiation norms, a thirteenth month or the time to decide.

A non-EU hire normally needs a Type A work permit from the voivode, preceded by a labour-market test (the district office’s information, 14 to 21 days) unless the occupation is on the regional shortage list; the employer pays PLN 400 for contracts over three months.

Two shortcuts exist: the EU Blue Card needs a salary of at least PLN 13,355.34 gross a month in 2026, far above entry pay, while a graduate of a Polish full-time course is permanently exempt from permits. A foreign student on a full-time course can work without a permit during the degree.
Raise it at the first interview; centres used to foreign staff will know the process, others will think of the labour-market test. EU and EEA citizens need no permit.

Portals: Just Join IT for tech, the Civil Service board for public posts, the public employment services’ Zielona Linia; career pages of PKO Bank Polski, KPMG, EY, PwC and Deloitte for students and graduates.
Fairs and career offices: the University of Warsaw Career Office lists faculty fairs and career days; KPMG’s World of Audit workshops are held in October.
Business-services centres hire in volume by language; their employers are listed by ABSL, the sector association.
Leaving the data-processing clause (klauzula RODO) off the CV, which many recruiters expect.
Missing the programme window: KPMG’s workshops are three dates in October and its recruitment has ended for this year; PwC’s summer programme is closed for 2026 and starts again in July.
Treating the centres as safe: automation runs in more than 74% of them and the junior share is falling.
Relying on old intake figures: the 100 to 200 interns per Big Four firm quoted in the press date from 2010.
Answering a question about your past salary: since the 2025 amendment an employer may not ask for it.
Western banks’ centres work in English with a second European language as a paid extra; local banks such as PKO recruit in Polish (its pages are in Polish).
KPMG asks for very good English for its audit internship and tests English online; the Big Four’s client work is in Polish. No page states a certificate level.
In the service centres English is the working language and a second language earns an allowance of PLN 600 to 2,000 a month; foreigners are 19.6% of staff.

Tech firms and the Just Join IT board work largely in English, which is why 668 of 19,988 offers are junior and the competition is international; no language certificate is mentioned on the pages we read.
Civil-service posts are advertised in Polish and the board has a filter for offers open to foreigners; we found no page stating a Polish level.
In 2025, 91.2% of Polish tertiary graduates aged 20–34 who finished within the last three years were in work (EU 85.3%), and unemployment among 15-to-24-year-olds was 12.2% (EU 15.2%).

PKO says over 60% of its interns continue working with the bank; Warsaw University of Technology says 44% of its graduates had a job before graduating. We found no national conversion rate for internships.

EU, EEA and Swiss citizens work with no authorisation.
Staying over three months, register your stay at the voivode’s office by the day after the three months end; the certificate is free.
Register your address (meldunek) at the town hall within 30 days of moving in; it gives you a PESEL number at no cost.
Student visa and temporary residence permit
Get the national student visa (D09) at a consulate; the first residence permit lasts 15 months and is applied for online on the MOS portal, where the university signs its part.
Full-time (stationary) students may work without limit and with no work permit; part-time or weekend students need one.
A non-EU student with a permit from another EU country in an EU programme needs no Polish visa or permit for up to 360 days, after the university notifies the Border Guard.

For graduates of the last two years or students outside the EU, with a written traineeship contract at a host approved by the interior ministry; up to six months, renewable once.
Full-time students in Poland can do internships with no permit.
Permit for graduates of Polish universities
After a degree or doctorate in Poland, apply while still lawfully resident: nine months, once, to find work or start a business.
Graduates of full-time Polish programmes are exempt from work permits for life: any employer can hire them directly, with no labour-market test.

A contract of at least six months and a three-year degree, or five years of experience (three in the last seven for IT and managers); no labour-market test, and a spouse may work at once. Apply online through MOS.

The employer first gets a work permit from the voivode, usually after a labour-market test by the job centre, then you get a D visa and apply for the single permit online before the visa runs out.

Researcher permit, and doctoral schools
A master’s degree and a hosting agreement with a research body approved by the science ministry; no work permit is needed for the project.

Poland has working-holiday agreements only with New Zealand, Australia, Canada, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, Chile and Argentina.
For citizens of those countries aged 18 to 30 (35 for Canada): a 12-month D visa with work allowed and no permit, usually not convertible inside Poland.

Up to 90 days in any 180; work only with an authorisation obtained before you start.
Schengen visa
Nothing to arrange in advance: work is open to you, and registration is needed only if you stay more than 3 months.

Since 27 April 2026 every residence application goes through the MOS portal (mos.cudzoziemcy.gov.pl), signed with a Trusted Profile; paper applications are set aside unexamined. For a work permit, your employer completes and signs its annex from a link MOS sends.

Register your address (zameldowanie) at the local municipal office within 30 days of moving in, with passport or ID, residence document or visa, and a lease signed by the owner; EU citizens must once they stay over 3 months, others once they stay over 30 days. It is free; a paper certificate costs 21 PLN.

Staying over 3 months, register your stay at the voivode’s office by the day after the 3 months end; students bring enrolment, a statement of means and the European Health Insurance Card. The paper certificate is free and valid 10 years.

Attend the voivode’s appointment for fingerprints; once the decision is positive, pay 100 PLN to collect the residence card. The stamp duty for the application is 440 PLN for work and 340 PLN for study or research.
The 11-digit PESEL number, needed for tax, work contracts, public health care and digital ID, is given free when you register your address; without a lease yet, you can ask for it for tax purposes.
Your employer must register you with ZUS within 7 days of hiring, which brings public health cover (NFZ). Students under 26 on a civil-law contract (zlecenie) pay no ZUS or income tax.
Students and trainees without a job use the European Health Insurance Card.
Students without cover take private insurance of at least €30,000, or voluntary NFZ insurance at about 55.80 PLN a month for foreign students.

Activate the Trusted Profile (Profil Zaufany), the state’s digital ID and e-signature, in two minutes through a Polish bank (mBank, PKO BP, Santander, Pekao, Millennium, ING, Alior), or online at pz.gov.pl with a check in person at a tax office, ZUS or the voivode’s office. It is free.
The registration certificate lasts 10 years.

File for a new permit by the last day of your legal stay: you then stay legally until the decision, but may work only if you already could, or are renewing a single permit with the same employer and job.

The MOS certificate or the voivode’s stamp is not a travel document: you may leave by a direct route home, but cannot return with it, and must not travel in Schengen once your visa or visa-free days run out.
Since 27 April 2026 residence applications are accepted only online through MOS, which needs a Trusted Profile (Profil Zaufany); paper applications are dismissed.
A pending application does not by itself let you work, and its certificate is not a travel document: you may leave on a direct flight home, but cannot re-enter Poland with it.
Decisions take 6 to 12 months in Warsaw and Kraków, against a legal 60 days.
The switch to the MOS portal and the end of the passport stamp are still settling in.
The Mazowieckie and Małopolskie voivode offices are structurally overloaded.
Banks often refuse an account to people holding only the application certificate.
Private landlords are often reluctant to confirm your address registration.

Lisbon holds about 60% of Portugal’s information and communication jobs and 58% of its finance and insurance jobs, with Porto a clear second; energy, retail and banking groups run graduate programmes there. The one strong card is tax: IRS Jovem exempts most of a young graduate’s income in the first years.

Portuguese is mandatory in the Novobanco and BPI trainee programmes and Jerónimo Martins asks for fluent Portuguese and English; EDP’s Global Graduate Program is the exception, and says Portuguese is not required.
BPI’s 12-month Trainee Program took applications in February and March 2026 and started in September 2026.
Novobanco’s 9-month Young Talent Program took applications from 20 April to 14 June 2026 and started in September 2026.
IEFP’s Estágios +Talento, a six-month internship for graduates up to 35, takes applications from 12 October to 7 December 2026, or until the budget runs out.
IRS Jovem exempts income for those aged up to 35: 100% in the first year of income, 75% in years 2–4, 50% in 5–7 and 25% in 8–10, capped at €29,542; worth about €7,200 in year one at €45,000.
Average gross pay for all Portuguese employees was €1,611 a month in the first quarter of 2026, against a central one-bed rent in Lisbon of about €1,425.

Nova SBE’s master’s in management ranks 2nd in the FT 2026 table, with 100% employed at three months, 93% international students and 10th place for international mobility, so many graduates work outside Portugal.
EDP’s Global Graduate Program is an 18-month programme of three rotations from September, one of them abroad; Portuguese is not required, and the 2026 applications are closed.

Eurostat counts 829,750 people in work in the Porto metropolitan region in 2021: 25,760 in information and communication (second in Portugal, after Lisbon) and 11,690 in finance and insurance (second in Portugal, after Lisbon). The region’s GDP was €39.2 billion in 2022.

Eurostat counts 1,474,000 people in work in the Lisbon metropolitan region in 2021: 79,860 in information and communication (60% of Portugal’s 133,230 and 12th of 152 European metropolitan regions) and 47,950 in finance and insurance (58% of Portugal’s 82,360 and 14th). The region’s GDP was €87.4 billion in 2022, 36% of Portugal’s €242.3 billion.
In the Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) Lisbon ranks 61st in the world, up 14 places, and is outside the Western European top 15.

Startup Genome’s GSER 2026 puts Lisbon’s Ecosystem Value at $35 billion, above the global average of $25 billion, with $316 million of early-stage funding between the second half of 2023 and 2025 against a global average of $554 million.
Startup Genome’s GSER 2026 ranks Porto in the 51st–60th range of emerging start-up ecosystems, in the top ten in Europe for funding runway and the top 20 for its AI-native cluster.
Portugal’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 5.7% in August 2026, and 19.8% for under-25s, against 6.1% and 15.4% in the EU.
In 2025, 83.9% of Portuguese tertiary graduates aged 20 to 34 who left education up to three years earlier were in work, against 85.3% in the EU.
Average monthly gross earnings (ganho) of employees in Portugal were €1,576 in 2024, against €2,121 for establishments in the municipality of Lisbon and €1,930 in Porto.
EDP, the energy group, has its headquarters at Avenida 24 de Julho 12, Lisbon.
Galp, the energy group, has its headquarters at Avenida da Índia 8, Alcântara, Lisbon.
Caixa Geral de Depósitos has its headquarters at Avenida João XXI 63, Lisbon.
The Banco de Portugal, the central bank, has its headquarters at Rua do Comércio 148, Lisbon.
NOS, the telecoms group, has its headquarters at Rua Actor António Silva 9, Lisbon.
Jerónimo Martins, the food-retail group, has its headquarters at Rua Actor António Silva 7, Lisbon.
OutSystems, the software company, has its headquarters at Rua Central Park 6, Lisbon.
REN, the grid operator, has its headquarters at Avenida Estados Unidos da América 55, Lisbon.
Banco BPI has its headquarters at Avenida da Boavista 1117, Porto.
Banco Comercial Português (Millennium bcp) has its registered headquarters at Praça D. João I 28, Porto.
Mota-Engil, the construction group, has its headquarters at Rua do Rego Lameiro 38, Porto.
Sonae, the retail and investment group, has its headquarters at Lugar do Espido, Via Norte, Maia, in the Porto area.

INE’s median rent of new leases, per square metre, in the 12 months to March 2026 was €9.50 in Portugal, €17.22 in the municipality of Lisbon (17,144 new contracts) and €14.29 in Porto (7,574); in the first quarter of 2026 alone Lisbon’s was €17.42. It is a rent per square metre of all homes, not the rent of a one-bedroom flat.

Galp’s Generation Galp, a one-year traineeship for people who have finished or are finishing a master’s degree, has run since 1998 and more than 500 current employees joined through it; the selection runs through screening, an online assessment, group dynamics and a pitch, a business case and a final interview, and the latest applications are closed.

Jerónimo Martins’ Trainee Programme in Portugal, for master’s graduates preferably in management, hotel management, economics, finance, engineering or technology who are fluent in Portuguese and English, began a new edition in January 2026; in 2025 it received more than 1,400 applications and had 11 participants.

Sonae’s Contacto programme, created in 1986, aimed in 2026 to recruit more than 80 young talents who are finalists or recent graduates in fields including economics, management, information technology, data analysis and artificial intelligence; applications closed on 6 April, assessment days were held in Porto and Lisbon in April, the programme starts in September 2026, and pay is promised above the average starting pay of the general “técnico superior” career.
In the Financial Times 2026 master’s in management ranking Católica Lisbon is 25th (three-year average pay $99,125, 97% employed at three months) and Católica Porto 66th ($55,831, 100% employed).

In Portugal many graduates start through a professional internship (estágio profissional), often part-funded by the state employment service, before a firm offers a contract. Large groups and the shared-service and tech centres in Lisbon and Porto also hire graduates directly, some in English.
State-supported professional internship (Estágios +Talento)

IEFP’s Estágios +Talento is open to people up to 35 registered with IEFP who hold a bachelor’s, master’s or doctorate. The gross monthly grant is €1,181.69 at bachelor’s level and €1,289.11 at master’s level; IEFP pays 65% of it, or 80% in some cases, such as when the host hires the intern full-time on a permanent contract within 20 working days.

In an evaluation from 2016, 38% of IEFP interns found a job within 12 months, and only 16% at the firm where they trained. The next application window runs from 12 October to 7 December 2026, or until the budget runs out.
Graduate programmes of banks, energy and retail groups

BPI (12 months), Novobanco (9 months), EDP (18 months), Galp (one year), Jerónimo Martins (two years) and Sonae (Contacto, more than 80 places in 2026) all run annual programmes, mostly with applications between February and June and a September start.
Places are scarce: Jerónimo Martins took 11 people from more than 1,400 applications in 2025. The Big Four also run graduate programmes; KPMG Portugal added 223 recent graduates in 2024.
University job fairs and career days

Técnico’s Jobshop (28 to 30 April 2026) calls itself the largest university job fair in Portugal; Nova SBE’s career fair on 17 September 2026 brought 43 organisations, including Bain, Accenture, KPMG, the ECB and the OECD; Católica’s RUMO in Porto in November 2025 had 67 companies.
Posted vacancies, including shared-service and tech centres
Net-Empregos, which calls itself Portugal’s largest job portal, showed 61,690 active offers on 8 October 2026, with a filter for internships (estágio).

Tech employers in Lisbon are mostly foreign engineering hubs, and recent lay-offs hit junior developers first; Landing.jobs, a tech job platform with an office in Lisbon, also offers visa and relocation help. This is also the usual route for the experienced hire.
Public-sector competitions (procedimento concursal)

Public bodies open competitions under the general public-employment law (LTFP) and publish the notice in the Diário da República and in full on the Bolsa de Emprego Público (BEP). A municipality’s notice of August 2026 for one civil-engineering post gave 10 working days to apply.
Personal recommendation (a cunha)

A personal recommendation still opens doors in smaller firms; international centres and the large groups rely on ads, fairs and structured programmes. No survey read measures how many hires come this way.

Expats rank Portugal last of 31 countries for career prospects, and unemployment among under-25s was 19.8% in August 2026 against 15.4% in the EU; in a slowdown the subsidised internship becomes the main door.

The programme calendar runs from February to June: BPI opened in February and March, Sonae’s Contacto closed on 6 April, and Novobanco took applications from 20 April to 14 June 2026. Most programmes start in September.
The state internship has its own window, from 12 October to 7 December 2026; outside programmes and internships, vacancies are posted all year.

Nova SBE’s master’s in management is 2nd in the FT 2026 table, with 93% international students, and Católica Lisbon is 25th (97% employed at three months); many Nova graduates work outside Portugal, so its pay figure is not Portuguese pay.
Employers recruit visibly at Técnico (Lisbon), Nova SBE and Católica (Porto), where Banco de Portugal, BPI, CGD, KPMG, Deloitte and PwC were among the 67 companies at RUMO.
Foreign degrees need no recognition for most private-sector jobs; the DGES offers automatic recognition for €32.20 if you want a certificate of the Portuguese equivalent.
Técnico Lisboa’s Jobshop, run by the students’ union AEIST, took place from 28 to 30 April 2026 on the Alameda campus, with workshops, roundtables and a finalist check-in.
The Nova SBE Career Fair of 17 September 2026 had 43 organisations from 50 markets, about 2,500 students expected and, for the first time, Citi, the ECB, the OECD and TikTok.
Católica’s RUMO in Porto was held on 12 and 13 November 2025 with 67 companies from banking, pharmaceuticals, IT and human resources, with CV sessions for students.

BPI’s 12-month Trainee Program (applications in February and March, start in September, open-ended contract) takes bachelor’s and master’s graduates in economics, management, engineering, mathematics or IT; Novobanco’s 9-month Young Talent Program accepts any field for corporate profiles.
Caixa Geral de Depósitos, Banco de Portugal and BPI were among the 67 companies at Católica’s RUMO in Porto in 2025.

The Big Four run graduate programmes for economics, management, law, engineering and technology graduates; KPMG Portugal added 223 people through its programme in 2024. KPMG, Deloitte and PwC were all at Católica’s RUMO in Porto.

Accenture, Arthur D. Little, Bain & Company, KPMG and Simon-Kucher took part in the Nova SBE Career Fair of September 2026, which also held Talent Breakfasts for students of the school’s international master’s in management and finance.

EDP’s 18-month Global Graduate Program has three rotations from September; Generation Galp is a one-year traineeship; Jerónimo Martins’ two-year Trainee Programme takes master’s graduates preferably in management, economics or finance.
Sonae’s Contacto, created in 1986, aimed to recruit more than 80 people in 2026 from economics, management, information technology, data analysis and artificial intelligence.

Central and local government hire through competitions under the LTFP, published on the BEP; the post in the notice read was permanent, required a degree in the field and professional-body membership, and was open for 10 working days.

Lisbon’s tech employers are mostly foreign engineering hubs, the largest being Mercedes-Benz.io with about 1,100 people, but recent lay-offs hit junior developers first and hiring now centres on senior engineers. Consultancies such as Capgemini run trainee academies for computer-engineering graduates.
Novobanco’s programme has a technology profile that requires a STEM background, and BPI asks for advanced digital literacy in its IT department.
Sonae’s Contacto lists data analysis and artificial intelligence among its target fields in 2026.

The big programmes recruit once a year: BPI in February and March, Sonae until early April, Novobanco from 20 April to 14 June, the state internship from 12 October to 7 December; ordinary vacancies are posted all year.
Galp and Jerónimo Martins ask for a master’s, while BPI and Novobanco accept a bachelor’s or a master’s degree.

Access to most non-regulated professions is free and depends on each employer; the DGES recognises foreign degrees as a Portuguese bachelor’s, master’s or doctorate (automatic recognition €32.20, within 30 days of a complete file; level and specific recognition at public universities, within 90 days). Regulated professions need the competent professional body.
Programmes and the Big Four visibly recruit at Técnico, Nova SBE and Católica fairs, but the programmes read ask for a degree and tests and name no list of schools.
The entry at graduate level is the professional internship (estágio) of about six months, not a dual-study degree; IEFP’s scheme is for graduates registered with the service.
Public bodies hire through competitions under the LTFP published on the BEP, but the graduate programmes read are all at banks, energy and retail groups and the Big Four.

The residence visa for subordinate work needs a work contract or a promise of one (Lei 23/2007, art. 59), so the employer has to commit before you move; EDP says Portuguese is not required, but Novobanco and BPI make it mandatory. See Visas for the rules.
A headshot is common but not mandatory, usually in the right-hand corner; E-Konomista calls a photo customary in Portugal, unlike in Brazil.
E-Konomista advises one page, two at most, with a 3 to 4 line summary; Expatica says no longer than three sides of A4. Europass is widely recognised, though its templates look dated.
A cover letter (carta de motivação) is not always required but may help you stand out; if sent, it is typed, one page, and addressed to a named HR person where possible.
References are not required in the application; Expatica suggests writing that they are available on request.
Programmes ask for an online application with a CV and academic information; no source read asks for certified or apostilled copies at this stage.
Salaries are often not advertised; they are usually discussed in the first interview, where the interviewer typically asks about your salary expectations (gross, salário bruto).

Labour Code art. 17 bars an employer from asking about a candidate’s private life, health or pregnancy unless strictly necessary and justified in writing; no programme page read mentions a background check.
Large groups and international centres hire through portals, fairs and programmes, while a personal recommendation (a cunha) still opens doors in smaller firms.

The programmes are applied for online, with online tests, a group exercise and interviews; Expatica notes that online or phone screening is increasingly common, though a first interview is usually face to face.

Portuguese is mandatory in Novobanco’s and BPI’s programmes and fluent Portuguese and English are asked by Jerónimo Martins; English is enough at EDP’s graduate programme and in many service and tech centres.

Novobanco’s programme has four stages: an online application, online tests of logical reasoning, behavioural profile and language, a group exercise on business challenges, and individual interviews. BPI adds presentation videos, an assessment centre and final interviews with business managers.
Galp’s selection runs through screening, an online assessment, group dynamics and a pitch, a business case and a final interview.

An ordinary job interview lasts 30 minutes to one hour, usually face to face, with HR or the department manager; some firms add several rounds or a skills test. Use the formal você unless invited otherwise.

Dress follows the job: a suit for senior finance, casual for a start-up. Punctuality is “a must” at work even if relaxed in private life. Candidates may face aptitude, language, personality and technical tests.

Probation (período experimental) on a permanent contract is 90 days for most workers, 180 days for technically complex or highly responsible roles and 240 days for management; on fixed-term contracts it is 30 days from six months’ duration and 15 days below.

The 2019 reform’s 180 days for first-job seekers was declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court, but only for those previously on fixed-term contracts with other employers of 90 days or more.

Portuguese pay is 14 salaries: a holiday subsidy and a Christmas subsidy, the latter due by 15 December, are paid on top of the 12 months, and both can be paid in monthly instalments. Holiday is at least 22 working days a year.

A permanent employee resigns with 30 days’ notice up to two years of seniority and 60 days above; BPI’s trainee programme starts on an open-ended contract, while Novobanco’s is a 9-month paid project. Pay is usually raised in the first interview, not after the offer.

The residence visa for subordinate work requires a work contract or a promise of one, or recognised qualifications and an individual expression of interest from the employer (Lei 23/2007, art. 59 n.º 5); the article does not set a quota or labour-market test, so ask for the contract or promise early.
Highly qualified work needs a contract of at least six months at a minimum pay set in the law (art. 61-A), so raise the permit at the offer stage.

Most graduate programmes read do not state a nationality rule; Novobanco and BPI make Portuguese mandatory, Jerónimo Martins asks for fluent Portuguese and English, and EDP says Portuguese is not required.

Nova SBE’s career fair, with 43 organisations from 50 markets and an international focus, and Landing.jobs, which offers visa and relocation help, are where employers used to hiring across borders are easiest to find.
Posted vacancies: Net-Empregos (61,690 active offers on 8 October 2026), the IEFP portal for job offers and registration, and Landing.jobs for tech.
Graduate programmes and fairs: Talent Portugal lists trainee programmes (BPI, Novobanco) and a fair calendar; the employers’ own pages carry EDP, Galp, Jerónimo Martins and Sonae.
University fairs: Técnico’s Jobshop (April), the Nova SBE Career Fair (September 2026) and Católica’s RUMO in Porto (November).
Public sector: competition notices appear in full on the Bolsa de Emprego Público (BEP) and as an extract in the Diário da República.
Missing the window: BPI opened in February and March, Sonae closed on 6 April, Novobanco ran 20 April to 14 June, and the state internship runs only 12 October to 7 December 2026.
Applying to a programme where Portuguese is mandatory without it, or assuming English is enough: only EDP says so, and Jerónimo Martins asks for fluent Portuguese and English.
Sending one generic CV: E-Konomista lists generic CVs, unexplained gaps, keyword stuffing and an objective statement as errors, and recommends a summary of 3 to 4 lines tailored to each application.
Treating the odds of a big programme as normal: Jerónimo Martins took 11 people from more than 1,400 applications in 2025, so apply to several programmes and keep the internship route open.
Arriving late: punctuality is a must at work in Portugal even if time is relaxed in personal life.
BPI asks for a proficient command of English and makes Portuguese mandatory; Novobanco’s online tests include language proficiency and Portuguese is mandatory.
Jerónimo Martins asks for fluent Portuguese and English; EDP’s Global Graduate Program is the exception, saying Portuguese is not required.
The foreign engineering hubs in Lisbon and the Landing.jobs platform advertise across Europe, so English is often enough there; Novobanco’s technology profile still lists Portuguese as mandatory.
Public competitions are published in Portuguese in the Diário da República and on the BEP, and the selection runs in Portuguese; expect to need it.
The 38% of IEFP interns in work within 12 months (16% at the same firm) is from a 2016 evaluation, before the current +Talento scheme, and is the only conversion figure found.

In 2025, 83.9% of Portuguese tertiary graduates aged 20 to 34 who left education up to three years earlier were in work, against 85.3% in the EU, while unemployment among under-25s was 19.8% in August 2026.

Nova SBE’s 100% employment at three months comes with 93% international students and a high mobility rank, so it does not measure staying in Portugal; no source read gives the share of programme graduates who stay.

Get the D4 visa at a consulate before you travel; it carries your appointment with the migration agency AIMA, where you receive the residence permit.
Students may work, employed or self-employed, with no fixed cap on hours as long as the work stays secondary to studying; no separate authorisation is needed.
A non-EU student with a student permit from another EU country can study here up to 360 days with no visa, once AIMA is notified.

Up to 90 days in any 180, with no work. Arriving through another Schengen country and not staying in a hotel, send an entry declaration to AIMA or the police within three working days; missing it costs €60 to €190.

Workers up to 35 pay no income tax in their first year, then 75%, 50% and 25% of it is exempt over ten years, on up to €29,542.15 a year.
Researchers, university teachers and staff of certified R&D and tech projects who were not tax-resident in the previous five years pay a flat 20% for ten years.
Insist on a lease the landlord registers at the Finance Portal, with electronic rent receipts: it is your proof of residence for every later step.

Get the residence visa at a Portuguese consulate before you travel (€110 for work, valid 120 days, with your biometrics appointment at AIMA): since the expression-of-interest route closed in 2024, entering without one leaves no way to regularise and risks a 3 to 5-year Schengen entry ban.
Foreign criminal records expire 90 days after issue, so do not request them too early.

Get a certificate of residence (atestado de residência) from the parish council (junta de freguesia) with your registered lease; without one, two residents registered to vote in the same parish must sign in person that you live there.

Staying over 3 months, register within the following 30 days at the town hall (câmara municipal) for the EU citizen registration certificate (CRUE): €15, valid 5 years, with ID, tax number and work contract or employer’s statement. Missing the window costs €400 to €1,500.
At your AIMA appointment you apply for the temporary residence permit: for work €247.30 at the desk or €185.60 online; the first permit lasts 2 years, then renews for 3.

First get a 9-digit tax number (NIF) from the Tax Authority: you need it for work, leases, utilities, bank and university. EU residents need no tax representative; others can avoid one by accepting the tax office’s electronic notifications.
Then ask for a social security number online (“NISS na Hora”) with passport and NIF; it is issued in 24 to 72 working hours and needed for any job.

Register at your local health centre for a national health service user number (número de utente), with ID, NIF, the parish residence certificate and your residence document or receipt, to get a family doctor.
The registration certificate lasts 5 years.
The AIMA receipt with a QR code makes your stay legal and lets you work while you wait, but only in Portugal: until you hold the card, fly home only on direct flights with no Schengen stopover.
The 5 years for citizenship count from the day you applied for the permit, not the day it was granted.
The AIMA receipt and Portugal’s extensions of expired visas are valid only in Portugal: fly home only on direct flights, never through another Schengen airport, until you hold the card.
Criminal-record certificates expire 90 days after issue: request them too early and the application is rejected.
Insist on a lease registered with the tax office and electronic rent receipts; without one, the parish residence certificate needs two local voters as witnesses.
Registering for the CRUE after your 120th day can cost a fine of €400 to €1,500.
AIMA appointments and “fast-track” services sold on social media are scams: the only channel is aima.gov.pt.
The qualified job-seeker visa waits for the order listing eligible skills; its funds requirement (€2,760 or €3,280) is also unconfirmed.
AIMA appointments for new visas and family reunion often take 6 to 12 months, beyond the 120-day visa.
Lisbon and Porto town halls may ask EU citizens for a work contract and parish certificate, beyond the sworn statement the law requires.
Getting the parish residence certificate is hard for people renting informally, a large part of the market.
Whether tax offices apply the exemption from a tax representative to non-EU residents who accept electronic notices.

Graduate evidence is thin: the graduate programmes of the sovereign fund and of QatarEnergy are for Qataris, and no source read gives jobs by role. Read the UK’s advice on regional attacks.

Qatar’s labour law, Qatarisation rules and sponsorship practice for graduates are fully verified in visas_immigration/qatar/qatar_visas_immigration_guide.md.
Entry for EU passports and tax were not researched; average pay is whole-country and by activity, with no entry pay and no figure for Doha alone.
