The Qatar Investment Authority’s one-year Journey graduate programme requires a Qatari national or the child of a Qatari mother; its international hiring is for highly experienced specialists.

The Qatar Financial Centre onboarded 1,135 firms in the first half of 2026, 37% more than a year earlier, for a total of over 4,700; the largest groups of new firms were technology and innovation (544), media (173) and consulting and professional services (166).

The UK Foreign Office reports strikes and retaliatory attacks by Iran in the region, Qatar included, since 8 July 2026, and warns of flight cancellations and airspace closures; it does not advise against travel to Qatar as a whole.

The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) ranks Doha 52nd of 117 financial centres (48th in the March 2026 edition), fifth in the Middle East and Africa after Dubai (9th), Abu Dhabi (13th), Casablanca (38th) and Riyadh (46th); Kuwait City is 60th.

Startup Genome’s 2026 report counts over 300 technology start-ups in Qatar, which raised $58.7 million (QAR 214 million) of venture funding in 2025, nearly double the year before, with 93% of deals at early stage and more than 22 incubators and innovation platforms.
Qatar’s real GDP grew 2.9% in the third quarter of 2025 against QAR 180.9 billion a year earlier, with non-hydrocarbon activities up 4.4% and 15 of 17 economic activities growing.

In 2023 Qatar’s 28,856 paid workers in financial and insurance activities averaged QAR 29,403 a month and its 25,965 in information and communication QAR 28,517, against QAR 11,025 for all 2,171,062 paid workers (author’s weighting of the male and female averages).
The National Planning Council’s open data give Doha municipality 1,186,023 residents, about 40% of the country, from the 2020 census base that its tables repeat for 2020 to 2024.

Standard employment contracts in Qatar are registered in Arabic and English on the Ministry of Labour portal, EY's Doha graduate programme for nationals asks for excellent written and verbal communication in Arabic and English, and Qatar Living's CV guide says Arabic matters more for government, semi-government and some customer-facing roles; no source measured English at work.

Graduate recruiting in Qatar runs on university fairs rather than one national season: the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies held its 9th fair on 21 January 2026 with about 30 organisations, the Qatar Foundation Alumni Office its Education City Job Fair on 15 February 2026 for Qatar Foundation students and alumni, Lusail University its third fair on 22-23 October 2025, and Qatar University's fair of 11-14 September 2023 had 73 employers; QatarEnergy says its graduate assessment may take up to 90 days.

Foreign nationals were 83% of Qatar's private workforce and 94% of its total workforce in 2023, the national strategy aims for 20% Qatari participation in the private and semi-private workforce by 2030, and the World Bank's modelled youth unemployment rate for Qatar was 0.559% in 2025; no graduate-specific unemployment or time-to-first-job figure was found.

QatarEnergy’s graduate pages describe a programme for "recent Qatari graduates", with a selection process that can take up to 90 days, and its vocational and scholarship programmes are for Qataris and children of Qatari women.

Qatar’s flagship graduate programmes are for Qataris: QIA’s Journey Program requires Qatari nationality or a Qatari mother, QatarEnergy’s graduate track is for “recent Qatari graduates”, and EY’s Doha graduate programme read is open to Qatari nationals only. Law 12 of 2024 makes private employers give priority to Qataris, and foreign nationals were still 83% of the private workforce in 2023, so foreign graduates are hired into roles outside the nationalisation scheme, mostly by international firms that sponsor the permit.
Direct application or recruiter, with the employer as sponsor

No survey ranks the routes in Qatar. Aetna’s relocation guide says people outside Qatar usually apply online or through an agency, and may be interviewed by phone or video by a recruiter in Qatar or by an adviser in their home country; the whole process can take weeks or months and Ramadan or summer slows it.
The employer then starts the work visa and the Ministry of Labour approval; the worker cannot start on a tourist or visa-waiver status.
Personal introductions and networking

Aetna’s guide calls regional recruitment informal and “all about connections”, and says word of mouth often finds the next job once you are employed. It is a relocation guide, not a survey of graduate hiring.
Campus recruiting at Qatari universities and the Ouqoul platform

Qatar University’s annual career fair brought 73 employers from energy, industry, finance, business, education and health to its students on 11–14 September 2023; the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies’ 9th fair on 21 January 2026 had about 30 public and private organisations; Lusail University held its third fair on 22–23 October 2025.

The Ministry of Labour’s Ouqoul platform is built for private employers to recruit expatriate graduates of Qatari universities for roles outside the nationalisation scheme; its second phase, with graduate registration, is limited to alumni of universities linked to the platform.
Part-time student jobs and the graduate visa extension (Jusour Sahem)

Jusour’s Sahem programme offers part-time jobs to students at accredited Qatari universities, and The Peninsula reported in July 2023 that it also offers recent graduates of Qatar-based institutions, aged 18 to 28 and on institution-sponsored residence, a one-year visa extension to look for work.

The library’s visa guide finds no stand-alone internship visa: a student or graduate from abroad cannot intern on a tourist or waiver status, so the internship route works for those already resident as students.
National graduate programmes (for Qataris)

QatarEnergy’s graduate track is for recent Qatari graduates and its assessment may take up to 90 days; QIA’s one-year Journey programme requires Qatari nationality or a Qatari mother; EY’s Doha Qatar Graduate Program posting is “for nationals” and runs online assessments, a recorded video interview and a recruitment day before an offer. A foreign graduate cannot use them.
Company transfer

Aetna’s guide writes its benefits section mainly for intra-company transfers and secondments, with health cover and accommodation; for a graduate this is a later route, after a first job at the group elsewhere. This is our reading.

There is no national season: graduate fairs fall in January and February (Doha Institute on 21 January 2026, the Education City Job Fair on 15 February 2026) and in autumn (Lusail University on 22–23 October 2025, Qatar University in September 2023).
QatarEnergy says its graduate assessment may take up to 90 days, so a Qatari applicant starts months before the intended start; the pages read give no opening or closing months for any programme.
For students at Qatari universities, Jusour’s graduate visa extension gives one year to find a job after graduating.

Qatar University’s Career Development Center runs the annual fair and a student-employment programme; the Education City Job Fair is organised by the Qatar Foundation Alumni Office for Qatar Foundation students and alumni only, so access to the fairs follows the university you attend.
Foreign universities do not recruit here: the Ouqoul platform’s graduate side is open only to alumni of Qatari universities. We found no ranking of schools by Qatari employers.
Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, 9th Career Fair: 21 January 2026, 9:00 to 16:00, about 30 public and private organisations, mainly for its own students and graduates.
Education City Job Fair 2026: 15 February 2026, organised by the Qatar Foundation Alumni Office for Qatar Foundation students and alumni only.
Lusail University Career Fair: 22–23 October 2025, its third edition, under the patronage of the Minister of Labour, who launched the university’s link to Ouqoul.
Big Four graduate roles in Doha may be sponsored by the local firm, unlike Saudi postings that require an existing work right.
EY’s Doha Assurance graduate programme read is for Qatari nationals with excellent written and spoken Arabic and English; we could not open any posting that is open to foreign graduates.

QatarEnergy’s graduate programme is for recent Qatari graduates, who may be posted to any QatarEnergy location; companies tied to QatarEnergy and petroleum operations are exempt from Law 12’s Qatarisation duties.
QIA’s one-year Journey graduate programme requires a Qatari national or the child of a Qatari mother; its international hiring is for highly experienced specialists.

Law 12 of 2024 makes private employers give priority to Qataris and children of Qatari women and hire expatriates only if no suitable Qatari is available; priority-group job seekers register with the Ministry of Labour.

Qataris are targeted at 20% of the private and semi-private workforce by 2030 under the national development strategy, after Law 12 of 2024 came into force in April 2025; IT roles for foreigners are mostly experienced hires.
University fairs cluster in January and February and in September and October; the pages read show no single national season and no programme with published opening months.
No posting or programme page read asks for a master’s degree; the national programmes read ask for being a recent graduate and, for EY, fluent Arabic and English. This is our reading.

Qatar Living describes a chain for every degree: the home-country higher-education authority, the home foreign ministry, the Qatari embassy, then Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs with the bonafide letter, transcript and degree. The library notes Qatar is not in the Hague Apostille Convention, and engineers and architects must also register with the Ministry of Municipality.

Access to fairs follows the university you attend (Education City’s is for Qatar Foundation students and alumni only; the Ouqoul graduate side is for alumni of linked Qatari universities); we found no ranking of schools by employers. This is our reading.
We found no apprenticeship or dual-study route into graduate jobs; the library finds no stand-alone internship visa, and Sahem part-time jobs are for current students. This is our reading.

State-linked bodies run the headline graduate programmes (QatarEnergy, QIA) but they are for Qataris; we found no figure for the public sector’s share of graduate hires, so for a foreign graduate the weight is our reading.

Residence is tied to an employer-sponsored work visa and the Ministry of Labour approves each quota; Law 12 lets employers hire expatriates only when no suitable Qatari is available, and the Ouqoul platform targets expatriate graduate roles outside the nationalisation scheme. See Visas for the rules.

Qatar Living’s CV guide (August 2026) says a professional headshot is commonly expected in Qatar and the Gulf, especially in the private sector and client-facing roles, though some employers treat it as optional and a few prefer none.
The same guide says a first-job CV should be one tight page; it also asks for nationality, date of birth and often marital status on the CV.
None of the programme and posting pages read mention a cover letter; EY’s nationals programme runs on an application, online assessments and a recorded video. This is our reading.
Qatar Living lists references as an optional last section of the CV that is commonly included; none of the programme pages read asks for them with the application.

A foreign degree goes through the attestation chain ending at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Qatar, and the library’s visa guide requires legalised degrees and certificates because Qatar is outside the Apostille Convention.

We found no page saying Qatari employers ask for a salary expectation with the first application; the contract is registered on the Ministry of Labour portal, and the legal minimum is QAR 1,000 basic plus QAR 500 housing and QAR 300 food. This is our reading for the application stage.

The state does the checking for a foreign hire: degrees are attested at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the library’s guide has a medical commission screening and a fingerprint record at the Ministry of Interior before the residence ID is printed.
Aetna’s guide calls regional recruitment informal and built on connections, with introductions valued; recruiters and agencies handle applications from abroad.

Applications and first interviews can be made from abroad by phone or video, and the library says the electronic work-entry visa is issued before travel; the medical test, fingerprints and ID card follow in Doha, and work cannot start on a tourist or waiver status.

English is the usual language of the international firms and free-zone companies, and standard contracts are registered in Arabic and English; Qatar Living says Arabic matters more for government, semi-government and some customer-facing roles. This is our reading for English at work; no source measured it.

EY’s Doha graduate programme for nationals runs five steps: apply, online assessments, a prerecorded video interview answering behavioural questions, a recruitment day or interview if shortlisted, then an offer. QatarEnergy says its graduate assessment may take up to 90 days.

From abroad, Aetna says you may have a phone or video interview with a recruiter in Qatar, and some processes include a trip to Qatar to meet key contacts over several days; Ramadan and summer slow things down. We did not establish interview dress norms or assessment-centre practice for foreign graduates.

Probation may last up to six months, and only once with the same employer; an employer ending it for unfitness must give at least one month’s notice. Standard contracts are registered in Arabic and English on the Ministry of Labour portal.

Commoner Law’s guide gives notice of one month up to two years of service and two months beyond (its own citations show a five-year threshold, so check the statute), and an end-of-service gratuity of at least three weeks of basic pay per year after one full year.

The legal minimum is QAR 1,000 basic plus QAR 500 for housing and QAR 300 for food, and the employer pays the work visa, medical and ID fees. We did not establish whether graduates negotiate, how long employers give to decide, or entry pay.

Law 12 of 2024, in force from April 2025, makes private employers give priority to Qataris and children of Qatari women; expatriates may be hired only if no suitable Qatari is available. Employers must notify the Ministry of Labour of vacancies, report new employee data every six months and train Qataris; penalties run from warnings to suspended immigration transactions and fines of up to one million riyals.

Companies tied to QatarEnergy and petroleum operations are exempt, and the Ministry may set a Qatari percentage for each sector once the Cabinet approves its plan. Foreign nationals were 83% of the private workforce in 2023, against a national target of 20% Qatari participation by 2030.

The library records that Decree-Laws 18 and 19 of 2020 removed the no-objection certificate for changing employer and Law 13 of 2018 the exit permit for most private-sector workers; the employer must still obtain the Ministry of Labour quota and the work visa. Ask early who sponsors, which entity employs you and whether the post sits inside the nationalisation scheme. This is our reading for the last point.

Public and platforms: the Ministry of Labour’s Ouqoul platform for private employers recruiting expatriate graduates of Qatari universities, and Jusour’s Tawzeef (an AI-assisted platform linking job seekers with employers and recruitment agencies) and Sahem (part-time student jobs and the graduate visa extension).

Employer pages: QatarEnergy’s careers portal (careerportal.qatarenergy.qa, graduates for Qataris), and EY Qatar’s graduate postings for nationals; we could not open the Qatar Airways, QNB or other Big Four pages.

University services and fairs: Qatar University’s Career Development Center (counselling, employer relations, a student-employment programme and the annual fair), the Doha Institute’s January fair, the Education City Job Fair for Qatar Foundation students and alumni, and Lusail University’s October fair. Qatar Living’s career-fairs guide lists the year’s events.
Applying to the national programmes (QatarEnergy graduates, QIA Journey, EY for nationals) as a foreign graduate: they require Qatari nationality or a Qatari mother.
Starting work, a trial day or an internship on a tourist or visa-waiver status: the library cites Law 21 of 2015, with fines up to QAR 50,000, up to three years in prison and expulsion.
Leaving the country after entering on the work visa but before the residence ID is printed: the library says the entry visa lapses and the process restarts.

Leaving the degree unattested: every degree goes through the home-country chain and the Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and Qatar is outside the Apostille Convention, so start the chain before the offer.
Treating a Qatar University or Education City fair as open to all: Education City’s is for Qatar Foundation students and alumni, and the Doha Institute’s is aimed at its own students and graduates.
EY’s Doha graduate programme for nationals asks for excellent written and verbal communication in Arabic and English; we found no posting for foreign graduates that states a level.

Standard employment contracts are registered in Arabic and English, and the Qatar Living CV guide asks you to state your Arabic level and says Arabic matters more for government, semi-government and some customer-facing roles. No source tested English at work; this is our reading.

Law 12 of 2024 gives Qataris priority in private jobs, and Qatar Living says Arabic matters more for government and semi-government roles; the national programmes read are for Qataris and run in Arabic and English.
IT postings for foreigners are mostly for experienced staff, and we found no page testing English or Arabic for graduates in software, data or cybersecurity. This is our reading.

The World Bank’s modelled youth unemployment rate for Qatar was 0.559% in 2025 (0.573% in 2024); it is a modelled series and says nothing about graduates specifically, and we found no return-offer or time-to-first-job figure for Qatar.

Foreign nationals were 94% of Qatar’s total workforce and 83% of its private workforce in 2023, so the market for a foreign graduate is large, but roles inside the nationalisation scheme are reserved for Qataris.

Student visa and student QID

Qatar University, HBKU or an Education City campus sponsors the visa, converted on arrival into a student residence permit after the medical and fingerprints. You need proof of funds or a full scholarship.
Qatar is not in the Apostille Convention: previous degrees need the full consular legalisation chain. Students may work only on campus, up to 20 hours a week, or in internships registered on Sahem.
Fees
visa QAR 200 + medical QAR 100 + QID QAR 500
Internships

There is no internship visa. Internships through Sahem are only for students already resident in Qatar; an internship on a visa waiver is illegal work, and companies almost never sponsor a temporary work visa for one.
Graduating student extension
Graduates of a Qatari university aged 18 to 28 can extend residence one year to look for work, and move to an employer without leaving. Others get a 30-day grace period.
Work visa and QID

The employer obtains a quota and registers your contract with the labour ministry, then issues the work entry visa; in Doha you complete the medical, fingerprints and Qatar ID within 30 days. The employer must pay every visa and recruitment cost.
Since 2020 you may change employer without a no-objection certificate, giving one or two months’ notice. The QFC and free zones process skilled hires faster.

Qatar has no working-holiday agreements; unauthorised work means up to three years in prison, a QAR 50,000 fine and a Gulf-wide ban.

Qatar is not in the apostille convention: Italian and EU documents and degrees go through a five-step consular legalisation chain, ending at the Foreign Ministry in Doha.

After the infectious-disease screening at the Medical Commission, the Qatar ID (QID) is printed, valid 1 year (QAR 1,000, paid by the company), and sent by Q-Post. Do not leave Qatar before it is printed: the entry visa lapses and the process starts again from abroad.
A positive result for HIV, hepatitis B or C, or lung scars from tuberculosis, even healed, means the permit is refused and you are deported.
The QID number is your identifier for government services through Metrash.
Health insurance is compulsory for all non-Qataris; for residents, your employer pays it in full.

Open an account with your employer’s salary certificate; it is linked to the Wages Protection System. Landlords usually ask for 12 post-dated cheques: a bounced cheque is a crime that brings a travel ban, and the bank freezes the account when the final settlement arrives at the end of a job.
Neither the entry stamp nor the application receipt lets you work: working before the work visa is issued is a crime punished with arrest, fines up to QAR 50,000 and deportation.
Leave Qatar before the Qatar ID is printed and the entry visa lapses: the process restarts from abroad.

Family visas formally need QAR 10,000 a month (6,000 with company housing); salaries in between are decided case by case.
Sector quotas for hiring Qataris are set by changing ministerial decrees.

Country brief: hubs, employers, pay and standing

Graduates in Romania most often enter through the software, engineering and shared-service centres of international firms in Bucharest, Cluj, Iași and Timișoara, which recruit students through internships and hire in English. Local firms lean more on contacts.
Internships at international and tech firms

No survey ranks the routes in Romania; this is first because the programmes found are mostly internships. Junior specialists in the service centres earned a mean of about €1,625 a month gross in 2024.
UiPath’s Bucharest software internship is a three-month, full-time, paid summer placement, and its listing says successful interns have the possibility to become full-time employees.
Stagii pe Bune, a summer internship scheme for IT students in Bucharest and Iași, says it has offered over 8,000 internship positions in 18 years and had more than 16,000 student applicants.
Graduate and trainee programmes

Vodafone Romania’s Discover Graduate Programme runs for two years, rotates participants through three business areas and can end in a destination role; applications are in English, and the 2027 intake closes on 6 November 2026 for a start on 11 January 2027.

KPMG’s Business School audit internship has asked for top students in economics, polytechnic or mathematics studies and runs for two years in Bucharest or eight months in Timișoara and Cluj; the listing read was for the 2024 campaign and is closed.
Career days and job fairs

The University of Bucharest’s career department held Career Days on 13–14 November 2024 with 11 employers in person and five online; Politehnica Timișoara’s twice-yearly fair reached its 24th edition in 2024 with 55 firms.
Hipo.ro lists its Angajatori de TOP fairs in Timișoara on 16–17 October 2026 and in Bucharest on 30–31 October 2026.
Direct application through job portals

EURES names BestJobs, eJobs, Hipo and Lugera&Makler as the main private portals, and says employers must declare all vacancies to the national employment agency ANOFM, whose listings are in Romanian only.

For experienced hires, ABSL’s 2025 report says business-services recruitment has become more cautious, with employment growth slowed to an average of 5%, and that companies want experienced professionals with specialised expertise.
Public-sector competitions
Civil-service posts are filled by competitions run on the ANFP’s national portal (concurs-national.anfp.gov.ro), by post or in an extended national competition.
The government portal posturi.gov.ro pools vacant contractual posts of public bodies and showed about 2,585 active posts across 3,230 institutions on the day it was read.
Referrals and contacts
At local, family-run and smaller firms, being introduced by someone who works there counts for more than a portal application. This is our reading; no survey was found.
Vodafone’s graduate programme closed on 15 November 2025 for a start on 12 January 2026, and on 6 November 2026 for a start on 11 January 2027: apply in the autumn for January.

Internships are mostly summer ones: UiPath’s lasts three months and Stagii pe Bune describes its placements as summer practice, so the applications that matter are in the spring and earlier. We did not read their opening dates.
University fairs fall twice a year: Politehnica Timișoara’s was in April 2024, the University of Bucharest’s in November 2024, and Hipo’s Angajatori de TOP are in October 2026.

A resignation notice cannot exceed 20 calendar days for operational posts or 45 for management. Full-time is 40 hours a week; the minimum gross wage from 1 July 2026 is RON 4,325 a month. Fixed-term contracts can run up to 36 months.

For a non-EU hire the employer files for a work authorisation (aviz de angajare) with the immigration inspectorate: vacancies must not be fillable by Romanians, EU/EEA citizens or permanent residents, and hiring must fit the annual quota set by government decision.

The fee is €100, or €25 for a foreign student hired after graduation; the inspectorate decides within 30 days, extendable by up to 15, and the employer must have operated for at least one year in the field and owe nothing to the state budget.
The library’s visa guide records the 2026 quota as 90,000 newly admitted foreign workers (Government Decision 1,169/2025), and EU Blue Card hires as exempt from the quota and the labour-market test.
Ask early, at the first interview or in the application, and ask whether the employer has filed the procedure before. This is our reading; no page states what employers want to hear.

The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Russia because of its continuing invasion of Ukraine; it reports an increased risk of British nationals being detained, Russia’s record of holding foreign nationals as leverage, a high likelihood of terrorist attacks, and drone attacks disrupting airports.

The US State Department rates Russia Level 4, do not travel, citing the war with Ukraine, the risk of wrongful detention, arbitrary enforcement of laws and terrorism, and tells US citizens in Russia to leave immediately.
St Petersburg is Russia’s second-largest city; its gross regional product in 2023 was RUB 10,908 billion, about EUR 117.5 billion at the official average exchange rate.
The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) ranks Moscow 100th and St Petersburg 104th of 117 financial centres (103rd and 110th in March 2026), the only Russian centres listed.

The Fortune Global 500 of 2026 lists Sberbank (rank 64), Rosneft (109) and Lukoil (239) as headquartered in Moscow and Gazprom (89) in St Petersburg; Fortune gives them 291,795, 302,100, 88,950 and 501,000 employees. Fortune’s pages say nothing about sanctions: read the sanctions claim before any dealings with Russian companies.
The mayor of Moscow told President Putin that the city had 13.3 million residents on 1 January 2025, after natural growth of 4,800 in 2024.

The rating agency Expert RA, citing the Moscow city government’s own estimate, reports Moscow’s gross regional product in 2023 at RUB 31.8 trillion, 4.0% more than in 2022 in comparable prices, and says the city accounts for about 20% of the GRP of all Russian regions.

St Petersburg had 5.563 million residents on 1 January 2025 according to Petrostat, the regional statistics service; a Centrum Balticum policy briefing notes that Gazprom has moved its head office to the city from Moscow, and that foreign-trade statistics for the port stopped being published after April 2022.

Large Russian employers such as Yandex and Sber recruit students through paid internships of three to six months, and the job site HeadHunter ranks universities by how much employers want their graduates, with HSE University first. The UK and US advise against travel to Russia and EU sanctions bind EU persons, so for most readers of this guide this describes the Russian market rather than a route to take.
Paid internships at large IT and finance employers

No survey ranks the routes in Russia; this is first because the large employers found recruit this way. Yandex planned 2,800 interns in 2025, 20% more than the year before, paid under the Labor Code for three to six months, and says 54% of its 2024 interns moved to full-time posts.

Sber’s internship through its School 21 lasts three to six months on a temporary employment contract and pays 73,700 RUB a month at full employment in Moscow; it is a chance to receive an offer of permanent work.
Job boards: hh.ru and SuperJob
hh.ru is the largest Russian job board and has a section for young specialists; SuperJob’s Start of Career section promotes practice and internships with leading employers.
University career centres and job fairs
MISIS’s spring job fair on 30 March 2026 brought together 5,200 students and about 60 employers, with express interviews and job invitations.

HSE University’s Career Development Centre lists vacancies and internships, offers over 500 consultations a year and reports over 150 partner companies; its project career schools in 2026 were run with Avito, PSB and Yandex Cloud.
Referrals and networks
We found no survey of how much introductions count in Russian graduate hiring; this is our reading that they matter at smaller firms.
Spring is the visible season: MISIS’s fair was on 30 March 2026, and Yandex announced its 2025 internship season on 12 February 2025 with an event for candidates on 20 March.
Internships of three to six months fit the student calendar; Yandex lets interns combine the placement with study. We did not establish opening dates for Sber’s intakes.

HeadHunter’s ranking of 411 universities by graduate demand, built from more than 500,000 graduate CVs from 2021–2022 (published April 2023), put HSE University first overall and first among Moscow universities in law, economics and finance, and in HR and psychology.
HSE’s Career Development Centre and MISIS’s fair both bring employers onto campus; Sber says it values students of its School 21.

Sber runs its own paid internships; its School 21 route lists higher demand for Java, QA, DevOps and systems analysis and lower for Go and mobile development. Check that any Russian bank you apply to is not under sanctions.

Yandex hires interns for frontend, backend, mobile, analytics and machine learning, and since 2025 for marketing and PR, finance, product management, procurement, HR and law; nearly a third of its developers are former interns.
Avito’s project career school “Case laboratory of analytics” ran with HSE in May 2026; Yandex Cloud held a career school on AI solutions for social tasks with HSE in April 2026.
The visible peaks are in spring (MISIS on 30 March, Yandex’s event on 20 March) while the internships themselves run for three to six months; there is no single national season.
The internship pages read target students and recent graduates by level of study, not by degree; we found no page stating that a master’s is expected. This is our reading.

The library’s visa guide says foreign documents need an apostille and a Russian notarised translation: translations sworn in Italy or elsewhere in Europe have no legal value in Russia. We found no page on degree recognition, as the Rosobrnadzor site could not be opened.

HeadHunter publishes a national ranking of 411 universities by employer demand for their graduates, built on more than 500,000 graduate CVs, so the school is something employers measure. This is our reading of that ranking.
Yandex lets interns combine the placement with study and employs them under the Labor Code; we found no formal dual-degree system.
We did not establish the public sector’s weight as a graduate employer: the federal civil-service portal refused our connection. This is our reading.

Hiring a non-citizen runs through an annual quota and a work permit unless the post is on the ministry’s out-of-quota list; for EU and UK passport holders the UK and the US advise against travel and EU sanctions limit dealings with many Russian firms. See Visas for the rules.
hh.ru advises adding a professional, neutral portrait photo to the resume, first in its recommended order with the contacts.
hh.ru sets no page limit but asks for short, simple sentences and five to ten key tasks per job; for a new graduate one page is our reading.
The hh.ru resume form and the internship flows read (Yandex, Sber) use an application, a test and interviews, with no cover letter mentioned. This is our reading.
None of the pages read asks for references with the application. This is our reading.

hh.ru’s resume form puts the desired salary second, after the photo and contacts, and advises setting it 15–20% above current pay and in line with the market.
A foreign employee needs a biometric registration and medical screening after 90 days, and the employer must hold a work permit; we found nothing on routine reference checks for graduates.
Job boards, internships and university fairs take open applications, while smaller firms may lean on introductions. This is our reading.

The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Russia and the US rates it Level 4, do not travel; Yandex’s internship offers remote work only for some directions, and a foreign hire needs a permit and a visa through a consulate. This is our reading.

Yandex: choose a direction and apply online, then a test task, professional interviews and meetings with hiring teams; Sber’s School 21 route has four steps: questionnaire, testing, distribution across teams and formalisation of employment.
University fairs add express interviews on the day (MISIS, 30 March 2026). We did not establish the usual time from application to offer, dress norms or assessment-centre use.

CXC Global says the standard working week is 40 hours, open-ended contracts are the default and a fixed-term contract must be justified in writing, resigning employees generally give two weeks’ notice and salaries are paid at least twice a month.
We did not establish probation length, whether graduates negotiate, thirteenth-month practice or how long employers give to decide.

Hiring a non-citizen needs an annual quota application to the labour ministry by 1 July of the previous year, a vacancy published for at least 30 days at the employment centre, an employer permit, a personal work permit and an invitation; highly qualified specialists are outside the quota.

The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Russia (updated 18 September 2026) and the US rates Russia Level 4; the EU’s 21st sanctions package of 23 July 2026 adds to rules that bind everyone under EU jurisdiction, including bans on providing certain business, legal, IT and other services. Check any offer against sanctions with a qualified adviser first.

Employer programmes: Yandex internships, Sber’s School 21 internship, and the project career schools run with HSE by Avito and Yandex Cloud.

Internships

There is no internship visa. Students enrolled in Russia are covered; others can come only through a university traineeship on a study visa, or be hired as ordinary or highly qualified employees. An internship on a business or tourist visa means expulsion.

The RVPO stays valid 180 days after graduating, with the right to work. RVPO holders can apply for a permanent residence permit within three years of graduating, honours graduates at once; other graduates get a temporary permit outside the quota.

Riyadh is the finance and headquarters centre, with hundreds of multinationals licensed to set up regional headquarters there, and Dhahran is Aramco’s home. Every job is employer-sponsored. Read the UK’s advice on Houthi attacks, including on Riyadh.

No employer-stated entry pay for expatriate graduates was found.

Where demand is now
The Public Investment Fund’s 12-month Graduate Development Program is aimed at, and open only to, Saudi nationals; 1,033 graduates have enrolled over nine cohorts.

The labour ministry announced in January 2026 Saudisation of 60% in marketing and sales professions (in force from 19 April 2026), 30% in 46 engineering professions (from 30 June 2026) and 70% in 12 procurement professions, and announced a new phase from 2026 to localise more than 340,000 private-sector jobs.
Since 25 March 2024, 40% of roles such as business consultant, financial-advisory specialist and project manager in consulting firms must be held by Saudi nationals.

Since 1 January 2024 most foreign companies without a licensed regional headquarters in the Kingdom cannot win government contracts; a headquarters must hire at least 15 staff within a year, 3 of them C-level, and is exempt from Saudisation for 10 years.

The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel within 10 km of the Yemen border and all but essential travel from 10 to 80 km of it, now including Abha and Khamis Mushait; since 13 July 2026 the Houthis have launched missiles and drones at Saudi cities, Riyadh among them.
The Saudi Ports Authority and DP World are expanding the container terminal at Jeddah Islamic Port, a SAR 3 billion investment raising capacity from 1.8 million to four million TEU.

The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) ranks Riyadh 46th of 117 financial centres (61st in the March 2026 edition), fourth in the Middle East and Africa after Dubai (9th), Abu Dhabi (13th) and Casablanca (38th); Doha is 52nd and Kuwait City 60th, and Jeddah is not listed.
Startup Genome ranks Riyadh third among the Middle East and North Africa’s start-up ecosystems in 2026, after Tel Aviv and Dubai, and puts Abu Dhabi fourth.

The investment minister said on 8 November 2023 that Saudi Arabia had issued 180 regional-headquarters licences, against a target of 160 for the year, and the state news agency later headlined that 450 foreign investors had been licensed; a foreign company that wants government contracts must base its regional headquarters in Riyadh.

As of the second quarter of 2025 Saudi Arabia’s unemployment rate was 2.8% overall and 6.8% for Saudis, 52.8% of employed Saudis worked in the private sector, and 35.8% of Saudis had tertiary education against 24.4% of expatriates.

In the second quarter of 2026 the Riyadh region’s three largest employing activities were construction (1,403,894 employees), administrative and support services (937,517) and wholesale and retail trade (678,141); its registered employees numbered 7,672,179 and the Saudi unemployment rate was 4.2%.

The Eastern Region had 5,125,254 residents in the 2022 census; in the second quarter of 2026 its largest employing activities were construction (928,796 employees), manufacturing (323,110) and wholesale and retail trade (260,954), and the Saudi unemployment rate was 5.3%.
Fortune’s 2026 Global 500 ranks Saudi Aramco fifth in the world, headquartered in Dhahran, with revenue of $445.5 billion and 76,664 employees; Aramco itself reports a workforce of more than 76,000.

Aramco’s page for international applicants asks for a minimum of five to 10 years of applicable experience, in engineering, geosciences, drilling, R&D, finance, law and administration, and names no graduate programme for non-Saudis.

SABIC’s student and fresh-graduate programmes in the Middle East and Africa say they "attract and nurture young Saudi talents", and its Basic Operation Training states "The applicant has to be Saudi".

PwC Middle East’s postings for Riyadh and other Saudi offices require candidates to be eligible to work without PwC sponsorship, while for Qatar and the UAE sponsorship "may" be available; BCG Saudi advertises Visiting Associate roles in Riyadh for students graduating between November 2026 and September 2027 without stating nationality rules.

The 2022 census puts the population of Riyadh city at about 6.9 million, Jeddah at about 3.7 million, Mecca at about 2.4 million, Medina at about 1.4 million and Dammam at about 1.4 million; Riyadh, Makkah and the Eastern Province hold about 67.5% of the Kingdom’s 32,175,224 residents.

Saudi employment documents must be issued in Arabic, and standard Qiwa contracts are Arabic or Arabic and English side by side with the Arabic prevailing; Riyad Bank's 2026 graduate programme asks for advanced English; no source measured the English or Arabic level employers require of graduates.

Graduate recruiting in Saudi Arabia runs on university fairs and rolling postings rather than one national season: King Abdulaziz University held its 13th Career Forum in Jeddah on 6-8 April 2026, KFUPM its fair in Dhahran on 28-30 April 2026 with more than 70 organisations, and PwC Middle East's Riyadh graduate postings for 2026 appeared on 17 November 2025 and 8 July 2026; for an expatriate, the work visa takes 8 to 14 weeks in practice.

The Saudi unemployment rate was 6.4% in the first quarter of 2026 and 6.5% in the second (3.1% and 3.0% overall), with 13.8% for Saudi men and 20.4% for Saudi women aged 15 to 24 in the first quarter; only 42% of employed Saudis with tertiary education worked in the private sector in 2025; no graduate-specific unemployment figure and none for expatriate graduates was found.

Hays's Salary Guide 2026 for Saudi Arabia has 74% of firms planning to grow headcount in 2026 and 62% having grown in 2025, with recruitment activity in Riyadh (69%), Jeddah (43%) and the Eastern Province (37%), concentrated in tech, construction, property, finance and banking.

Jisr's 2025-2026 hiring report found Saudis were 41% of new hires, Riyadh took more than half of all new hires, and close to 60% of HR leaders expected expatriate numbers to shrink further, with foreign hiring focused on highly specialised roles.

Saudi graduate programmes are built for Saudi nationals: PIF’s, SABIC’s and Aramco’s graduate intakes are for Saudis, and Aramco hires internationals only with five to ten years of experience. Saudisation quotas reach into marketing, sales, engineering and consulting.

In the hiring report of the HR-software firm Jisr, Saudis were 41% of new hires and close to 60% of HR leaders expected expatriate numbers to shrink further, with foreign hiring focused on highly specialised roles. An expatriate graduate therefore competes mainly for specialised and transfer roles, and most of the graduate schemes we could read are for Saudi nationals or ask for an existing work right.
Referrals and personal introductions

The US-Saudi Business Council’s review of its members’ comments (October 2019) calls referrals from current staff the top hiring method and a first source for entry-level professional posts, ahead of online listings (LinkedIn, Bayt, Naukrigulf, the government’s Taqat portal) and agencies, whose results varied with local knowledge. It is an informal review by one business council, not a survey.

A 2017 Durham doctoral thesis, based on interviews with 30 Saudi employees and managers at two telecom companies, finds wasta (informal influence, often through an intermediary) increasingly used in recruitment, promotion and training. It is a small study of Saudi staff and does not show how it works for a foreign graduate at a multinational.
Direct application or recruiter, with the employer as sponsor

Hays’s Salary Guide 2026 for Saudi Arabia (reported by EnterpriseAM, May 2026) has 74% of firms planning to grow headcount in 2026 and 62% having grown in 2025, with recruitment activity in Riyadh (69%), Jeddah (43%) and the Eastern Province (37%); the growth is in tech, construction, property, finance and banking.

MHRSD’s rules on private-sector job advertising and interviews (reported in September 2025) require vacancies to follow the national occupation classification and appear on approved platforms or the employer’s own site, give candidates at least three working days’ notice of an interview and require the outcome within 30 days. After an offer, the library puts the real time to a work visa at 8 to 14 weeks.
Transfer within an international firm
Foreigners usually reach Riyadh as experienced staff or through a transfer from another office; some Big Four postings require the candidate to hold a work right already.

Aramco’s page for international applicants asks for a minimum of five to 10 years of applicable experience, and Aramco’s Saudi page, not this one, is where its student programmes and graduate jobs are listed.
Graduate schemes (for Saudi nationals)

The graduate schemes we could read are for Saudi nationals: PIF’s Graduate Development Program (1,033 graduates over nine cohorts), SABIC’s student and fresh-graduate programmes (“young Saudi talents”), KPMG’s Hamaat programme (nearly 300 young Saudis in its first cohort in 2024, as part of the firm’s nationalisation drive) and PwC’s 2019 intake (all 104 who joined in Saudi Arabia were Saudi citizens, about 35% of them women).

Riyad Bank’s 2026 Fursan Al Riyad programme is a six-month rotation for graduates with 0 to 1 years of experience and advanced English; the listing states no nationality rule and has expired. PwC Middle East’s Riyadh graduate postings for 2026 (Consulting on 17 November 2025, Assurance on 8 July 2026) now show as filled, and the library records that PwC’s Saudi postings ask for a work right without PwC sponsorship.
Campus recruiting at Saudi universities

KFUPM’s Career Fair in Dhahran (28–30 April 2026) had more than 70 organisations and over 11,000 visitors, with Aramco as platinum sponsor and Riyad Bank as gold sponsor; King Abdulaziz University’s 13th Career Forum was held at the Jeddah Superdome on 6–8 April 2026. KFUPM says its fair is for its students and graduates and external attendees; KAU’s page does not say who may attend.

A student on a Saudi student Iqama may not take private-sector work off campus; the library describes a route for graduates: a company on Qiwa with Nitaqat capacity can take over the sponsorship before the student Iqama ends, otherwise the graduate must leave and restart as a work-visa applicant from abroad.
Research internships (KAUST) and the lack of an internship visa

KAUST’s Visiting Student Research Program takes STEM undergraduates (third year or above) and master’s students with a GPA of at least 3.5 out of 4 for 2 to 6 months at USD 1,000 a month, with tuition, a private room and return airfare; it is open all year, and those finishing their degree within a year of the start date qualify. It is research, not an employer internship that converts to an offer.

The library finds no stand-alone internship visa: a company would have to sponsor a Qiwa temporary work visa (SAR 1,000, 90 days, extendable to 180) for a foreign graduate, and Middle East Briefing reports these had not been issued since 28 April 2025, with no resumption date announced. Interning on a tourist eVisa is prohibited.

There is no national season: the fairs read fall in April (KAU on 6–8 April 2026 in Jeddah, KFUPM on 28–30 April 2026 in Dhahran), and postings appear at different times of the year (PwC Middle East’s Riyadh graduate programme for 2026 was posted on 17 November 2025 for Consulting and on 8 July 2026 for Assurance; Riyad Bank’s programme on 7 April 2026).

Quota dates shape what employers can hire: marketing and sales 60% from 19 April 2026, engineering 30% from 30 June 2026, accounting 50% from 27 October 2026 and project management 70% from 14 February 2027.

For an expatriate the lead time is the work visa: the library gives 4 to 6 weeks officially and 8 to 14 weeks in practice, and the qualification check (QVP) adds about 15 days, so an offer has to come three months or more before the start date.
Fairs are run by universities for their own students: KFUPM’s (with Aramco as platinum sponsor) and King Abdulaziz University’s are the two with 2026 dates we could open, and both are in the Kingdom.

We found no ranking of foreign schools by Saudi employers; what counts at the visa stage is that the degree can be verified (QVP accreditation, an apostille and a sworn Arabic translation). This is our reading of the employer side.
KFUPM Career Fair, Dhahran: 28–30 April 2026, more than 70 organisations, over 11,000 visitors and more than 300 career-coaching sessions; Aramco was platinum sponsor.
King Abdulaziz University, 13th Career Forum: 6–8 April 2026 at the Jeddah Superdome, with employers and job seekers under one roof.

Accounting is being localised in five phases from 27 October 2025: 40% of 44 accounting roles in firms with five or more people in those roles (Saudis counted at a minimum of SAR 6,000 with a bachelor’s degree), rising to 50% from 27 October 2026 and to 70% at the end. The library adds that accountants need SOCPA accreditation before the licence on Qiwa.

Ten marketing occupations and nine sales occupations carry a 60% Saudi quota from 19 April 2026 for establishments with three or more workers in them, so a foreign marketing or sales graduate competes against a quota.

Hays’s guide puts technical and digital skills (49%) and business and analytical skills (46%) at the top of what employers want in 2026; procurement roles carry a 70% Saudi quota and project management 70% from 14 February 2027.

Riyad Bank’s Fursan Al Riyad graduate programme (six months, Riyadh) asks for a bachelor’s degree, 0 to 1 years of experience and advanced English and states no nationality rule; PIF’s programme is for Saudis only.

Only 42% of employed Saudis with tertiary education worked in the private sector in 2025, up from 19% in 2015, so state and state-linked bodies still employ most Saudi graduates; the national employment platform Jadarat, launched in August 2024, is aimed primarily at Saudi citizens.
Consulting firms must keep 40% of quota roles Saudi, and Riyadh offices are staffed with Saudi graduates first.

Aramco, STC and government-linked bodies such as the data and AI authority SDAIA are steady recruiters of Saudi graduates in software, data and cybersecurity, with structured mentoring; the giga-projects prefer people who already have a specialism.
We did not establish the Saudi quota for IT roles: sources read give conflicting percentages and none is an official text.
STC’s academy was set up to train Saudi graduates in cybersecurity and data analysis.
University fairs cluster in April (KAU, KFUPM) and programme postings come at different times of year (PwC in November and July, Riyad Bank in April); the pages read show no single national season.

The graduate programme page read asks for a bachelor’s degree and 0 to 1 years of experience, and Aramco asks internationals for years of experience rather than a degree level; neither mentions a master’s as an advantage. This is our reading.

Foreign degrees are verified, not just accepted: work-visa applicants from many countries must obtain Qualification Verification Program (QVP) accreditation online (USD 93, about 15 more days; one law firm lists 19 countries, unofficially, and the portal decides which applies), and the library requires an apostille, which Saudi Arabia has accepted since 7 December 2022, plus a sworn Arabic translation. Engineers need Saudi Council of Engineers registration (5 years of experience for foreigners) and accountants SOCPA accreditation.

The fairs read are run by individual universities for their own students and the biggest sponsors are state-linked (Aramco, Riyad Bank); we found no ranking of schools by employers. This is our reading.

We found no apprenticeship or dual-study route into graduate jobs for foreigners; the library finds no stand-alone internship visa and describes co-op training only for students enrolled in Saudi universities. This is our reading.

Only 42% of employed Saudis with tertiary education worked in the private sector in 2025 (19% in 2015), and the largest graduate schemes (PIF, Aramco, SABIC) are state-linked and for Saudis; for a foreign graduate the public sector is largely closed.

Every foreign hire is employer-sponsored and the employer pays the visa quota (SAR 2,000) and the expatriate levy (SAR 9,600 a year); but foreign hiring is focused on highly specialised roles and employers need Nitaqat room (Medium Green or above) to sponsor at all. See Visas for the rules.

A Saudi CV guide (April 2023) calls a neat, conservative professional photo common practice, while noting some experts caution against photos. MHRSD’s interview rules bar discrimination by gender, age or marital status.
The same guide says to keep the CV to two to three pages depending on experience, starting with contact details and a phone number with the international code.
The programme page read (Riyad Bank) lists no cover-letter requirement, and the CV guide read does not mention one. This is our reading.
None of the programme and posting pages read asks for references with the application; the contract stage brings the checks. This is our reading.
Degrees and certificates must be apostilled with a sworn Arabic translation, and the QVP accreditation is needed before the work visa is stamped and the Iqama issued.

We found no page saying Saudi employers ask for a salary expectation with the first application; the salary is set in the Qiwa contract, and no entry pay for expatriate graduates was found. This is our reading for the application stage.

Checks run through the state for a foreign hire: the QVP qualification check, a pre-departure medical on the official form, an apostilled criminal-record certificate and a second medical in the Kingdom (Efada) before the Iqama.

Referrals from staff are the top hiring method in the US-Saudi Business Council’s 2019 review, and a 2017 study of two telecom companies finds wasta used in recruitment; recruiters and agencies are used with mixed results.
A foreign fresh graduate rarely fits a programme; every role needs an employer-sponsored permit.

MHRSD’s rules allow interviews in person, remote or by phone, and the work visa takes 8 to 14 weeks in practice after the contract is accepted on Qiwa, so a search can start from abroad but work cannot start on a tourist eVisa.

English in multinationals and in Riyad Bank’s graduate programme (advanced English), but employment documents must be in Arabic, with an English copy common and the Arabic text prevailing; Arabic is increasingly expected as roles are localised.

MHRSD’s rules on private-sector interviews (reported September 2025) require the employer to tell the candidate the format (in person, remote or phone), the date and the time at least three working days ahead; a panel of at least two Saudi members including an HR specialist; and a result within 30 days of the interview, with reasons given to unsuccessful candidates. Interviews may not discriminate on grounds such as gender, age or marital status.

After an accepted offer the contract is issued on Qiwa and the work visa follows; the library gives 4 to 6 weeks officially and 8 to 14 weeks in practice, and the QVP qualification check adds about 15 days.

We could not open the selection steps of any graduate programme (PwC’s and KPMG’s Saudi postings show only “filled” and Aramco’s hiring-process page returned an error), so the number of rounds, online tests, assessment-centre practice, interview language and dress norms are not established here.

Employers must issue contracts on the Qiwa portal; expatriates can only be on fixed-term contracts (one guide adds a maximum of four years), and a contract is normally in Arabic, often with an English copy, the Arabic text prevailing if the two differ.

Probation can last up to 180 days (raised from 90 by the amendments in force since 19 February 2025), must be written into the contract, and either side may end the contract during it without notice or compensation. Employers must provide housing and transport, or equivalent compensation.

On indefinite-term contracts notice is 30 days for the employee and 60 days for the employer, and a resignation is deemed accepted if the employer does not reply within 30 days. The library gives the end-of-service award as half a month’s pay per year for the first five years and a full month after, and on resignation nothing under two years, one-third from two to five years and two-thirds from five to ten.
We did not establish whether graduates negotiate, how long employers give to decide, or entry pay; no employer-stated entry pay for expatriate graduates was found.

Under Nitaqat, employers are rated Platinum, Green (low, medium or high) or Red, and only Medium Green and above can apply for new visas, renew work permits or transfer sponsorship. A new three-year phase launched in 2026 aims at more than 340,000 additional private-sector jobs for Saudis, and profession-specific requirements apply even when a company meets its overall ratio.

Quotas by role: consulting 40% of quota roles (since 25 March 2024); marketing and sales 60% (from 19 April 2026); engineering 30% (from 30 June 2026, firms with five or more engineers, and only Saudi Council of Engineers-registered engineers count); accounting 40% rising to 70% in five phases; project management 70% from 14 February 2027; administrative support 100% from 4 October 2026.

Regional headquarters licensed under the 2024 rule must hire at least 15 staff, three at C-level, and are exempt from Saudisation for 10 years. The library says foreign graduates cannot get the engineer title (the Saudi Council of Engineers asks foreigners for 5 years of certified experience), and a downgrade to technician costs the right to a family visa.

The employer bears the visa quota (SAR 2,000), the expatriate levy (SAR 9,600 a year, or SAR 8,400 for compliant employers), the Iqama fee (SAR 650 a year), health insurance and return travel; the worker pays only the dependants’ levy.

Public platforms: Jadarat, the unified national employment platform launched in August 2024 (it brought together Taqat and Jadarah), is aimed primarily at Saudi citizens; for expatriates the contract runs through Qiwa (qiwa.sa) once an employer has hired you, and the qualification check through the QVP portal (qvp.qiwa.sa).

Boards named by employers in the US-Saudi Business Council’s 2019 review: LinkedIn, Bayt, Naukrigulf and Taqat.sa (now succeeded by Jadarat). Hays’s Salary Guide 2026 is a recent read of where recruiters see demand.

Employer pages: Aramco (careers for international applicants and for Saudi applicants), PwC Middle East’s graduate postings, Riyad Bank’s careers site (careers.riyadbank.com.sa) and SABIC’s student and fresh-graduate programmes; most are for Saudis (see Common mistakes).

University services and fairs: the KFUPM Career Fair (April), King Abdulaziz University’s Career Forum (April) and KAUST’s Visiting Student Research Program (admissions.kaust.edu.sa/study/internships) for STEM students.

Applying to the Saudi-only schemes (PIF, SABIC, KPMG Hamaat) as a foreign graduate, or assuming a PwC or Aramco page is open to you: Aramco’s international page asks for five to ten years, and PwC’s Saudi postings ask for a work right without PwC sponsorship.
Working, doing a trial day or interning on a tourist eVisa: the library cites arrest, up to 6 months in prison, a fine of up to SAR 50,000 and deportation with a ban on return.
Leaving the country after entering on the work visa but before the Iqama is issued: the library says the visa lapses at the border and the whole procedure restarts abroad.
Starting the degree check late: QVP accreditation (USD 93) adds about 15 days and must clear before the visa is stamped, and the apostille and sworn translation come before it.

Expecting an engineer’s title as a new graduate (the Saudi Council of Engineers asks foreigners for 5 years) or planning to move to a rival in the first 12 months: the library says a worker cannot change employer before 12 months of service, except for serious breaches by the employer.
Riyad Bank’s 2026 graduate programme lists advanced English among its requirements and states no Arabic level; the pages read give no test or certificate.

Employment documents must be in Arabic and standard Qiwa contracts are Arabic or Arabic-English side by side, with the Arabic prevailing; advertised posts follow the national occupation classification. No source measured the English or Arabic level employers ask of graduates.

Public and state-linked employers recruit Saudi nationals mainly through the national platform Jadarat, and employment documents must be in Arabic; we found no page stating an Arabic level. This is our reading for the language.

Technical and digital skills are the most wanted capability in Hays’s 2026 guide (49% of employers), but we found no page testing English or Arabic for graduates in software, data or cybersecurity. This is our reading.

The Saudi unemployment rate was 6.4% in the first quarter of 2026 (Saudi men 4.9%, Saudi women 9%) and 6.5% in the second, against 3.1% and 3.0% for the whole labour force; for Saudis aged 15 to 24 it was 13.8% for men and 20.4% for women in the first quarter. These are all-education figures: we found no graduate-specific unemployment, return-offer or time-to-first-job figure, and none for expatriate graduates.

Saudis made up 41% of new hires in Jisr’s 2025–2026 report, and Riyadh took more than half of all new hires; the World Bank counts 35.8% of Saudis with tertiary education in 2025 against 24.4% of expatriates.

Apply through the Study in Saudi portal: a long-term educational visa for a full degree, with a student iqama sponsored by the university; a short-term one for language courses and exchanges up to a year.
Students may not work off campus at all; only paid research or teaching assistant roles at the university.

There is no internship visa. KAUST’s Visiting Student Research Program takes STEM students for 3 to 6 months with a stipend, housing and the visa paid; a company hosting a graduate must sponsor a temporary work visa. Internships on a tourist or business visa lead to expulsion.

EU and UK citizens get a one-year multiple-entry eVisa or a visa on arrival, up to 90 days a visit, with no work or internships.
eVisa, insurance included

Check and accept your contract on Qiwa, do the medical screening (Tasheer from Italy, Wafid elsewhere), apostille your degrees and a criminal record no older than 3 to 6 months, and collect the work visa sticker at a Tasheer centre.

Within the first 30 days, register your National Address with Saudi Post (SPL). Leases are signed digitally on the government platform Ejar, which needs your residence permit (iqama) and Nafath login.
At the border you get a 10-digit border number; within 90 days of entry your employer must pay the expat levy (SAR 9,600) and the iqama fee (SAR 650) and issue your iqama on Muqeem.
On a single-entry work visa, do not leave before the iqama is issued: the visa lapses at the border and the whole process starts again from abroad.
Once you have the iqama, move your SIM from the border number to it, activate Absher at a self-service kiosk, and set up Nafath, the face-recognition login for government services and banks.
Within 30 days, have the local medical check, uploaded to the Efada system (SAR 150 to 300); your employer activates your health insurance with the Council of Health Insurance.
A payroll account at a Saudi bank (SNB, Al Rajhi, Riyad Bank, SAB) needs an active iqama, the National Address and Nafath: with the border number alone you cannot open one.
To travel abroad with an iqama you need an active exit and re-entry visa on Absher; leaving without one, or coming back late, cancels the iqama and brings a 3-year ban on returning to work.
Before the iqama is issued you cannot leave: the single-entry work visa lapses at the border. Afterwards every trip needs an exit and re-entry visa on Absher.
A positive test for HIV, hepatitis B or C, syphilis or TB scarring in the local medical means deportation and a ban across the Gulf.
Resign before two years and you get no end-of-service award.
Italians who do not register with AIRE within 90 days remain tax residents in Italy, which then taxes the Saudi salary.
Foreigners pay no Saudi pension contributions, and there is no pension agreement with Italy: those years are a gap.
Most Saudi fees were not re-checked against official tables in the latest review.
Temporary bank accounts on a border number exist on paper; in practice new hires wait 30 to 45 days for a salary account.
Compound housing in Riyadh is saturated by companies moving regional headquarters there.

Corporate graduate programmes recruit in English but many roles need Swedish, youth unemployment is high at 24.3%, and since June 2026 non-EU students may work only 15 hours a week in term.
